div.head: CHAT and GOSSIP.
div.p: CHAT and GOSSIP.
By MARjORIE.

King Ferdinand and Queen Marie of Roumania., The new King of Roumania is a prince of the House of Hohenzollern, but so far he has shown little sympathy with his relatives of that kind. His Consort has been described as beautiful, charming and accomplished. She is rather tall and fair, is a fine horsewoman and drives a team of horses with great skill. She is also fond of motoring, and drives her car as well as she manages her steeds. Queen Marie belongs to the Orthodox Greek Church, as do also her son and daughters,,although King Ferdinand is a Roman Catholic, in common with the other princes of his branch of the Hohenzollerns. Fireless Cookers. _ _ _

Economy is the order of the day, and a fire- ' less cooker should find a place in every house- ho: this winter, for it saves gas and coal to a surp;.sing extent. Canadians and Americans use these cookers extensively, and those at- tached to the German armies are said to have saved the lives of many soldiers during in- clement weather. Miss Clementina Black has started an industry for the making of the simplest form of fireless cooker, viz., the hay- box, which is made entirely by women thrown out of employment by the war. The effort therefore deserves support. The boxes cost only a few shillings, are well made, and ought to prove a blessing to the bachelor woman.

British Made Fabric Gloves.. The making of fabric gloves, and the material of which they are composed, has hitherto been largely in the hands of the Germans and Aus- trians. Labour, <!specially that of women, is cheaper on the Continent than it is here, and hence it has been difficult for British manufac- turers to compete for the trade. They are, how- ever, now experimenting, and hope shortly to

Cheese Savoury. One and a half ounces cheese, three ounces bread crumbs; grate the cheese, or chop into small pieces; mix with bread crumbs, a little seasoning, and sufficient milk to make into a thick batter; bake twenty or thirty minutes a buttered dish.

Bottling Fruit (no sugar). Thoroughly warm bottles in oven, then fill with quite sound ripe fruit; return bottles to oven till fruit begins to discolour (about 15 minute,,, fn t. moderate oven), then fill bottles with ling water, leaving room for two-inch layer oi 'nelted mutton fat, which, when cold, seals up hPi fruit.

Unripesned Outdoor Tomatoes.—Slice six pounds of green tomatoes into an earthenware vessel in layers, sprinkle each layer with salt, let it remain twelve hot.rs, then drain off salt and watsr. Put .the toma- toes in a saucepan ready for boiling, add enough vinegar to cover well, add also 41b.. to lib. sliced onions, ioz. bruised ginger, tor. cloves, Oz. peppercorns, ioz. mustard seed. NB.—This is quite the nicest pickle we know. Pickled Herring.

Professor Hopkins says: "The effect of pick- ling upon the digestibility of the herring seems to be somewhat greater than that of smoking, but the difference is not large and probably not of practical importance. Changes occur in the flesh of the fish after pickling, but if it is eaten within a period of, say, six months, there is every reason to believe that it remains whole- some and without any appreciable loss in its nutritive value." MY DEAR, CHILDRFN,-
We shall soon be having Christmas with and oh ! what a happy time we shall spend. If there is snow on the ground you can make a snow man and then throw at him with snow- balls.
Before I write my next letter you will have celebrated Guy Fawkes' Day. Will you have many fireworks?
I hope none of you are as unfortunate as
I was when a little boy. On one occasion I slipped when near a big fire and burned my hand very badly, but it soon got better. I did not get too near a fire after that. Your loving UNCLE NED.

div.head: WOMAN'S WORLD.
div.p: WOMAN'S WORLD.

more extensively put British made fabric gloves on the market. Meanwhile patriotic women will do well to buy the fine Milanese, Lisle, or the Nenvel white washable leather gloves, for both are entirely British in make. The former are summer, rather than winter, gloves, but many people wear them throughout the year. They are not cheap, but they are durable; they are also well-shaped, well-cut, and very well- made. The same may be said of the Neuvel washable white leather gloves, for the making of which the skins of animals, indigenous to this country, and prepared by a new process, are used. This process permits the glove to be I washed again and again, and yet to retain its good shape, colour, and softness of texture. It is finding favour with men for evening dress.

Features of This Winter's Modes. Adversity has its uses, and even this terrible war which is costing so much in precious lives and treasure, may be made to serve a useful purpose, if the lessons it teaches are only learnt as they ought to be. Among the minor advan- tages already gained is the quieter and better taste in dress everywhere evidenced since the beginning of August last, that fateful month which brought the grave issues of life and death home to every woman in this country. It is to be hoped that the grotesque in fashions has been eliminated, that the freak is doomed, and that common-sense and restraint will reign in the future, as at present. Although the drastic changes in modes contemplated by designers some months ago have not, in consequence of the war, beeii carried out, this winter's styles offer a complete contrast to those of last year. The distinctive features of fur coats, for in- stance, are belted waists, a broad fur band at the hem, and close fur collar at the throat. Pleated and Gathered Furs.

• —.._.__ The shapes also are utterly different, and the fulness below the waist necessitates tl3e employ- ment of short-haired or closely-clipped peltry. How to drape and• to pleat fur with success would have puzzled the furriers of forty years ago; those of to-day have accomplished this feat. Sable, ermine, and the less expensive pelts can now be draped as easily, and as grace- fully as velvet or satin. Fur is moreover gored

than half the price of a barrel, and that a bar- rel will contain some 800 to 850 herrings, it will be realised that pickled herring provide a very valuable form of food at a very low price with the advantage that the food is in a state of pre- servation in which it can be stored for consider- able periods. The wholesale price of one pickled herring would be about one half-penny. The retail price would necessarily be higher, but it is obvious that if the statement that "two salt herrings contain as much protein as need enter into the daily diet of the average working man" can be relied upon, that amount of daily protein can be provided at a sum not largely in excess of one penny. To Wash Chiffon Veils. _ .

A good method of washing a chiffon veil is to put it in a glass fruit jar, half full of warm soap suds, let it stand a few minutes, fasten on the cover securely, and shake the bottle vigor- ously. Then drain off the water and replace with clean. It is as well to rinse twice, shak- ing the bottle each time. Then hang the veil without wringing it, on a line in the open air, and when dry it should be as soft and fluffy its when new, and none the worse for the water. bath. Veils that are soaked with rain, should be stretched out and hung over a rail to dry.

and pleated, and even gathered as a matter of course. The sleeves of fur coats are cut on magyar and kimono lines. These, however,,de- mand great skill in their manipulation, to be really successful. A heavy military braid is fre- quently used for the buttons of a fur coat, old the sash-like belt; or one made from the many fur substitutes, which deserve to be popular, so wonderfully do they imitate the natural skins. The coats of these fabrics now shown in the best shops are by no means expensive when the cut and finish are taken into consideration, and this winter everyone will be compelled to con- eider the cost of new clothes.

The Vogue for Black. There is not much colour to be seen in the evening dress department this season. Before war broke out—or, to be more accurate, last spring—designers settled among themselves that there should be the loveliest of the old shades of blue and rose for evening wear, but the out- break of hostilities placed the black toilette in the foreground. It is, however, considerably lightened by much jetted lace, and by the clever introduction of white on the corsage. A large flower of a deep rich hue also affords relief when worn on the corsage of a black or dark gown. There is much veiling of white with black filmy lace, and vice versa. The wearer of a coloured corsage with a black tulle skirt, so popular in the 'seventies—with a difference, of course—was to have been revived, had not cir- cumstances changed fashion's decrees.

New Umbrellas. A wedding present that meets with general approval from recipients is a highly ornamental umbrella handle, quite ready to put on. En tout cas and umbrellas, made of silk, match in colour the dresses with which they are worn, and have very ornate sticks and handles, the latter being frequently studded with gems of the same tint. A crimson silk umbrella, for instance, has a handle adorned with garnets. The sticks are coloured and Often very long. Crystal, carved ivory, tortoiseshell and wrought gold , furnish the suniptuous handles of umbrellas de luxe, prepared before the _out- break of war, but it is doubtful if these expen- sive articles will find purchasers this winter.

Jenkins: "Well, the fact is, old chap, that it's not through ill will or bad feeling, or any- thing like that, you know; only you and Mrs. Possmore have borrowed so many things from me that when I see your place it makes me feel quite homesick."

IReturnee. Wedding Present. After a fortnight a wedding present of a small I Irish terrier, about eleven weeks old, has been iteturned by a young couple living at Streatham to, the donor (the wife's mother) on account of it destructive habits. During this time, the "Moil" says, the puppy has scattered a tea breaking. several pieces; broken a china teapot; been found curled up in the tea-cosy surrouno\ed by tea leaves; dug a hole in the lawn; eat\en parts of a straw work-basket; up- rooted a thed of lilies; killed a sparrow; hidden the wife's stockings in his kennel; and eaten the tassels off the table-cover. His jast exploit was a mad fight with a dog four times his own size.

AN OLD ,ACT. An Act of Parliament wihich was passed in the reign of George 111., an is still in force, exempts members of the Yeomanry from the ballot for the Militia, allowO them to ride through a toll-bar WbPD in uniform without paying, and also relieves them fi-om the tax on powder for the hair Such pirivileges were highly valued in 1804, when the Act was passed; but as yeomen are not now liable for the Militia ballot, as toll bars have been abolisheO, and as hair powder is no longer izt request, ,these favours have ceased to have any practical varute.

div.head: CLEVER SPIES.
div.p: CLEVER SPIES.

Just before the Russo-Japanese war a hawker of cakes was caught wandering about:a Russian fort. A sentry had frequently allowed him to pass through the gates, thinking the man was merely intent on selling his cakes to the soldiers in the garrison. The hawker wandered out of the recognised paths, and walking boldly into the fort itself, got close to the guns. He was arrested, and thoroughly searched, but nothing could be found to make the Russians' think he was a spy. He was therefore allowed to go. As a matter of fact he was a spy and the plans he had stolen were hidden in one of the cakes in his basket. Another excellent hiding place for plans and Maps was discovered by chance by the Russians during the war. A coolie was arrested in the Russian lines, and was ordered to receive 50 strokes with the bamboo which he carried with him. While the punishment was being in- flicted the bamboo split open and the officer present was astounded to see little packets of I rice paper fall to the ground. He picked them up and found that they contained details of the number of guns and men, an also a description of the defence works erected by the Russians. This "coolie" turned out to be no other than c.o. colonel in the Japanese Army. He was shot immediately.

GOLD IN SEA WATER. Gold can be found in sea water, but the amount is so small that it is doubtful if it would pay for the cost of extraction. The gold is, of course, in solution, and is estimated to average from half a grain to one grain per ton of sea water. The value of that would be about two- pence.-' It would need a lot of water and ex- pense to extract sufficient gold t'o make m sover- eign.

div.head: HINTS ON HEALTH. Useful Information in Popular Language.
div.p: HINTS ON HEALTH. Useful Information in Popular Language.

For a disinfectant for a sink, pour down a gallon of boiling water mixed with two table- spoonfuls of soda and a teaspoonful of ammonia. This Will dissolve all greasy matter in both sink and pipe. Children's Meal Hours.

------- Children should be taught to be regular at their meals, and to take nothing between them. This rule applies to infants as well as to older children. The practice of feeding the little one every time it cries is- a dangerous one to its weak digestive organs. An infant's stomach, though it needs food at more frequent intervals, two to four hours, according to its age, requires the same regularity which is essential to the maintenance of healthy dige,stion in older per- sons. Diet. -

_ Our diet is apt to be one-sided, says a writOr in the "Family Doctor." It often does not con- tain the different nutritive ingredients in the proper proportions. We consume relatively too much of the fuel ingredients of .food—those which are burnt in the body and yield heat and muscular power. Such are the fats of meat and butter, the starch which makes up the larger part of the nutritive material of flour, potatoes, and sugar, of which such enormous quantities are eaten. Conversely, we have relatively too little of the protein or flesh-forming substances, iikthc, kart of natant and fish, and tha glutan of wheat, which make muscle and sinew, and which are the basis of blood, bone, and brain.

To Destroy the Bed-bug. In an interesting series on "Insects and War" In the "British Medical Journal," Mr. A. E. Shipley writes about the bed-bug. In all fumi- gating experiments every crack and cranny of a house should be shut, windows closed, keyholes blocked, and so on. A good method of fumiga- tion is that of burning sulphur. Four ounces of brimstone are placed in a saucer, which in its turn is placed in a larger vessel. This protects the floor of the room from a possible overflow of ,the burning material. After all apertures have been successfully plugged, four or five hours of the sulphurous fumes are said to be sufficient to kill the bugs, but to ensure success a longer time is needed. Another more localised method of destroying these pests is the liberal applica- tion of benzine, kerosene, or any other petroleum oil. These must be introduced into all crevices or cracks with small brushes or feathers, or in- jected with syringes. In the same way oil of turpentine or corrosive sublimate has proved effective. Boiling water is also effective when it can be used, and recently in the poorer quarters of London the "flares" which painters use in burning off paint have proved of great use in ridding matchboarding, or wainscoating, or wood or hoarding, of bugs. Passed quickly along, the flame does not burn the wood, but it produces a. temperature which is fatal to the bug and to its young and to its eggs.

div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 31, 1914. FARM AND GARDEN.
DANGER OF FEEDING NEW HAY.

New hay, says "Farm and Home," will cause some horses to scour badly„ so badly that the source of supply has to be changed and treat- ment adopted to stop the purging. It is liable to produce other evidence of digestive derange- ment, and certainly has riot the feeding value or conditioning effect of good old hay. Carters, coachmen, and grooms often attribute the lack of condition in the majority of horses at this season to the changing of the coat, and no doubt in the main correctly, but there is every reason to believe that this condition, or rather lack of it, is aggravated by the use of new foods, in many cases unwittingly. It is really no easy matter to distinguish new foods, whether oats or hay, from old, and very often it is the effect on the animal that first leads to the discovery of its being immature. It is easy enough if we see the hay in the stack, when its outside ap- pearance and thatch tells its tale pretty clearly, but to all but the expert it is very difficult to form a reliable opinion from a single truss. Well-saved samples may retain their perfume for two, or even three or four years,' but will have lost much of their feeding value. Very old toy becomes dry, tasteless, innutritious, and unwholesome.

div.head: BARLEY AS_A FATTENING FOOD.
div.p: BARLEY AS_A FATTENING FOOD.

_....__ _ Fifty years of sheep feeding trials cohducted on all the best feeding breeds of sheep and lambs in fairly large quantities particularly attest to the value of barley as a fattening food either in the form of grains or in its natural form. It is an eminently starchy food, yet the results are much beyond those of oats, which is supposed to be the best balanced natural food for live stock that we possess, short, perhaps, of grass. Most of the experiments, it is true, are concerned with barley mixed with other con- centrated food, but in the five recorded cases where it was used alone almost as good results were obtained, 1.951 b. increase per week, the others reaching up to 3.151 b., with an average of 2.31 b. per head, live weight. These high results do not seem to be accidental, for both malt and grain, show up well. Barley is known, too, to be an excellent pick-me-up fin run-down cart horses, by. those who have tried it steeped, and in the East barley is valued '.for nag horses in spite of the heating properties wilich are com- plained of in the cooler West.—" Agricultural Economist and Horticultural Review."

div.head: FARM PRODUCE FOR HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES.
div.p: FARM PRODUCE FOR HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES.

The Board of Agriculture and Fisheries are taking steps, in consultation with the War Office, with the object of facilitating the pur- chase by the military authorities of farm pro- duce, such as forage and vegetables, direct from the farmer. With this object in view the Board have appointed an Organising Committee. There will be set up for each county or, in certain cases, for groups of counties, a Farm Produce County Committee, consisting of eight tenant- farmers 'of recognised standing, who will be nominated jointly by the president of the Royal Agricultural Society of England, the chairman of the Farmers' Club, the chairman of the Central and Associated Chambers of Agri- culture, and the president of the National Farmers' Union. Sub-committees will be ap- pointed and weekly meetings will be held to discuss and settle the prices for the ensuing seyen days at which farmers and others in the county might be reasonably expected to dispose of their farm produce for the use of His Majesty's Forces. A County Committee will also invite farmers to submit samples and to quote prices for the various classes of proauce which the military authorities may desire to purchase in the district. A purchasing officer of the Army will attend, whenever possible, the meetings of the County Committee and of the sub-committees, and will intimate beforehand, as far as practicable, the classes and quantities of produce he desires to purchase. The County Committee will invite farmers to \attend the meetkngs in order that they may submit `their offers for the consideration of the purchasing officer. The War Office have undertaken to pur- chase, as far as practicable, through the County Committees, but necessarily reserve the 'right to refuse offers which the committee may obtain, in cases where the purchasing officer can make better arrangements elsewhere. The County, Committee have discretionary power to make 'arrangementg with any Agricultural Co-opera- tive Association or other body of organised farmers, for the purpose of assisting them in any but their advisory work.

div.head: IN THE GARDEN.
div.p: IN THE GARDEN.
ROOT PRUNING AND LIFTING.

Complaints are often heard that fruit trees go too much to wood and do not bear. The only remedy for this is root pruning in the case of established trees, and lifting in the case of Young trees. Now is a good time to carry this work out, as if planting is done while the leaves are still on the trees the formation of new fibres is the more quickly encouraged.

div.head: PLANTING FRUIT TREES.
div.p: PLANTING FRUIT TREES.

Though rather too early to think of planting fruit trees, it is well to make preparations for so doing by digging out the holes, renewing the soil if need be, and where necessary putting in some broken bricks, or such like, where the water collects or the soil is too wet to plant. The weather at the present time is favourable to such work, and it can be carried out more quickly than when deferred till later. By doing the work now the trees, if they have to be pur- chased from a nursery, can, if the weather is open, be planted immediately on their arrival, and the ground being fairly warm, they have a ?hence to get established before severe weather 18 Upon us, more especially if the precaution is taken when spreading out the roots tp mix with them a little good soil to encourage them. lii the case of standard trees it is also advisable to fix the stakes in position before planting, as by doing this all danker of injury to the roots is averted.

EARLY FLOWERING CHRYSANTHEMUMS. Now that the dull October days are with us, and there are but few flowering plants in the garden, with the exception of the Michaelmas daisies, it is pleasing to fall back on the .early flowering chrysanthemums in their many and varied colour shades, from the purest white to almost crimson. Not only do the colours of the flowers vary, but the forms, too, are many. In many gardens ere this the dahlias will have been cut down, but the early flowering chrysanthe- mums seem to brook no harm from early frosts. and the blooms continue to open freely, and if the weather keeps mild; with no heavy rains, a succession of bloom will be maintained for some weeks to come. In order to see these at their best let the plants grow naturally with no disbudding of the flowers. In this way shoots bearing five and six blooms may be had. An- other valuable trait in these early flowering chrysanthemums is that they last so well when cut, while they do as well in the town garden as in the country, the only exception being that the flowers of the country grown plants are brighter. In many gardens if the stools are given protection in the way of a little coal ashes they will live through the winter, but I have always found it best to lift the plants when flowering was over, and plunge them in a frame. In the following spring it is an easy matter when growth is on the move to divide them and grow them on in pots or boxes until the time comes round in April to again plant them out. —" Farm and Home."

div.head: OUR TACTFUL MLAMML
div.p: OUR TACTFUL MLAMML
Alderman Peacock Thanked for Year's Services..
PRAISE FROM ALL SIDES.

The last meeting of the Town Council for the current municipal year was held at the Town Hall on' Tuesday evening, when the members took the opportunity of expressing, in more than mere formal fashion, their thanks to the Mayor (Alderman Peter Peacock) for the tact- ful, manner in which he has presided over their deliberations for the past twelve months, and for the excellent service he has rendered the town daring a most trying period in its exist- ence.

The expressions of thanks that were uttered were linked with an expectation of further favours to come, in view of the fact, already announced in our columns, that the genial and populq Alderman has consented to take on the onerous duties of the Chief Magistracy, and all that it involves in the way of civic and social duties, for another twelve months.

div.head: "UNVARYING COURTESY AND IMPAR-
div.p: "UNVARYING COURTESY AND IMPAR-
TIALIT`i:I;

On the official records the Council's appre- ciation will be stated in the following form : That the best thanks of this Council be presented to Mr. Alderman Peter Peacock, J.P,, for the satisfactory manner in which he has discharged the responsible duties devolving upon him as Mayor and Chief _ Magistrate of the borough during the past year, and for the unvarying courtesy and impartiality displayed , by him when pre- siding over the deliberations of the Council, and in his _intercourse with its members."

The foregoing resolution was proposed by Alderman BOLTON, who said that the Manner in which the Mayor had discharged the duties of his high office had fulfilled the greatest expectations of all his friends and fellow- councillors. It had been really surprising to see how he had kept the unruly members of the Council in order and had succeeded in making them all a happy family. He was certainly to be congratulated upon his year of office, and they only hoped that his second year as Chief Magistrate would be equally suc- cessful. In Alderman Peacock as Mayor they had the right.man in the right place. (Hear, hear.)

div.head: "A GOOD BUSINESS MAYOR."
div.p: "A GOOD BUSINESS MAYOR."

-- Alderman TxxxioN, in seconding, said he was sure that all the members of the Council were more than satisfied, more than pleased; aye, more than delighted, with the manner in which Alderman, Peacock had carried out the duties of the Mayoralty.. When he voted for the worthy Alderman as Mayor twelve months ago he had no doubt that he would make a good business Mayor—a Mayor who would discharge the duties. appertaining to the office with credit to himself and advantage to the Council. His greatest expectations had been exceeded. Not only did .the resolution ought to record Alder- man Peacock's unvarying courtesy to the Coun- cil, but it should go further and speak of his unfailing courtesy in his intercourse with the inhabitants of the town at large. (Hear, hear.) He had known no party or sect. He had not known what it was to have time to himself. He had always been at the service of the people of the town, and if he had heard of any cases in which the sympathy and help of the community, or of individuals, were needed, it had not been too much trouble for him to investigate them personally. (Applause.) He had not only tried to be courteous and helpful to the members, but also to the inhabitants at large. The time he had given to the work of the borough was sur- prising; probably he had given more hciurs to the duties of the Mayoralty than had any pre- vious occupant of the chair.

"THE MOST INDEFATIGABLE MAYOR." The DEPUTY MAYOR (Councillor Joseph), in supporting the resolution, said Alderman Pea- cock had had a most arduous year of office, and ;,he had , proved - himself the most indefatigable Mayor that, Probabb% Warrington had ever had. He had tried hard to make his year of office useful and popular, and lie had succeeded. (Hear, hear.)

Alderman BENNETT added his tribute. Alder- man Peacock, he said, accepted office in a year of exceptional stress—a year that was unique in the history of the town and of the country. He had risen to the occasion and had upheld the best traditions of the high office. (Applause.) Alderman SMETHURST said that the amount of • time and work which the Mayor had put in had been astounding to the people of Warrington. Councillor BROADHURST said that although he was one of those who was very much opposed to the election of Alderman Peacock, he felt that he had had in the Mayor one of the best friends of his life. (Applause.) Councillor ARCHER thought the Mayor's prac- tical sympathy with all that went on in the town had been recognised.

THE MAYORESS. Alderman JAMES EVANS thought some of the praise was due to the Mayoress—(Jiear, hear)— without whose gracious help the Mayor cottld not have carried out his duties so effectively. Mrs. Peacock had proved a most amiable and charm- ing Mayoress, and she had been of wonderful help and assistance to her husband. (Applause.) Councillor OSBORNE said that during the sum- mer the climatic conditions had not always been of the best, but the Mayoress had always brought sunshine wherever she had attended. (Hear, hear.)

• Councillor 'ASHFORD held that Alderman Pea- cock had done his duty as Mayor so well that it would be a difficult job for the gentleman who had to follow in his footsteps. Councillor PEMBERTON said that the sacrifice which the Mayor was called upon to make when he first took his seat had been of benefit to the whole of Warrington. (Hear, hear.)

BRO. PEACOCK AND SISTER PEACOCK. Councillor CHRIMES referred specially to the Mayor's work in connection with the Friendly Societies,, and said he could safely say that all the members of such societies in the town fully appreciated and valued to the full every- thing the Mayor had done for them during the past year, and previous years. Incidentally Councillor Chrimes mentioned that the Mayor- ess—Sister Peacock—was a member of the first ladies' Court established in the town.

Councillor Goron said that although they had not always agreed, yet he had found the Mayor invariably courteous, and kindly and consid- erate even, for the weaknesses of his fellow- members. The amount of work he had done for the town was unique, and he had always tried to be helpful and sympathetic. (Hear, hear.)
Councillor SKELLAND associated himself with the eulogies of the previous speakers. The resolution was then put and carried with applause.
THE MAYOR'S RETROSPECi.

div.head: 4Slrenuous Year.
div.p: A 4Slrenuous Year.

In acknowledgment, his WORSHIP said that` the manner in which the Council had received the resolution of thanks to himself and the Mayoress for their services made it very difficult for him to give a proper reply; difficult because he felt, from the bottom of his heart, that he was not capable of expressing fully the extreme gratitude which he felt. The position of Mayor was not a sinecure, and if it were not for the loyal and hearty support which had at all times 'been accorded to him by, the Deputy Mayor, his colleagues in the Council, the officials and the members of the public in general, be should not have been able to merit their approval, as shown by the resolution which had been passed.. They had had fillies in the Council when feeling. had run high, but, on the whole, their debates had been carried on without any spirit of rancour, overy member striving to do his best in the interests el/ the good old town which they were privileged to serve. It was true that he had laid himself out to merit the confidence which lidel been reposed ~.in him. His omnivorous Lappetite for work 'had stood him in very good . tend, and when he had done all that he felt •:vas required of him in the interests of the \ tti‘ 14, wn and in .the discharging of the duties of the ffice whfih he was honoured to hold, little time i qd been left for pleasure or private busi- ness. ."--..
527 iii,tIBLIC ENGAGEMENTS. Apart from ;11:N.Y....f1y civic engagements, he

could not possibly detail all the calls that had been made,upon him, but suffice it to mention that his list of social, religious and other en- gagements had been very heavy indeed, as would he readily seen when he stated that during the year he had held office he had fulfilled 192 public engagements. In addition, he had attended no fewer than 335 committee meetings of the Council and had endeavoured to beat his old friend, Alderman Smethurst, who was the 'pre- vious record-breaker. (Laughter and applause.) On top of that he had also attended to his duties as a member of the Education and Insurance Committees, whilst he had also found it neces- sary, in the interests of the borough, to pay visits to various cities and other boroughs in the United Kingdom. Those visits had not been made with any idea of personal gratification, but for the purpose of learning something from other places which might be of benefit to the good old town. (Hear, hear.) In passing, he might say that he had made those visits at his own expense. (Laughter.) He had managed to dovetail in all this work a visit abroad.

div.head: AN EFFORT THAT WAS USELESS.
div.p: AN EFFORT THAT WAS USELESS.

He would pot say much about the part he had endeavoured to play" in regard to the British Empire by endeavouring to cement a better feeling between Germany and England, but the expense of going to Cologne had been entirely thrown away. (Laughter.) The trip he made to Brussels he would always remember with feelings of gratitude to the Bel, gian people, and he would never forget the man- ner in which, as Mayor, it had fallen to his lot to, in some measure, repay the kindness shown to himself, the Mayoress, and other Mayors of E4ngland, by the good people Of Brussels, by wel- coming and entertaining the unfortunate refu- gees who were at present being housed and cared for in the town.

Continuing his Worship said that all through his Mayoralty his idea had been to spare no effort or sacrifice of comfort in discharging his duties as Mayor faithfully and conscientiously to the satisfaction of the Council and the town. He had endeavoured to satisfy the dictates of his heart in doing the duty nearest and dearest to him—in endeavouring to promote, the better- ment of th9.people who were not so fortunate as qne would wish.
NOBLE CONTINGENT FOR THE FRONT.

"Before leaving the meeting to-night," the Mayor continued, "I would just touch for a moment upon the present international crisis. We in Warrington have sent a noble contingent forward to help our country in her hour of need. (Applause.) It has been my privilege as Mayor to wish them 'God-speed,' and I know, come what may, our King, God bless him, has no more loyal subjects than the inhabitants of Warrington. All of us cannot fight, but we at home will do our -utmost to keep the old flag flying and help by every means in our power those in whose hands the interests of our great Empire rest." (Applause.) Before concluding, his Worship referred with gratitude to the assistance accorded him by the various officials of the Corporation, and thanked the Councilefor the kind references which had been made to the Mayoress, who, he said, had helped him splendidly. He felt that any sacri- fices he had made—and he had made some—had not, been in vain. (Hear, hear.) _ _ _

Ald,rman Peacock 'also referred in words of regret to the losses the Council, had sustained by the deaths of Alderman Forshaw and Conn; cillor Birtles, whilst he also mentioned the un- fortunate tanners' strike and the outbreak of war. With these exceptions, the time of lib Mayoralty had been one of the most pleasant tittles of his life.:''

div.head: "GOD SAVE THE KING."
div.p: "GOD SAVE THE KING."
The Mayor was loudly applauded and the members of the Council spontaneously sang the National Anthem.

Osborne had performed a great public duty by calling attention to the matter, which, in his (the speaker's) opinion, was a very serious one and served to demonstrate how necessary it was for Warrington to have a Government audit of its accounts. He ventured to think that any firm in the town—however large it might be—that had two different accounts would feel very, very uneasy with regard to their book-keeping. He knew that if he had anything to do with such a concern his mind would be very uneasy indeed. It seemed to him that Councillor Osborne had struck the right note. The mistake which had been made was that the Council as a body had been expected to shut its eyes, open its mouth, and swallow whatever any committee liked to put in it. The Gas Committee had been for years practically a secret committee. This was the first time since he became a member of the Council, twelve years ago, that he had known what the actual reserve of the Gas Department was. Now he found it was almost equal to a year's rate, totalling as it did .R 43,760. He thought that, after the Auditor's report, the Council could not do less than appoint a com- mittee to investigate the whole platter from top to bottom. Councillor GOUGH said he was not a little bit surprised at the discrepancies which had been pointed out, wheh they considered that some of the members had been sitting on the Gas Com- mittee for\ twenty-five year. (Laughter.) They wanted new blood on the committee, and only when they got it would they begin to know the true particulars, and the Auditor would not have to make such serious remarks in respect to the accounts.
ALDERMAN TINNION PROTESTS AGAINST ".BOLSTERING UP THE RATES."

Alderman Tnn.lioN, replying on behalf of the Gas Committee, said he did not find the least I fault with Councillor Osborne's attitude. The Councillor had taken the matter up in the proper spirit. But he did emphatically object to the assertions or insinuations which had been made by others with reference to the action of the Gas Committee. Councillor Osborne, in dealing with the differences in the two accounts, had admitted very fairly that in the end the accounts presented were absolutely correct. On the other hand, the suggestion had been made that there were discrepancies. The fact was that it was a question of accounts and not of discrepancies at all. It all came to what he (Alderman Tinnion) had said long ago—that the Gas Committee should no longer be a committee to bolster up the rates of the town. It had long been a question of "How much can you get out of the Gas Committee?" and consequently the committee had not, to his mind, been working on the best principles. They ought to make the gas cheap; to make it for the consumers, and let the manager have the benefit of making and selling it cheaply. The Alderman went on to refer to the money set aside for the re-sheeting of the gas holders, and said that when that sum was earmarked the committee were told that the gas holders were beginning to show signs of wear and tear. The manager said to them, in effect, that the principle adopted by the committee had been to make a very con- siderable profit and allocate it to the rates; he did not want to create any great disturbance in the amount contributed to the rates, but pointed out that if the gas holders were to be re-sheeted in one year at a cost of £7,000 to £B,OOO, it would mean that they would have the rates "bobbing up kind down." The result was that, on the advice of Mr. Haddock, the committee allocated in two different years a sum amount- ing to £7,000 odd. Then came a period when the profits were not so large as they ought to be, although the requirements of the finance department of the Corporation were just as great. Feeling that it was not desirable to have to continually increase the rates the Finance Committee said to the Gas Committee: "You have some money which you are not using. Mr. Haddock took rather a pessimistic view at the time, and the holders have lasted better than he thought they would, and as long as you are not using the money we think you ought to band it over to us for the alleviation of the rates."
Made £8,000; Paid Away £ll,OOO.

So, because they could not get the sum re- quired of them out of the profits the committee handed over a portion of that reserve, the result being that although the department made only £B,OOO profit this year, -611,500 had been given to the relief of rates. Having referred to coke as a drug on the market, Alderman Tinnion went on to say that, so far as he was concerned, an investigation committee could be appointed, and he would welcome Councillor Osborne as a member of it. The councillor who suggested it, however, probably knew less about the sub- ject than anybody else in the Council: He (Alderman Tinnion) resented the insinuation that there was anything wrong or, dishonest, and he knew an inquiry would reveal that the managtment of the works and the keeping of the accounts were fair and above board. The department was not quite s 6 well off as it had been. The bank balance on October 26th, 1913, was £10,958 9s. Id., whereas the balance on the corresponding day this year was only £3,185 2s. They were in the unfortunate position that, as a trading concern, they had a ready sale for their gas, but in its manufacture they produced coke and other residuals which at present were difficult to dispose of, partly owing to the war, for some of the by-products were sent to France and Germany in normal times.

COKE DEPOTS—A NOVEL SUGGESTION. Councillor OstfORNE suggested that the large accumulated store of coke with which the com- mittee at present found themselves saddled could be taken to various parts of the town, in which depots could be opened at which it could be sold cheaply. Why could they not take ad- vantage of the Tramways at night for the ,pur- pose of stocking the depots? It might be a novel suggestion, but it was certainly worth trying. Even if it proved to be unprofitable the first year, it would be a boon to the people and be the means of returning to them a por- tion of the profits they had helped to make. (Hear, hear.)_
Councillor FIRTH LINDLEY said that in order to test the demand for coke the Gas Committee had arranged for it to be delivered anywhere in the town.

FINEST COMMERCIAL MEN. Alderman BOLTON said the Gas Committee included the finest commercial men on the Council; they could make a profit where others would be bankrupt. Practically the whole of the profits of the Gas Department, the Alder- man added, were made out of consumers out- side the borough, who paid no improvement rates. It was the only chance the Corporation had of getting a bit of-their own back, and he was surprised that some people could not see through the holes in a ladder. (Laughter.) Councillor WILKINSON said he considered it was very wrong indeed for a member to take a report given by a particular department and then start making comparisons, as Councillor Osborne had done, between that and the Audi- tor's report. Nothing in the Auditor's report had anything whatever to do with the remarks of Councillor Osborne.

The MAron : Oh, yes; he has quoted the figures. Councillor OSBORNE : I quoted the figures sub- mitted in the two revenue accounts—the one submitted to the Auditor and the one placed before the Gas Committee. Councillor PEMBERTON : Members of the Fin- ance Committee do not understand figures. (Laughter.) The MAYOR: Councillor Osborne was quite in order. The minutes containing the Auditor's report were then formally approved.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 31, 1914.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 31, 1914.
FRIENDLY SOCIETIES and the WAR
Difficulties Which will Have to be Faced.
"EXAOINER" SPECIAL.

Not the least perplexing of the difficulties raised at the present time is the effect of the war on Friendly Societies. The funds outgoing in death benefits and sick payments must necessarily reach a remarkably. high figure. Although the incomes may be smaller, the officials will have to deal with greater liability, for the pick of their members —fine, strong, young men—are at present run- ning grave risks at the front. It must be admitted that some -branches will suffer little, if anything at all, but where the members are drawn from industrial centres where Kitchener's appeal has been heartily re- sponded to, the position is serious.

div.head: NO "CONTRACTING OUT."
div.p: NO "CONTRACTING OUT."

Of course, some societies have a rule in which it is stated that any member leaving the United Kingdom or joining the Army or Navy, shall \ cease to be in benefit. Although these rules exist, an Act of Parliament lays it down that no member's interests shall be imperilled by his being in the Army or Navy. This is clearly set forth in the Friendly Society Act, 1896, wherein it is stated that " a person shall not by reason of his enrolment or service in the Militia (which includes the Territorial Forces by Order in Council dated March 19, 1908), or as a naval coast volunteer, royal naval volunteer, naval artillery volunteer, or in ally corps of yeomanry or volunteers whatsoever, lose or forfeit any interest in a Friendly Society or branch, whether registered or unregistered, which he possessed at the time of his being so enrolled or serving, or be fined for absence from, or non- attendance at, any meeting of the society or branch if his absence or non-attendance is occa- sioned by the discharge of his military or naval duty, as certified by his commanding officer; any rules of the society or branch to the contrary notwithstanding."

' The most common interpretation of this clause is that a member on returning to civil life shall be in exactly the same position on the society's books as he was when he joined the force. For instance, if a member joins the Army to-day, and is five weeks in arrears, he will still be five weeks in arrears when the war is over. Similarly, if a member is out of sick benefit when he listens to the call of the King and country, he will be out of that benefit when he returns; or if his arrears are so heavy that he is. out of death benefit when he joins the Army or Navy, no death payment will be made if he unfortunately happens to be killed. The time occupied by the war will be counted as nil; it will be overlooked, so that, in all respects, the member's absence will be likened to going away one minute and coming back the next. It is patent therefore that no society can fore- go the claims of its members even if it wished to do so.

Another point to be borne in mind ill-that the majority of the absent members will not be in a position to continue their usual contributions. These can be met by drawing upon the benevo- lent funds of the lodge, or by making a levy upon the members who remain behind. It is understood that these systems are being adopted by certain orders. It is also possible to make the benevolent fund and the levy divide the responsibility for raising an amount sufficient to equal the contributions of the men who are in the services. In these times it behoves every Friendly Society man to rally round his stan- dard and facilitate the work of his officials.

div.head: CIVIC CHURCH-GOING.
div.p: CIVIC CHURCH-GOING.
Corporation Listen to Striking
War Sermon.
"GOD WILL REPAY !"

The Mayor and Corporation paid an official visit to Bewsey-road Wesleyan Church on Sun- day morning, when the preacher was the Rev. W. Thompson Derry (circuit superintendent). Included in the large congregation besides the Mayor and Mayoress (Alderman and Mrs. Peacock) were: Aldermen Bennett, James Evans and Tinnion, and Councillors Osborne, Haw- thorn, Henshall, Halliwell, Dickenson, Lashford, Gough, Skelland, Shaw, Chrimes, Locker and Lindley, whilst accompanying them were the following officials: Messrs. A. T. Hallaway (deputy town clerk), J. Fairhurst (borough treasurer), W. H. Woodcock (borough collector), M. A. Piercey (assistant borough surveyor), A. S. Elliott (assistant director of education), C. Madeley (librarian), J. M'Adam (assistant librarian), W. T. Flood (nuisance inspector), R. Whitfield (head gardener), and A. Bottomley (clerk to the Board of Guardians). Messrs. J. W. Hayward, J. Upson, J. Bailey, W. Furness, R. T. Fair- dough and T. Pemberton (borough magistrates) were also in attendance upon his Worship.

div.head: PRESENT "HOLY WAR."
div.p: THE PRESENT "HOLY WAR."

Taking for his text the well-known words "Righteousness exalteth a nation," the preacher referred to the war, and said it had been called "a holy war." Men had smiled at the expres- sion and termed it rather extravagant, but he held that if the war were based upon righteous- ness it was a holy war—and a holier war than the Crusaders in ancient times waged against the unbelievers who held possession of the Holy Sepulchre. It was a holy war because it chal- lenged the dictum that "right was might." It was a righteous war because it was dictated by. truth, sblemn pledges solemnly renewed. 'Whether other nations kept their word or not, or whether cynical Germany violated her pledges, England was bound to maintain hers. It was religious war because it was waged on behalf of liberty. The sanctity of the poorest home was as dear to its inmates as the sanctity of a palace, and a nation, worthy of being called a nation, would part with life itself rather than part with the homes of its people. People who were only keen about their own freedom did not know the meaning of the word.

div.head: Live And Let Live.
div.p: Live And Let Live.

To be free they must live and let live—to be free they must be free and free others. If they were true lovers of freedom they would always do that. "We have," continued the preacher, "fought great battles in the past on behalf of our own freedom, and we have also engaged in keen constitutional struggles. We have inter- ested ourselves in the freedom of other nation- , alities, such as Italy and Portugal, and once more the call has come to us, and we have re- , solved as a people that Britain shall not live if Belgium dies. The present war is just because it is a matter of honour. Whether we were bound by treaty or not, we were bound by friend- ship with France to prevent her being robbed of her colonies. If we had played fast and loose we should have stained the fair name of our country. It has been said to me that our right- ' eousness is under a suspicion because we are allied with the authors of Belgian atrocities in the Congo, and the persecution of the Jews and reformers in Russia. The answer to the former is that the late King Leopold was responsible to the latter, that it has all been brought about by political religious bigotry. The true answer is that whatever these nations have done hitherto, in this crisis.they have chosen, the 'right course, and therefore we are right in standing shoulder to shoulder with them. In bumble confidence and thankfulness we say this is a righteous war, and on all hands we can see a source of ,exalta- tion.
"This Colossal Crime."

Referring to the loyalty and patience of those who were left at home, the preacher said: "Greater love than this hath no man, that he lay down his life for his friend." God said: "Vengeance is Mine! I will repay !" and He would do so, although He might employ human agents to help Him in the task of punishing those who were responsible for the present colossal crime against humanity, and in taking such strong measures that its repet'tion would be prevented. They should redouble their efforts to bring those who had suffered through the war from the depths of despair and misery.

div.head: SCHOOL PLAYFIELDS.
div.p: SCHOOL PLAYFIELDS.
Should Secondary Scholars be Specially Favoured?

div.head: LONG DISCUSSION AT COUNCIL MEETING.
div.p: LONG DISCUSSION AT COUNCIL MEETING.

At the monthly meeting on Monday night the Warrington Town Council had before them a recommendation by the Education Committee to the effect ,that the offer of Mr. William Powell to let to the committee a piece of ground for the purpose of an athletic field for the use of the scholars at the Secondary School be accepted, the clear rental of the same to be £6O per annum, on a seven years' agreement It was fnrther recommended that the landlord of the field at present used by the school be given notice to terminate the tenancy. WHY NOT USE VICTORIA PARK?

The recommendation gave rise to a lengthy discussion, inadgurated by Councillor ARCHER, who, after Councillor Roberts had formally moved the adoption of the committee's report, said he would rather, the resolution, referred to above, had been more explicit as to the position of the field, but, apart from that and kindred questions, it appeared to him that the time was not opportune for the Council to em- bark upon an expenditure of ..t420, extending over seven years, for the purpose of providing a playing field for one school, seeing that in the midst of the town they had just acquired an addition to Victoria Park, which it was proposed to allocate to a 'similar purpose. The point might be raised that the Town Council had no right to set apart that ground for such. a purpose as this field Was intended, but his' answer was that already every Saturday six teams played on the ground which the Town Council had allocated for the purpose of en- couraging outdoor sport. He contended that just as the use of the additional ground was granted to those six teams, so could a part of it be allocated th the Secondary School for a like purpose. Seeing what the country was going through, this was not the time when public money should be spent for the purpose proposed by the Education Committee. If land was to be set apart for the games of the Secondary School, he contended that the Coun- cil should also give facilities to the children in the elementary schools. Councillor CHRIMES, who seconded, said that, like Councillor Archer, he did not think this was the time to incur expenditure on a playing field, nor did he believe in providing a field for the Secondary School and leaving out the sdholars of the elementary schools. (Hear, hear.)

FACILITIES FOR ALL THE CHILDREN. Alderman BENNETT said that because at the present time the Education Committee were not proposing to provide suitable recreation grounds for the elementary schools that was no reason why they should withhold such a ground from the Secondary School. Personally, he felt that ample facilities ought to be provided for all the children of the town, and he should not feel that the Council had completed their duty until they had done that, but he did not think that the fact that the Council were not asked to go the whole hog at the present moment was a reason for withholding the facilities proposed for this one particular school. Facilities for physical exercise were exceedingly necessary and helped in the rearing of a healthier and stronger race, and because they could not be procuftbd for all the children at one and the same time it was no reason why they should be denied to part of the children. At the same time he was not altogether con- vinced as to the complete suitability' of the site of the proposed playing field, and he thought it might be possible to find a play- ground in a position that was more central and more in touch with the school. It was quite a long walk from Padgate Station to the ground in question. Alderman BOLTON said that if the sort of thing proposed by the Education Committee went on the ratepayers would soon be in the position of not knowing whether they were paying for education, gymnasia, or what, and added that it appeared to him that the com- mittee were still trying to spend all the money they could on every fad they could create.

Committee were conferring a favour on those children who were in a better position to get recreation than were the children in the ele- mentary schools. He was not satisfied that the resolution of the committee did justice as between the two classes of schools.

Councillor JOSEPH thought there was a great deal in the argument put forth that the elementary schools should also be provided for, and said that since the meeting of the Educa- tion Committhe more than one person bad urged upon him the objection, from the moral point of view, of the boys and girls attending the Secondary School being sent so far out into the country. Councillor ROBERTS hastened to assure the Doctor that the boys and girls were always under proper supervision. Councillor PEMBERTON announced his intention of voting for the amendment. A VOICE: Of course you would. (Laughter.) Councillor PEMBERTON : Why? The Voice: Because you always do. (More laughter.) WHY NOT PLAY "ON OUR OWN PREMISES"?

Councillor PEMBERTON went on to say that be could not understand why the Corporation went on buying land suitable for recreative purposes and then kept on paying other people money for playing fields for the school children. Why could not the playing be done on their own premises? There was ample room in the Vic- toria" Park. extension for a dozen secondary schools to play on. It was not fair to, or in the interests of, the children in the elementary schools that the scholars of the Secondary School should be singled out for this special favour. The majority of the children in the Secondary School lived in very nice districts and their friends had gardens, or other plam, for them to play in; whereas the parents of tlpa elementary scholars lived, often, in back-to- back houses, or in courts, that afforded no proper facilities for the physical recreation of the little ones. _ _ _

Councillor GOUGH said that the Council had recently purchased an extension of Victoria Park, and he thought part of it ought to be allocated for the purposes of recreation for the Secondary School children. He advised that the committee's minute, be sent back for re- consideration, with a view to further and fuller particulars being provided. . Councillor CRAIK said he considered that the proposed play-field was altogether too far out of the way. Councillor WILKINSON pointed out that one thing that had been overlooked was that the scholars at the Secondary School who belonged to the school tennis club each paid 3s. a year, and that that realised about £33 towards the £6O which it was proposed to nay as rental for the whole ground. "So you are being asked to be very wasteful with public money, are you not?" asked the speaker, in sarcastic tones, add- ing, "Will the gentlemen who condemn this site as being too far away find us another one nearer, and at a suitable price?" (Cries of " Victoria Park.") He considered the Council were getting a bargain if they adopted the committee's recommendation.

div.head: NO NEW QUESTION_.
div.p: NO NEW QUESTION_.

Councillor- lisxsnALL, after remarking that he thought they were all agreed on the principle of providing a playing field for the scholars of the elementary schools, went on to point out that the Council were not asked to deal with a new question at all, as the Secondary School had already had a playing field for some time, and all that was proposed was to change over from the old one to one more suitable. To say that the Secondary School should not have a playing field until they could get a recreation ground for the elementary schools was very much like " cutting off one's nose to spite one's face." Granting the principle of providing a recreation ground for the Secondary School, the question merely resolved itself into one of retaining the old ground at Padgate, or going in for a new and more suitable ground at Fearn- head. The agreement submitted by the Edu- cation Committee was terminable any year after the first year, so that all the Council were asked to commit themselves to was an expen- diture of £6O, whilst, from the agreement, the risk was not on their side, but on that of the lessor. If they terminated the agreement next year, the lessor, apparently, was going to lose 'money. He would not like the Council to vote against the committee's ,proposal on the ground that the elementary schools had not yet got a recreation ground, but, rather, let them sup- port it, and then go in for a similar playing field for the scholars in the ordinary day schools.

THE CLAIMS OF THE POORER CHILDREN Alderman JAMES EvsNs said that, if it were right for the Secondary School to have a re- ciestion ground such as the committee proposed surely it was about time that body also con- ‘idered the advisability of adapting the prin- ciple, generally, to the elementary schbols. He contended that they were not justified in spend- ing £6O a year on one school's recreative facilities whilst they did practically nothing for the recreation of those children whose posi- tion in life rendered them less able to provide facilities for themselves. (Hear, hear.) "Are you going," the Alderman asked, "to back up the school that can very well provide for itself, so far as the individual scholars are concerned, and leave out all those whose station in life renders them unable to provide at all? If we are going to. embark on this question at all, it is my feeling that we should have one general recreation ground for all the schools in the town." Councillor BROADHURST said that the inference to be drawn from what Councillor Archer had said was that the provision of the proposed playing field had sonzething to do with the drawing of class-distinction—that it was pro- viding for the recreation of the classes and not of the masses—and he (the speaker) could assure them that if, in his opinion, that were so, he would vote for the amendment; but he knew for an absolute fact that there was no question .of class-distinction about the business, and that was why he supported the Education Committee. Alderman Bolton had raised the question of economy, and on that score alone he (Councillor Broadhurst) submitted that it would be in the best interests of the ratepayers to effect the proposed change of grounds. As to the drawing of the contrast between the Second- ary and the elementary schools, he did not think the Council ought to take up a dog-in- the-manger standpoint. By voting for the committee's proposal the Council would only be carrying on the system introduced some time ago, and if they could extend similar privileges to the elementary scholars, by all means let them do so. NEW PROPOSAL WILL SAVE MONEY. Alderman SMETHURST supported the commit- tee's proposal and pointed out that instead of , spending between .V7O and £BO as they had been doing, the Council would only be called upon to pay £6O. Much had been Said about the ' want of playing-spaces for the elementary ' scholars, and, in that connection, he might say that many a time he had wondered why the playgrounds surrounding the ordinary day schools could not be left open so that the children could go into them and play during the hours when the school itself was closed. Otherwise, he could not help thinking that the playgrounds that had been provided were largely a waste of money. Councillor Gomm, in supporting the amend- ment, opined that by singling out the Secondary School for a special play-field the Education,

div.head: COMMITTEE CHAIRMAN'S PROMISE.
div.p: COMMITTEE CHAIRMAN'S PROMISE.

Councillor ROBERTS, replying to the debate- on behalf of the Education Committee, said he was extremely sorry that certain statements had been made that night,, which had not the slight- est foundation in fact, and no relation to the question at issue. He guaranteed that, al- though he was absolutely in agreement with the suggestion, whenever the Education Com- mittee came forward—as it certainly would do in view of the challenge thrown out that night —with a proposition to provide a playing-field, or fields, for the scholars of the elementary schools, some of the same objectors would be found prominent in objecting to that also. Well, he would see that they had their oppor- tunity. He did feel a little bit hurt when he knew how persistently and consistently opposition came from the same quarter in re- gard to every question of a progressive nature which the committee brought forward. The proposition submitted to the Council that night was one of the most democratic that was ever submitted to them. Reference had been made to the station in life and social position of the children of the Secondary School, and more colossal ignorance of the facts had never been displayed in that Council Chamber. The children of the Secondary School—and he was proud of the fact—were, as to 75 per cent, of the total number, free scholars—worthy chil- dren of working men and working women whose brains had come to the top and who by virtue of that fact had found themselves free students, and to talk about them and their parents being in a position to find the boys and girls with opportunities for physical advancement was nonsense. It only showed what utter balder- dash certain members of the Council were only too glad to use in order to throw dust in the eyes of others. No secondary school in the country stood higher in regard to the results of its work—regard being paid to the material it had to work upon—than did the Warrington Secondary School. One of the Town's Finest Institution& It was one of the finest institution the town had got, and he was surprised that councillors should get up and say that the children of working men, who had found their way to the school by merit and brain power, should have denied to them the privileges accorded to those who, being better off, were able to enjoy the privileges of the endowment of a rich school, privileges that were given them without stint or limit. He regarded the committee's pro- posal as one of the finest things that they could do, in that the carrying out of it would help to make the children of working people both mentally and physically fit. Councillor Got an: Could not the committee have joined the elementary schools in the pro- posal? Councillor ROBERTS replied that the question of providing play-fields for the elementary schools was a big matter, but it was one of the first things the Education Committee would give the Council the opportunity of voting upon. It had been suggested that the school might join with the elementary schools in using the Victoria Park, but those who made the sugges- tion overlooked the fact that the average age of the children in the Secondary School was higher than that of the scholars in the ordi- nary day schools. Many of the scholars in the Secondary School were just emerging from boy- hood and girlhood into manhood and womanhood, and the committee wanted to give them every opportunity for physical development, and that entailed something more than the occasional use of Victoria Park for a few hours. Eight or ten years ago the scholars of the Secondary School started an athletic club of their own, and out of their own meagre purses they raised £2O or £3O a year, but the time came when it was impossible to carry on unless somebody came to their rescue to keep them out of debt. Then it was that the com- mittee felt that they should under f• • the work, and they did so with the full Iction of the Council, and had continued to do so for eight years. The onl- diffPience between the old position and the 1, •w were (a) the financial differences, and (b) the physical situation of the propose 4 ground. Not a New Departure. Councillor Gomm : Why do not you use Vic- toria Park? Councillor ROBERTS, continuing, said that it was extremely difficult to get land, sufficiently near the town for recreative purposes, and it was only when they got a wealthy firm who were willing to assist in the matter of terms that they were able to secure such a ground. On the question of finance the Education Com- mittee's proposal was going to save £2O or £3O a year. The play-field for the Secondary School was not a new departure, and the one proposed was going to involve less expense than had pre- viously been incurred for the same purpose. The £6O that had been mentioned was not the rent of the land, but it covered the cost of pre- paration of the tennis grounds, &c. As to the suggestion that part of Victoria Park should be used for the purpose in hand, he would point out that the Parks Committee had no power to allocate any part of the Park for the exclu- sive use of any school. On being put to the vote the amendment was lost and the committee's minutes were then approved.

div.head: DRINK, HER RUIN.
div.p: DRINK, HER RUIN.

Sad Story of a Mother's Neglect. The sad story of a mother's want of care for her offspring was told to the borough magis- trates on Tuesday, when Alice Louisa Vernon, or Morrow, of 3, Ford-street, was charged with neglecting her two children in a manner likely to cause injury to their health. Mr. A. Browne prosecuted on behalf of the N.S.P.C.C., and Mr. T. S. Steel, instructed by prisoner's mother, defended.

Mr. Browne said that the prisoner was before the Court on October 6th, and one instance which was mentioned then was that she had put her baby underneath the tap on account of its temper. The prisoner promised to be better, and he (Mr. Browne) took it upon him- self, much against the wishes of the Chair- man, to ask that the case'should be adjourned in order to give her another chance. The case was adjourned on her promising to be better, to sign the pledge, and to look after the children. She did sign the pledge and was very good for a fortnight, but she com- menced drinking again, and her conduct since had been such that her father begged of Mr. Wainwright to lock her up on the previous Thursday, when she was very drunk. Horrible Things the Inspector Saw. _ _ . .

The case might be said to have started first of all in Shrewsbury in April last, and Inspec- tor Anderson, of the N.S.P.C.C., would be able to tell the Bench of horrible things he saw there. Prisoner was supposed to be married to a man named Morrow, who was a clerk in the Military Depot at Shrewsbury. He had a pension of 2s. 6d. a day. Inspector Anderson, of Shrewsbury, was called to give evidence, but the Chairman (Councillor H. Roberts) asked if the case could not be shortened.
Steel: My instructions are to lay one or two lacts before you with a view to asking you to give her another chance. I agree that this case could be materially shortened.
The Chairman: Are you prepared to admit the material facts as alleged?

Mr. Steel: Yes, the ma-terial ones. Inspector Anderson said that the prisoner and the man named Morrow had been in a house in Shrewsbury for three months, and yet they had nothing unpacked when he called. The place was covered with straw, the whole of the house was dirty, the children were in a filthy state, and one child was lying on a pillow covered with grease. The children were in an extremely dirty condition. He went up into a bedroom, where there were bottles of beer under the bed, "find the place was in such a condition that he could not stay in it. _ _ _

div.head: Left the Child •Alone for Hours.
div.p: Left the Child •Alone for Hours.

- . - In answer to Mr. Steel, witness said he knew that Morrow was preparing to go to the front. Inspector Wainwright said that since the adjournment he had visited prisoner three times. He had frequently cautioned her about going out and leaving her child alone for hours at a time. She was very dirty and had ad- mitted that the iivhole trouble was caused through drink. She had told him that her husband had sent her £7 to buy furniture. Dr. Peacocke said that the prisoner's action of placing the child under the tap had caused unnecessary suffering. Mr. Steel said that drink was at the bot- tom of the whole sad story. From the evi- dence given by Inspector Anderson at a previous hearing they had gathered that the husband_ was of a somewhat similar nature to the prisoner herself. He understood that the husband was responsible in the first instance; he drank. so she started to follow suit. There was an element of jealousy in the case, and Inspector Anderson had told them that she had said she had only done as she had in order to spite her husband. She now, asked for a chance, instead of being sent to prison. In that case he could not help feeling that the spirit was willing, but the flesh was weak. Money had been sent to the prisoner to get int% a little house, and on Thursday the Was look- ing for one, and, having walked round the town for a long time, she went to a friend's, and that friend sent for some beer. She drank again then. She was willing to go to a home

for six months, and lie (Mr. Steel) suggested to the magistrates, whom, he was sure, were not desirous of sending her to prison if it could be avoided, that that was the best course that could be adopted. If there was a chance of reforming her, and getting her away from the longing for drink, he was sure she would be a good. woman and a good mother.

Prisoner broke down and wept as she called out: "I will be firm this time! I will be good, gentlemen!" The Chairman: You will either have to con- sent to go to a home, or we shall send you to prison. We will adjourn the case for six months, but if you leave the home before the expiration of that time you will come up for sentence.
The case was adjourned for seven days in order to see if a home can be found for the woman.
