THE EXAMINER,
SATURDAY, OCTOBER 31, 1914.

div.head: IMPERIAL GAMBLER.
div.p: THE IMPERIAL GAMBLER.

Whom God will destroy lie first of all drives mad. Never was the truth of this classical saying better justified than in the case of the .GERMAN EMPEROR. All the insane things he has done; s4t and since the outbreak of his insane war are too well known to justify recapitulation, but the new facts presented in the last few days may be reviewed. Three out- standing acts of madness which will surely be the deciding factor in an already nearly decided case against the EMPEROR have followed closely upon one another's heels. In the first place Germany, not content with hav- ing taken the Old World by the ears, has challenged the New World by gratuitously claiming the right to send troops to Canada because Canada has sent troops to England. The United States have been staggered by the sug- gestion, lAA now they know the world- wide nature of the aims of the slayer of European women and children, and the burner of ancient seats of learning, they may be trusted to take a keen and active interest in German doings for the future. The German dash for Calais is another sign of the incurable disease that holds the head of the Prussian Monster in its grip. For political pur- poses, apart altogether from military needs and strategy, Germans have been bundled towards the Straits of Dover to establish themselves there whateyer the cost. They have paid the price, but have not got the prize. In the extremely unlikely event of their suc- ceeding, they will have gained a barren victory. They will be there to frighten the people of England. We shall simply refuse to be frightened, and shall know that the hundreds of thousands of the enemy who will have perished in providing the show will not be available either for an advance upon Paris, or to defend the Rhine fortresses when we are under way for Berlin: It is strange how the campaign furnishes analogies as it proceeds. The KAISER deserted soldiering for politics when he rushed all his forces into East Prussia to drive out a small but brave Russian force and left his Austrian allies to be swamped by the main ttussian Army. He lost his allies then ; now he is completing the loss of the : million of his own me,n he announced, with so much complacency, that he could afford to lose to achieve his ob- ject of conquest. But to have lost a million men and achieved nothing is enough, to breed desperation of a still worse kind. It is, however, the third and latest ct that will tell most heavily against ,he KAISER. After having cast about .n vain for some respectable ally, he has joined forces with the Turk. Birds of a feather flock together, and this -combination will demonstrate to the world what we might expect if Ger- many won. The German mailed fist and the Turkish proclivities for gov- ernment by means of atrocities is a combination that would present it dismal prospect to humanity. We should say this move is about the best one`the KAISER could have devised for urging the rest of Europe to arm against him. Certainly the Balkan nations will do all they can to prevent the Turk from getting once more in the ascendant. The failure to get into •' •Id, nt will mean that the Turk ,
Mir

gap.desc: skipped/gap: fewer than 20 non-control characters after cleanup

div.p: will be banished finally from Europe, and European civilisation will make a fresh and encouraging start, shorn of the blighting influence of the Prussian Junker and the successors of the Great Assassin.

div.head: BRIDGE ENGINEER.
div.p: THE BRIDGE ENGINEER.

Mr. J. J. WEBSTER, the engineer for the new Warrington Bridge, died sud- denly yesterday_ Mr. WEBSTER was connected with Warrington by the closest ties, and his death will be deeply mourned by a large circle of friends. His best monument, locally, will be the great ferro-concrete bridge, part of which was opened by the KING last year, when Mr. WEBSTER was pre- sented to His MAJESTY. The whole bridge will be ready before the end of this year, and it is sad to reflect upon the reason why Mr. WEBSTER will not see the completion of his handiwork. Ordinarily a change of engineer during the course of work entails much delay, as well as expense, but, fortunately, Mr. WEBSTER had in Mr. FITZSYMONS a capable partner, who, as a matter of fact, has been responsible all along for the technical and detailed work con- nected with the bridge. i When the bridge was n part opened by His MAJESTY it was stipulated by LORD DERBY that there should be no other "opening." This condition will, of course, be observed, though there may be an unveiling of the tablet which was the subject of a discussion at the Council this week.

div.head: SENSIBLE DECISION.
div.p: A SENSIBLE DECISION.

This week the fovVrT"-EOrii-lcil were i asked to do a ridiculous thing—to pre- vent the Secondary School from having a recreation , ground because the 1 elementary schools had none. Coun- cillor HENRY ROBERTS, who made one of the best speeches of his life, had little difficulty in riddling the argu- ments of the proposal to give up the field, and he had the satisfaction of seeing the Council, which seemed to have been captured by the sophistries that were doing duty for argument, turn to his way of thinking and reject the proposal by a handsome ,majority. To put children who wish to play marbles in a field with young men and women athletes, intent upon hockey, tennis and cricket, would be a brilliant arrangement; but we scarcely think 1 it would assist in building up the nation physically in the way that Eng- land has been, and is being, built up on her playflelds. The last resort of the barren controversialist, the cry of the classes versus the masses, was adopted, but it was shown that at the Secondary School almost the whole of • the scholars are children of the Work- ing classes, who, in later life, will have to compete against the scholars at the Grammar School, who, although chil- dren of the better classes, have their recreation ground in connection with a school that is largely endowed. Coun- cillor ROBERTS, however, promised that the Education Committee should pro- duce a scheme for providing suitable playgrounds for the elementary school children of the borough. He does not expect to get the support of those who opposed the Secondary School field.

div.head: COKE.
div.p: COKE.

Councillor OSBORNE, in the course of his interesting review of the finances of the Gas Committee, succeeded in bringing forward once again the ques- tion of supplying coke in small quanti- ties. He favours the establishment of depots in various parts of the tow-n, where the poor could have their require ments met. To get over the expense of cartage to these distributing centres, he suggests that the tramway system should be used during the night-time to transport the fuel from the works. So far as a lay mind can see, there would be no objection to the lines being used for the purpose, but special waggons would have to be bought. Coke would leave any ordinary cars used in too grimy a condition to be used by passengers. There are, how- ever, two cars on the Manchester-road route that might with advantage be degraded into coke trucks. They roll in an alarming way, and keep passen- gers in anything but a pleasant state of mind.

div.head: RETAINED MILITARY DOCUMENT, Warrington Barman Sentenced at Assizes.
div.p: RETAINED MILITARY DOCUMENT, Warrington Barman Sentenced at Assizes.

Harold Dutton (20), a barman, who was re- cently charged at Warrington with unlawfully retaining a military document, contrary to the Official Secrets Act, 1911, was sentenced to ,six months' imprisonment by Mr. Justice Darling at the Liverpool Assizes on Thursday. Mr. A. R. Kennedy, for the prosecution, said that the document was very important and re- lated to lectures which were given at the head- quarters of the Army Service Corns. Prisoner had stated to the police that whilst he was a clerk at Portsmouth he kept an extra type- written copy of the document for himself, and used to show it to the men in his ranks just to " swank." He had shown it to a fellow-lodger in Warrington. Mr. Newman, for the defence, said the pri- soner made no secret that he had the document in his possession, and showed it to one or two people. He was not in any sense a spy. In sentencing Dutton, his Lordship said he hoped the military authorities would inquire into the matter, for it should not be allowed , to rest simply with the punishment of a sub- ordinate clerk.

div.head: Twenty in the Infirmary; Thirty-four at Haddon Court.
div.p: Twenty in the Infirmary; Thirty-four at Haddon Court.
FIRaT-HAMB BATTLE STORIES

Twenty of Britain's brave fighting men are at present quartered in the Warrington In- firmary, where they are recovering from wounds received in recent -battles on the Continent. Considering the extent to which they have suffered, they are a wonderfully cheery band of fellows, and those who have had the honour of shaking them by the hand and the privilege of a brief chat with them have come away with the feeling that there is nothing wrong with the old country whilst she can produce sons of such mettle as goes to the making of these wounded warriors. Never a complaint do they make; never a grumble do they utter, but they regard it all as part of the day's work, their only regret being that, for the nonce at any rate, they are prevented from rendering further service to their country. .

On Monday afternoon an "Examiner" man called at the Infirmary and was allowed to have brief chats with a few of the wounded men. Several of them he found in the semi-convales- cent stage—able to leave their beds. and spend a few hours in the all-too-small garden at the rear of the hospital. They were, in the main, quite ready to chat of themselves and their ex- periences, and as they trod the little piece of greensward they puffed with evident relish the pipes and cigarettes which thoughtful admirers had provided for them. And in this connection, why should not the little band of thoughtful ad- mirers who have so far found the wounded Tommies a few smokes become a big band? 'Cigarettes—and as everybody knows, or ought to know, in these days, "fags" are Mr. Atkins' pet predilection in matters Nicotinian—are very cheap and for the outlay of a few coppers one can confer quite a lot of pleasure on these gal- lant fellows. The address is: "P. Atkins, Esq., Warrington Infirmary." Enough said ! When the wounded " Tommies" arrived on Sunday they were met, and in cases where necessary, assisted by twelve members of the Warrington Corps of the St. John Ambulance Brigade.
Told to " Examiner " Reporters.

German guns are a bit thick," he told our representative, "and a sliver off one of them unholy shells caught me wheie it didn't oughter,' and here I am." "I was," Private Doyle went on to relate, "with an ammunition waggon. Me and the others were taking ammunition to the battalion and I was standing outside a house in e vil- lage, looking after a waggon and a pair of horses, when my little bit of trouble came my way. I had another four horses behind and some pack mules, but they were killed. Then one of the two horses in front was shot through the nose and I had to shoot the poor beast when I managed to get my waggon up to the trans- port column.

div.head: WOUNDED, BUT HELPED OTHERS.
div.p: WOUNDED, BUT HELPED OTHERS.

The first of the smiling Tommies to submit himself to the tender mercies of "The Ex- aminer" interviewer had his head heavily ban- daged, but he assured our man that his wound was "nothing to shout about" now, and told him to "fire away" with his questions, first of all stipulating that he was not to be asked to give his name. This plucky chap belongs to the Rifle Brigade, and he was wounded at La Chapelle, near Ar- mentieres, in the fierce fighting which raged in that neighbourhood on Sunday, October 18th. With the Brigade, the Leinsters, the South Devons, and a battery of Field Artillery, he was engaged in deen ding a two-mile length of rail- way. Suddenly they were submitted to a search- ing shrapnel fire by the enemy's guns, and, to use Mr. Atkins's own words, "it was too jolly hot to make you feel at home, like! We perse- vered, however, in the teeth of the murderous "guns and got to within a hundred and 'fifty yards of the trenches in which the enemy's rifle- men had taken up their positions. There we found passable cover, under shelter of which' we hastily constructed trenches for ourselves, in which we were ensconced for the remainder of the day, employing the hours in taking pot- shots at the Germans whenever one of them made himself visible and holding the ground whilst reinforcements were hurrying up and establishing themselves." "This little forward move of ours," said Tommy, with a touch of grief in his tones, "cost us about two hundred jolly good chaps! It was no picnic, I can tell you!" - TERRIBLE VIGIL IN A FARMHOUSE.

"When I got hit," he went on, `` I managed to crawl out of the way and retired to a farm- house, where I found six other chaps who had also got more than they wanted. There we stayed nursing our hurts for the remainder of the day, living in hopes of being picked up by the ambulance people at night, but hour after hour passed by, and 110 help came. I was the only chap hit in the head; the only one that could get about and handle things, for the others were all hit either in the arms or legs, or so badly damaged that they couldn't even crawl. So I did what I could for the others—it wasn't much; but it was all I could do. "We stayed in that building until 7.15 the next morning, and all the time we could hear the noise of the guns and hear the shells screeching, and we never knew when one of them might pay us a visit and put 'paid' to our account. Finding that nobody came to us, we decided in the early hours of the morning, just before daybreak, to see if we could find a field hospital, and so, crawling and hobbling as best we could, we made our way along hedge- rows and ditches for about two miles, until we got back to the village of La Chapelle Armen- tieres, where we knew there was a small field hospital. We found it, and you can guess we weren't half pleased. There the doctors got busy, on us, and they soon made new men of us. We stopped in the hospital ten hours, and then we were cleared out to make room for others, being sent to Armentieres itself. "JUST AS THE FUN WAS COMMENCING."

"Proni -t-hez..e we got, as -best we could, to a Red Cross train that was in waiting ten or eleven miles away, and then it was all right v‘ith us. We were taken to Calais, and from there to Boulogne, and the morning after our arrival at the last place they put on a boat, and—well, here I am, getting well and strong, and ready to have another smack at 'em as soon as they like! .

_ . "I'm sorry I got knocked out just as the best of the fun was commencing, for we were advanc- ing and carrying everything before us. We hear all these tales about German barbarism," added the anonymous warrior, "but I can only say that I have seen none of it." This particular Tommy also took part in the fighting on the Aisne. "We boys," he said, were entrenched near the river for twelve solid days, and I can tell you that they were not among the jolliest days I have spent, though they were some of the most exciting and uncom- fortable, for with guns, guns, guns banging and booming night and day you never knew what was going to happen next. After we got out of those trenches we were sent down to Soupier— just at the bottom of the hill on which we had been perched—to the rest camp, and I can tell you we wanted that rest. Whilst we were on the banks of the Aisne fifty of us were sent out with some of the Engineers to build a bridge, and although we were being 'shelled at like anything, not one of us got hit, and you can imagine we considered ourselves in luck's way. As regards the German artillery fire," he continued, by way of conclusion, "it's very good once the beggars get the range, but they seem to be a long while finding it. Their snipers are good hands at their trade. But as for their infantry—well, I wouldn't take the trouble to pick the beggars up."

div.head: BUSY GETTING BETTER.
div.p: BUSY GETTING BETTER.

Private George Thomas Sharp's stay at the front was a very brief one, but that was not his fault. He belongs to -Upchurch, Kent, and is in the Ist Buffs. He spent only a fortnight on French soil. He was hit in the forearm and the shoulder fighting in the neighbourhood of the Aisne, and he is now, as he phrased it, "busy getting better," so that he can go but and "have another smack at 'ern."

div.head: DIDN'T KNOW HE WAS WOUNDED.
div.p: DIDN'T KNOW HE WAS WOUNDED.

Private Charles Doyle, a "broth of a bhoy " from Dundrum,, Co.. Dublin—" an' that's in Oireland and.don't forgit it," he laughingly told our interviewer—is the life and soul of the little party of wounded, to one and all of whom he is affectionately known as "P,addy." He serves in the Lancashire Fusiliers, and he was wounded at Armentieres, being hit just above the ankle, with the result that he can only get about at the cost of great discomfort and pain. "The

div.head: "PLUGGED" IN THE ANKLE.
div.p: "PLUGGED" IN THE ANKLE.

" But before that I had to make him go about a mile and a half, though it hurt one to have to do so. As I drove down the road to the trans- port people kept shouting out to me 'Are you hit?' They noticed that I seemed to be suffer- ing with one of my feet. I shouted back ' but when I reached the transport and had time to attend to ray foot, I found that I had been ' plugged ' all right. My boot was full of blood and there was a hole near the ankle, from which more blood was welling. But I hobbled about as best I could and managed to fetch the wag- gon and both horses into a farmyard. I then noticed that the other poor beast had also been badly hit, and after taking the harness off I had to shoot that also, for it was quite evi- dent that, like its trace companion, it was unfit for further work. You will see how necessary it was to shoot the poor animals when I tell you that nearly a bucketful of blood ran away from the nose and mouth of one of them whilst I was making up my mind whether to destroy it or not. When I got off the waggon I found that I could not stand, and I was sent down to a con- vent which had been turned into a hospital. From there they sent me home as soon as they could."

div.head: THRILLING BAYONET CHARGE.
div.p: A THRILLING BAYONET CHARGE.

Private L. Williams, of the Ist Somersets, who belongs to Swansea, told our reporter that he was hit by the enemy at Ypres, about eight miles from Armentieres. The Somersets, he said, were ordered to reinforce the Inniskillens, who found themselves in a particularly tight corner and were beiug forced to retire before vastly superior numbers, having left many of their men prisoners in the hands of the enemy. "When we got up," he said, "the Irish-ers had had just about as much as they could be expected to stand. They had made a fight of it They weren't half glad to see us! Together we made a bayonet charge. Only those who have been in such a charge can have any idea of what it is like. You haven't time to think or to care about anything; you just rush straight on, shouting like mad! It didn't take us long to find that the Germans don't like our cold steel. All the time we were rushing on shrapnel was bursting over us lt was in this charge that I got wounded, a piece of shrapnel doing the trick." Private Williams went on to tell a story of treachery on the part of the Germans. "There was," he said, "a big place—a hospital, I be- lieve it had been—flying the Red Cross flag, but we got to know that the flag was a blind, and we made the discovery in an uncomfortable manner.

GERMANS MISUSE THE RED CROSS FLAG. "When we drew near Germans started firing at us from the windows and when we managed to make our way inside we discovered that the Red Cross flag was `all a blind,' for there were neither sick nor wounded on the premises. It was a dirty trick, but we made 'em sit up for it. Before we knocked off work that day," added Private Williams, "we got some of our own back, for we took three hundred prisoners. Armentieres wasn't half a sight, I can tell you. The houSes were nearly all knocked about, and it was pretty clear that the place had been looted, for clothes and all sorts of things were strewn about the streets. The German artillery fire is terrible, the shrapnel doing fearful damage, but the brutes are very faint-hearted when they see the bayonet; that makes 'em sit up and squeal." " "They're dirty beggars at fighting," added the interviewed, referring, of course, to the foe. "They have a knack of showing the white flag, and when our troops get within about a hun- dred yards of them they open a murderous fire upon them. I don't say this from hearsay; I've seen it with my own eyes and experienced it. The abuse of the white flag is so flagrant that we had orders to take no notice of it." _
The plucky private added that he was hit in the wrist, the bullet passing clean through. GERMANS FIRE ON WOUNDED.

Private Butcher, of the East Yorkshire Regi- ment, who was also in the charge at Armen- tieres had little to say about his own wound in the wrist, but condemned most strongly "the dastardly actions of the Germans in Shelling hospitals and firing on parties of wounded soldiers on the road. "We were fired on," he said, "as we went down a narrow lane, and we had to run through three ploughed fields in the teeth of heavy fire to get to the general Los- pital."

div.head: HOW GENERAL HAMILTON DIED.
div.p: HOW GENERAL HAMILTON DIED.

Private James Malone, of the Royal Scots, who received a shrapnel wound in the head in the fighting on the Aisne, spoke of the gallant manner in which General Hamilton met his death. "We were in a critical position," he said, " having lost eleven officers and 250 men in a few days. Captain asked General Hamil- ton to stay for a little time. General Hamilton agreed and was just talking to Captain Strutt, when a shell whizzed through the air and killed him. Captain Strutt was knocked down, and is suffering from concussion."

div.head: IRISHMAN'S GRIM HUMOUR.
div.p: IRISHMAN'S GRIM HUMOUR.

Irishmen are noted for finding humour in most unlikely places and things, and one com- patriot of Private Malone's, serving in the Royal Irish, certainly lived up to his country's reputation When he told the gallant private:— "You should have been here a month ago, and you would have seen the funniest sight of your life. Horses, guns, men and ammunition were all being blown up into the air together." Asked if he had seen any instances where Ger- mans had been brutal to wounded soldiers, Pte. Malone said, "No; I have not. I firmly believe that they treat our men as well as we treat theirs."

div.head: HIGHLANDER'S CONTEMPT FOR GERMAN SHELL-FIRE.
div.p: HIGHLANDER'S CONTEMPT FOR GERMAN SHELL-FIRE.

Wearing the kilts of the Highlander, Private John Lightfoot told our reporter that he had been serving with the Seaforths since the out- break of the war. He received a bullet wound in his arm at Armentieres, when his regiment were advancing on the enemy, who were in trenches about ,250 yards away. The Germans were stronger in numbers, but as he was being taken to the rear after the bullet had passed right through his arm he saw that his regiment was, to use his own' words, making " a telling impression." " What do you think of the German shell fire?" our man asked, and with a contemptible smile this sturdy Warrior replied, "It is no good at all. They might as well throw eggs at us, for all the damage they do. The Germans are good range-finders," continued Private Lightfoot, "for the simple reason that they are now retreating over ground which, when they were advancing, they had marked out." "This war," he added, by way of conclusion, "is cruel murder, but I can assure you we are having the best of it. The Germans deserve no mercy, the dirty, treacherous lot."

div.head: SAW GENERAL FINDLAY DIE.
div.p: SAW GENERAL FINDLAY DIE.

The terrors of shrapnel fire formed the chief experiences of Bombardier B. Jones, of the Royal Horse Artillery, who served with the L Battery at Mons and the Aisne. It will be remembered that though the losses of this bat- tery were considerable, it was distinguished by three of its members gaining the Victoria Cross. ' The bombardier told our reporter that the awful effects of the German shells could be judged when he said that six horses and a wag- gon had been buried in a hole made by shrap- nel. The battery he accompanied had a large experience of shrapnel fire at Mons, for they were caught unawares, and prepared to make a charge to save the guns. He was horse-holder to General Findlay, who was in command, and witnessed his death. "He (the General) was giving orders as to the position we should fake when a shell from a German siege gun burst close to him and a piece struck him in the neck. He died as he was being taken to the hospital. Fragments of the shell were scattered all over the place, and I secured one as a relic. I would not part with it on any consideration." During the second battle in which he served —that of the Aisne—the bombardier fell into the hands of the enemy, and was put under the charge of a guard in a neighbouring field. He kept a sharp look-out, however, and availed himself of an opportunity of slipping away un- observed, whilst his German companion was asleep..

Bombardier Jones had many thrilling experi- ences during the campaigns. He tells how on one occasion two small parties—British and Ger- man—met at a place occupied by the former, and had a "tussle without the gloves." The German soldiers were soon helpless, and begged the Britishers to "leave off." Another time the bombardier and a friend were standing in a barn, cooking some bacon, when a shell burst right overhead, killing the friend instantly. The farmer's legs were shattered also, but the bom- bardier was quite uninjured.

div.head: AVIATORS AND THE SPY. Brilliant Work By Our Airmen.
div.p: THE AVIATORS AND THE SPY. Brilliant Work By Our Airmen.

The principal note of interest in the stories related by Mechanic Kiddell (Royal Flying Corps), who has been incapacitated for a time by injuries received by the back-firing of a fly- ing machine motor, is the fine tribute he pays to the valuable and courageous exploits of the English aviators, with whom, he declares, the Germans cannot compare in point of bravery. On the Continent, he told a reporter, the British have many remarkably swift machines, and these, whatever the state of the weather, are flown every day. So far, they have "grounded" at least twenty of the enemy's machines, which never venture lower than 5,000 feet. Experience has taught the aviators out there to beware of German spies! Mechanic Kiddell tells how, at one time, the British airmen had run their machines into a large field just be- hind the firing line, where they were awaiting reports.

div.head: BENIEVOLENT-LOOKING HUMBUG.
div.p: A BENIEVOLENT-LOOKING HUMBUG.

Presently a benevolent-looking old gentleman strolled up; he said he was a Russian, but could not reach his own country because communica- tion was cut off. He had, he said, offered his services to the French military authorities, who had rejected them on account of his age. He intended now to volunteer for the British Army. After exchanging cigarettes with the airmen and chatting a little, he passed on to a village not far away, in which he was staying, and no sooner had he disappeared from view than the enemy commenced to shell the field—an experi- ence the aviators had not had before. They did not guess anything at the time, but moved their machines to a different position. "Half an hour later," continued the mechanic, "the pleasant stranger once more appeared, and had another chat. His departure was again succeeded by shelling.

div.head: CAUGHT AND SHOT.
div.p: CAUGHT AND SHOT.

" The neici-Ky--;(; inquired about the man, and were informed that the French had caught him signalling with a flash-light from the upper window of a house and had shot him as a spy. No one would have suspected him for a moment."

Passing on to the thrilling aerial experiences over the firing lines, Mechanic Kiddell described the tactics of a German machine which sud- denly vol-planed, after continually avoiding a British aeroplane, leaving it exposed to the enemy's guns. This manceuvre was unsuccess- ful, however, for the shell sailed to hit the machine, which was seen actually to pass through the smoke from the hostile fire, in a chase of the enemy, which was continued for miles. Mechanic Kicldell also recalled an excit- ing eight-mile drive in a motor car, which was pursued by an armoured German car, but eventually escaped, since the enemy dared run their car no farther.
No new cases have since been admitted, and none of the wounded soldiers have been dis- charged. Patrick Barry, of the 2nd Munster Fusiliers, is in a very critical condition, suffer- ing from lockjaw.

div.head: BRITON AND BELGIAN FRATERNISE Comrades in Misfortune at Haddon
div.p: BRITON AND BELGIAN FRATERNISE Comrades in Misfortune at Haddon
Court.

Scenes of great enthusiasm were witnessed outside Raddon Court Temporary Hospital on Saturday afternoon when six wounded British soldiers arrived from Manchester for treatment in thelospital by the Red Cross nurses. Their names, with descriptions of wounds, are as follows :
Private S. Leonard (Canterbury), let Batta- lion Buffs, septic wound in right arm. Rifleman A. Turton (Nottingham), 3rd Bat- talion Rifle Brigade, shrapnel wound under the heart.
Private S. Moreton (Bootle), Royal Welsh Fusiliers, shrapnel wound in each leg. . Private S. Robinson (Todmorden), 2nd Lanca- shire Fusiliers, bullet wound through left upper arm.
Private G. Nuckley (Bagshott), 2nd York and Lancaster Regiment, bullet wound in right ankle.

Private Isaac Herbert HelEwell (Sheffield), 2nd King's Own Yorkshire Light Infantry, bullet wound in the left ankle. The men seemed very cheerful when an "Examiner" man visited the hospital one day this week. Two of them were lounging in the day room with the Belgian soldiers, who are also being treated there. Our representative had no difficulty in getting the men to relate their experiences.
EXTRACTS FROM A SOLDIER'S DIARY.

I Private Leonard was very obliging and allowed ' The Examiner" representative to copy ex- tracts from an extensive diary which lie had kept. One extract reads: "We went to relieve the Fusiliers, who had lost all their officers bar I five. They left with us a dying German, who I had been shooting at the officers. Our first night in the trenches I shall never forget. The Germans opened fire on us and we returned it. Then the battle started and the noise of the rifles and shells was 'like hell on fire.' I had come off sentry-go and had been asleep, when the sergeant ordered me to get up and open fire at once. I got up and shouted for my rifle, but one of the other fellows, whose rifle was broken, had got it. I sat on the bank in the trench shaking with cold. After about five minutes I got another rifle, and began to fire away. Then I got a little higher up, and saw a long line of flame coming from the German lines. I then took aim as well as I could, and after 12 hours the firing began to slacken, and eventually died ' away. The second day was fairly quiet, except that in the afternoon two or three shells burst I over our trenches. For the following fortnight we stayed in the trenches. I caught my arm on a nail in the school where we were billeted, and blood poisoning set in." CONTEMPT FOR GERMAN RIFLE

With great pride Private Leonard showed our representative a rosary, which, he said, had been given to him by a little child. Asked what he thought about the Germans as fighters, the gallant private said: " Their artillery fire is very good, but their rifle fire is rotten." People in England, he added, did not realise the enor- mous amount of damage that had been done. If they did they would send far more men to join the colours. At the conclusion of the interview Private Leonartl gave our representative a pfennig piece, which he had got from a wounded German on the second day of the Aisne battle—" to keep as a souvenir."

div.head: WAR STORIES.
div.p: WAR STORIES.
SERGEANT BOAST'S INITIATIVE. Why He Was Mentioned in Dispatches
BRILLIANT ADVANCE GUARD.

Sergt. J. Boast, of the 2nd Battalion South Lancashire Regiment, who was mentioned in dispatches by General French, as reported in "The Examiner" last week, and who has been invalided home, writes to.us from "G" ward, Fazakerley Hospital, Liverpool, to say that several inaccuracies appeared in our account of the circumstances under which he earned recog- nition. Having explained that he has never seen Sir John French and that the incidents that led to his being mentioned did not occur at , Mons, Sergt. Boast says:— "It was during the advance, when we were driving the Germans before us. One night, I don't know the date, the 2nd Battalion South Lancashire Regiment, under the command of Major Ashworth, was marching along a road to take up an outpost position, when we were suddenly fired upon by the enemy. Before we realised what had happened Major Ashworth's horse was shot and some killed and wounded. However, the Battalion at once took up position in different parts and as best we could in the dark. It was at this time that I found that my platoon was being fired upon from a flank or rather a sort of cross-fire. Seeing some high ground close by, I took my platoon there, and finding I had a commanding position I went and gathered such men ash could and formed a fairly good firing line and beat down the enemy's fire..
"It was at this time that Captain Bagley (a very brave officer), of my battalion, not General French, came up, and asked who was in com- mand.
"1 replied, I, Sergt. Boast, am, sir.' He, Capt. Bagley, said, 'Good. Well done, Boast. Remain there until I find out tho exact posi- tions of the various companies of the Battalion.' I did so.

"The following morning our Battalion again moved out to take up a position as advance guard, when we became rather heavily engaged in a wood, and it was here again I assisted Cap- tain Bagley and my company officer, Captain Herbert, to form a three-sides square and by so doing we drove the enemy out of the wood, but it was not before we had suffered many casual- ties.

"Sergt. Britton, a well-known Warringtozi lad, was killed in this action. I saw him as we went over the ground we had been fighting on, and one would imagine he was asleep. His features were not disfigured in any way. It was on these two occasions that my name was ,brought before my C. 0., Major Ashworth, who is, and was at that time, in command."

div.head: "GERMANS A LOT OF Words Fail a Warrington Royal Irish
div.p: "GERMANS A LOT OF Words Fail a Warrington Royal Irish
Reservis-t.

The following is an extract from a letter received by Mr. E. Handley, •of the Victoria Vaults, Mersey-street, Warrington, from his brother, Private M. Handley, now serving with the 2nd Royal Irish Regiment. Private Hand- ley is a reservist; he served three and a half years with the colours in South Africa : "I don't think the war can last very long. At present the Germans are retreating all along the line. We keep capturing them in hundreds, and others who could escape give themselves up, as they are literally starving. They will give us anything for a tin of bully-beef. They must be a lot of . I can't give them a name bad enough, as the sights we see as we pass through the towns and villages are awful, beyond description. Old men, old women and children are lying dead in the streets. Their chief aim seems to be to destroy churches and hospitals, where the wounded are now lying. "We commenced the fight at Mons on the 23rd August, along with the Middlesex Regi- ment. We, the 2nd Regiment, were the first Infantry to open the ball—we lost terribly- -600 officers and men, and the Middlesex lost about the same. We retreated to a place •called Caurdry on the 26th and got another smashing. We are advancing now and have been in the trenches for fourteen days without a break.

" We occasionally see an English newspaper, but it is weeks old when we get it. I have just been reading a few letters from fellows who say they were at Mons. They write of playing marbles in the trenches with shrapnel shells and of having guessing competitions as to where the next shell will drop. This is all 'swank.' I can assure you, and my regiment will bear out what I say, that it is a miracle anyone was left alive. I saw more shells fired on that Sunday then were fired during the whole three years I served in the South African War. The German Artillery is great, but their Infantry are not worth taking into account."

SOLDIERS' RATIONS STOLEN. At. the Borough Police Court on Monday Ed- ward Kelly and Patrick Glynn, both of whom have no fixed abode, were charged with having been on the enclosed premises of Orford Bar- racks for an unlawful purpose.—The Chief Con- stable asked for a remand and said that the prisoners went to a corporal on duty at the en- trance to the barracks and represented that they wanted to see a man who had joined the Con- naught Rangers. The corporal told them he would be at his depot, and the men went away. They were seen to be acting suspiciously at the back of the barracks. They went to the dining hall and took their seats for the purpose of hav- ing tea. Taxed by the sergeant, they again lied and were handed over to the police. Observation had been kept on characters of that description hanging round the barracks. Prisoners had gone in with the intention of stealing rations in- tended for those who were brave enough to join the Army. Rations for 30 men had been missed in one day, and a number of overcoats had gone. —One; of the prisoners stated that he had come to join the Army on Saturday.—The Chief: You did not say that yesterday.—Prisoners were re- manded for seven days.

"I was, with others, crossing a ploughed field, when a shrapnel shell burst about ten yards away on my left, knock- ing my rifle from my grasp. I was spun round and sent down a little slope into a ditch. Here," he added, "I waited until dusk, when I made my way to a field hospital. At one of the hospitals where my injury was attended to, the members of the R.A.M.C. were particularly good to the wounded. Their sympathy was not uttered; it was practical, for they gave their own rations to the injured, at a time when they did not know when the next supply would reach them."

Referring to the German artillery fire, Pte. Robinson said that he did not for a single moment believe that it was as good as that of the British. The only difference was that the cternians indulged in wore of it.

div.head: In Memoriam Peals of Bells.
div.p: In Memoriam Peals of Bells.
Muffled peals will be rung on the bells of the local churches. to-morrow, All Saints' Day, in memory of those who have fallen in the war. Trees for Manchester-road. _

The Town Hall, Parks and Baths Committee, with the approval of the Town Council, have given instructions to their head gardener to plant suitable trees in the widened portion of Manchester-road. Market Prices.

Wheat was firmer and in good demand at Warrington Market on Wednesday, Sa. sd. to ss. 6d. per 781 b. being offered for good sound English wheat. Oats were a little easier at 3s. to 3s. lid per bushel of 451 b. Straw, a little better, sold at 20s. and 21s. per ton. F.o.r. XX flour fetched 335. per 280 lb., and bran sold at is. id. per 201 b.

div.head: Leather Workers Wanted.
div.p: Leather Workers Wanted.

According to the current issue of "The Leather Trades Review" employment in the Warrington district in this particular trade "is very good; in fact one of the troubles felt is a shortage of labour. Whilst there are always a certain number of men of the casual type, it is extremely difficult to get hold of any men with tanyard experience."

Week's Crop of Infectious Cases. During the week ending October 24th the Medical Officer of Health (Dr. G. W. N. Joseph) was notified of 39 cases of scarlet fever, three of diphtheria, eight of tuberculosis, one of enteric fever, and four of erysipelas. On the date mentioned there were 128 patients in the Borough Hospital, 92 of whom were suffering from scarlet fever, three from enteric fever, and 11 from diphtheria.
Death of Former Mayor's Sister-in-law. _

The death took place on Sunday of Mrs. Chrimes, who for the past ten years had been licensee of the Roebuck Hotel, Bridge-street. The deceased lady, who had attained the patriarchal age of 77, was a member of a well- known Warrington family. She was the widow of the late Mr. Peter Chrimes, and sister-in-law of a former Mayor of Warrington, Mr. Joseph Chrimes, who held office in 1855-6-7.

Present at the Council Meeting. The Mayor (Alderman Peacock) presided over the meeting of the Town Council held on Tues- day evening, and there were also present :—The Deputy Mayor (Dr. Joseph), Aldermen Bolton, Tinnion, James Evans, Pierpoint, Smethurst and Bennett, and Councillors, Broadhurst, Roberts, Dickenson, Gough, Craik, Hawthorn, Pember- ton, Lasbford, Cunnington, Chrimes, Chantler, Archer, Firth Lindley, Barton, Osborne, Skel- land, Shaw and Menshall, with the Town Clerk (Mr. J. Lyon Whittle).

div.head: £7500 for Improving Buttermarketstreet.
div.p: £7500 for Improving Buttermarket- street.

The minutes of the Paving and Sewerage Com- mittee submitted to the Town Council at their meeting on Tuesday evening, and approved by them, contained the following item :—" The Borough Surveyor having reported upon the paving of Buttermarket-street, it was resolved that Buttermarket-street be paved with litho- falt blocks, and that application be made to the Local Government Board for their sanction to the borrowing of the sum of £7,540, for the cost of paving Buttermarket-street ; the new passage behind Buttermarket-street ; Upper Bank-street, Factory-lane, and Orford-road.

Catholics and Belgians. The Catholics of Warrington have not been slow in taking their part in fulfilling the national duty of providing for the Belgian refugees, most of whom are, of course, co-re- ligionists. A committee, formed to carry out this pur- pose, consists of the following members drawn from the five parishes: Father N. V. Wilson, 0.5.8. (chairman and treasurer), Messrs. Felix Maginn, E. Massey, A. M. Crowe (hon. secre- tary), Misses Dolan (St. Mary's), K. Caldwell (Our Lady's), Mesdames Liston (St. ltary's), T. Bunch, Marsh (St. Alban's), Morris, Walsh (St. Benedict's), Crowe and Gibbins (Sacred Heart), together with the local clergy. Through the agency of this committee an appeal was made to all Catholics throughout the town. The response has been most gratifying, and a considerable sum has been already raised. . .

Out of this sum a substantial amount has been allocated to the Penketh Committee for the maintenance of the refugees at Hall Nook. Be- sides this, very considerable contributions in furniture and in kind have been made to the same establishment. The committee intend to continue their efforts and hope to be able to render assistance to other similar establish- ments for refugees, as the need may arise and opportunity offer. The present representatives of the Catholic Committee on the Hall Nook Committee are Rev. Father W. Rockliffe, Mr. Felix Maginn and Miss Dolan.

Bowling Prizes for Loyal Shepherds. The prizes won in the bowling main organised in connection with the Warrington District of the Loyal Order of Ancient Shepherds (A.U.) were distributed at the "Late Spring Rose" Lodge, Barley Mow, on Saturday, by the Mayor (Alderman Peter Peacock), who is an honorary member of the Order. The recipients were : 1, Richard Warburton; 2, Arthur War- burton; 3, Harry Higham; 4, W. J. Dainteth; 5, Wm. Sanders; 6, W. Ellison; 7, Pater Antro- bus ; 8, Jos. Ashton; 9, Peter L. Edgar; 10, Thos. Roberts; 11, Jas. Poole; 12, John Mather; 13, H. Savage; 14, H. Johnson; 15, H. Twigs; and 16, Isaac Mills. Consolation prizes went to the following :- 1, Fredk. Dale; 2, Thos. Atherton; 3, E. T. Rogers; 4, Samuel Leigh; 5, J. T. Harrison; 6, Thos. Potter; 7, J. Holcroft; and 8, Jas. Elli- son. A hearty vote of thanks was accorded his Worship, on the proposition of Bro. Peter L. Edgar, seconded by Bro. Jas. Parr, and, in acknowledgment, Alderman Peacock spoke of the good work performed by the Friendly Socie- ties of the country. Votes of thanks were ac- corded to the donors of the prizes, and also to the Chairman (Bro. J. Fulton-Smith), and dur- ing the evening the toast of "The West Lanca- shire Centralised State District" was honoured, Bro. H. W. Townley (secretary of the State Dis- trict) responding.—Bro. Brobbins entertained the company with a Musical selection, Bro. Johnson sang a song, and Bro. Jos. Ashton gave a recitation in the Lancashire dialect. '

div.head: Alderman Bennett and the Bridge Inscription.
div.p: Alderman Bennett and the Bridge Inscription.

At the monthly meeting of the Town Council on Tuesday evening Alderman Bennett called attention to the following ininute of the Bridges Committee: "That the Chairman, Deputy- Chairman, Mr. Alderman Tinnion and Council- lor Joseph be appointed a sub-committee, to settle the inscription on the panel for the north- east pylon of the bridge." He wanted to know whether the Council would have the opportunity of approving the proposed inscription, or were the committee to have plenary powers. He felt that the inscription should take the form of some suitable historic record pointing out that there had been a bridge on the site for hundreds of years, and that it had been associated with many historic events. Such an inscription would add to the dignity of the town, and would be a source of interest. So far as he could learn there were ono or two things on the proposed inscription that, to say the least of them, were unfortunate, whilst there were omissions; no reference, for instance,, being made to the par- ticular method of construction, nor, he believed, was it proposed to mention the name of Mr. J. Mansfield Cobb, to whose energy and constant attention much was due. He did not want this inscription to be a case of the "Three Tailors of Tooley-street " over again—the Cor- poration were the only people who seemed to be of any account. Ile proposed that the minute be referred back. Councillor Broadhurst seconded, but subse- quently withdrew his support to Alderman Ben- nett's proposition, on learning that the name of the late Alderman Forshaw, who played an iMPortant part in bringing about the widening of the bridge, would be included among the names on the inscription., Alderman 'Bunion said the town would have a good bridge when it was finished, and why on earth should not the names of the lot of them be put on it? (Laughter.) Alderman Bolton agreed, saying he. would rather have his name on a bridge than a grave- stone. For the want of a seconder, Alderman Ben- nett's amendment fell through.

div.head: AVeek's_Births and Deaths.
div.p: A AVeek's_Births and Deaths.

During the week ending October 24th 41 chil- dren were born in Warrington, as against 42 in the corresponding period of last year. The deaths numbered 18, the comparative figure being 22. Seven of the people who passed away were over 65 years of age.

Reason of Our Semi-dark Streets. In accordance with the requirements of the Defence of the Realm Act the Warrington streets are not now fully lighted. The electric lights have been reduced, but there has been no appreciable reduction in the number of lighted gas lamps. Present for Bible Class Teacher.

An enjoyable social was held by the Senior Men's Class of the Wycliffe Sunday School on Thursday evening in the Memorial Buildings. The occasion was the presentation to Mr. C. Eccles—who has retired from his position as their teacher, after nearly 30 years' service— of a large and suitably inscribed and framed photograph of the class. Many interesting speeches and items of entertainment were given.

Tontine Club Supper. About 60 members and friends of the Mersey Hotel Tontine Club assembled on the invitation of Mr. Burke at the headquarters, Mersey- street, on Monday evening to partake of a hot- pot supper. Afterwards a smoking concert was held, Mr. J. Howard, president of the club, being in the chair. The toasts honoured included that of the Allies. Several musical items were rendered, the artistes being Messrs. Houlton (concertina solos), H. Greening, Vose, A. Woods, W. Woods, Robinson, Burke, Raferty, Guest and 11. Blinkensop (songs).

Injured by Transport AVaggon. Whilst cycling along Sankey-street on Thurs- day noon, Henry Mortimer (16), 50, Gorsey- lane, employed by Messrs. Crosfield's, met with a serious accident The wheel of his cycle was caught in the tram line, and he was thrown under an Army transport waggon, which was Passing through the town with a number of others. The driver of the waggon applied his brakes and stopped the motor, but not before the front wheel of the waggon had crushed the Youth's leg badly. Mortimer is being attended for a lacerated leg at the Infirmary and is pro- gressing satisfactorily.—The bicycle was com- pletely smashed.

Nearly Seventy Years a Druid. The funeral of the late Mr. Wm. Barlow, a well-known Friendly Society worker, who re- sided at 39, Bewsey-street, took place at Hill Cliffe on Thursday. Mr. Barlow, who had reached the advanced age of 85, had been a member of the Druids for 67i years, and had been the treasurer of the Widows' and Orphans' Fund in connection with that Society since its inception. He had occupied every position it was possible to hold in the Order in this dis- trict. Amongst Mr. Barlow's recollections were the celebrations in the town on the occasion of Queen Victoria's coronation. Prior to the in- terment a short service was conducted by the Rev. Hugh Williamson in the Bold-street Wesleyan Chapel, with :which the deceased gen- tleman has been connected for about 60 years. The chief mourners were: Miss Barlow and Mrs. I. E. Barlow (daughter and daughter-in-law), Messrs. W., I. E., and J. Barlow (sons), the Misses Gladys, Dorothy, and Nancy Barlow (grandchildren), Mrs. Wilde, and Messrs. H. Wilson, B. Warburton, W. Wright, S. Rowe, E. Bradshaw, W. B. Forshaw, Levi Richardson, T. Cooper, and Coleman. Others present at the graveside were Messrs. W. Silcock, T. Baxter, F. Pendlebury, J. Cooper, C. E. Toft, S. Carter, and J. E. Hannan.

div.head: MR. J. J. WEBSTER
div.p: MR. J. J. WEBSTER
Death of Engineer of New Warrington Bridge.

Just on the eve of the completion of a task which was specially dear to his heart by reason of his local connections, Mr. John J. Webster, the engineer for the new Warrington Bridge, has passed away, his death occurring with pain- ful suddenness at his residence in Streatham, near London, yesterday morning. The deceased gentleman was born in Warring- ton in 1845, and was the son of the late Alder- man S. M. Webster, a former, Mayor of the town, whilst he was a grandson of the late Mr. John Webster, who had the honour of being a member of Warrington's first Borough Council. The bridge now being erected over the Mersey will, when completed, furnish a striking local monument to Mr. Webster:s genius as a bridge designer, a branch of engineering and architec- tural work in which lie excelled; indeed, he enjoyed a world-wide reputation, as numerous bridges in many parts of the globe attest. One of his triumphs was the Transporter Bridge which connects Widnes and Runcorn. EARLY DAYS AND FIRST TRIUMPHS. Mr. Webster was articled to a Manchester firm of engineers in the early 'sixties, with whom he remained ten years, spending the last four years of that period in the capacity of head draughtsman. Engagements with the authori- ties of Aberdeen Harbdur and Hull Docks fol- lowed, and he then became connected with the Ashbury Carriage Company, for whom he de- signed a number of bridges in India. His suc- cesses in that direction led to his appointment as chief bridge designer to Messrs. Thomas Brassey and Co., and whilst in their service he had the care of hundreds of bridges of various kinds, also of the construction of the great Landing Stage at Liverpool. Deciding to launch out on his own, Mr. Web- ster commenced a private practice as a bridge builder in Liverpool, but he soon transferred to London, where he established a high reputation as a consulting engineer. Amongst the structures he designed and car- ried out are the Northwich Town Bridge, the Portsmouth Bascule Bridge, Littlehampton Swing Bridge, and the new Conway Suspension Bridge, to mention but a few of the best known of many. He also enjoyed a great reputation as a designer of piers, and among others built those at Dover, Bangor, Minehead, Llandudno, Menai Bridge, Penmaenmawr, and Egremont.

DESIGNED THE BIG WHEEL. In open competition Mr. Webster was placed either first or second on fourteen occasions. *The Big Wheel, which for so long formed the chief attraction at Earl's Court, was a creation of his brain, and more recently he designed the Stadium, in which the Olympic Sports were held some few years ago. The constructional work of four of the largest buildings at the Franco-British Exhibition was also carried out from his designs, and quite recently he com- pleted the plans of a large transporter bridge for South America. -

Mr. Webster had several 'narrow escapes. He was nearly dropped from the top of the Big Wheel through the carelessness of workmen dur- ing his inspection, and on another occasion he came near to being drowned whilst engaged in diving operations at Hull. He often expressed to Warrington friends his desire to see the local bridge completed, and his pride in being asked to exercise his skill in the interests of his native town. The late Ur. Webster leaves a widow, but no family.

div.head: 350 RECRUITS STILL WANTED._
div.p: 350 RECRUITS STILL WANTED._
The recruits towards the 700 men needed from Warrington to complete the reserve battalion of the Territorials, now number 350, so that half of the number is still required.

div.head: ER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 31, CALL ro ARMS.
div.p: ER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 31, CALL ro ARMS.
MORE MEN WANTED.

Lord Kitchener is calling for more and more men. The safety of the Empire demands that all available men should forthwith be placed at the disposal of the War Office, which is now well organised and prepared to meet all de- mands made upon it by any number of recruits. Lord Kitchener has sent a notice to the works in Warrington saying that those who are carry- ing out the great work of providing the Army with supplies and equipment, are doing their duty for their King and country equally with those who have joined the Army for service in the field.
If men cannot be spared from the works there are many others, especially in country districts around, who are available and who would make splendid fighting material.

THE LATE MIDSHIPMAN DICKSON. -- Rev. W. Braceeamp and a Father's Brave Appeal. Addressing the new Reserve Battalion of the Warrington Territorials at St. Paul's Church on Sunday morning, the Chaplain (the Rev. W. Bracecamp) read the letter that appeared in our columns last week from Dr. Dickson, of Marlow, Bucks, the father of Midshipman Dickson, one of the victims of the H.M.S. Hawke disaster, and the brother of Mrs. John Crosfield. It was, said the reverend gentleman, the finest letter he had read for a long time, for it showed that the father's patriotism, notwith- standing the loss of his son, was as keen as ever, because he appealed to parents "over his son's watery grave," not to hesitate to send their boys into the battle line. As long as England possessed such men as Dr. Dickson, England was safe from her enemies, but if she had half- hearted and lukewarm men no one could say what the consequences would be.

div.head: "MY COUNTRY NEEDS ME."
div.p: "MY COUNTRY NEEDS ME."
RCN'. W. Bracecamp Says "Au Revoir " To Ills Flock.
OFF TO THE FRONT.

Two Warrington chaplains—the Rev. William Bracecamp, vicar of St. Paul's, and the Rev. H. F. S. Collier, vicar of Christ Church, Padgate, have, as we announced last week, been ordered to join their regiments, in which they will rank as major and captain respectively. A large congregation, on Sunday evening, attended the last service which their Vicar, the Rev. W. Bracecamp, expected to conduct at St. Paul's, before his departure for the front, where he will see active service with the Warrington Terri- torial Battalion, to which he acts as chaplain. Good Wishes from Wycliffe.

In the course of this service Mr. Bracecamp made a statement, which he prefaced by saying that he wished first to read a letter he had re- ceived from the Rev. T. T. James, pastor of the Wycliffe Congregational Church. The letter
ran:-

" Dear Mr. Bracecamp,—Very heartily my church and congregation wish to convey to you their good wishes and prayers, and to express the hope that as you go to the front you may be shielded from danger, and by the goodness of God be brought back safely again. We also wish for your church during your"absence every prosperity, and the constant sense of the Divine presence, and we pray that all the good work which is being done at St. Paul's may be fully maintained while you are away. "This message I was commissioned to forward you at our service this morning, and you will let me add my personal word of good-will. We shall not forget you. " With every good wish, _

div.head: "Yours very sincerely, " T. T. JAMES." A Message of Cheer for Tommy.
div.p: "Yours very sincerely, " T. T. JAMES." A Message of Cheer for Tommy.

The Vicar said that to receive such a letter, and to see so large a congregation, despite the unfavourable weather, almost overwhelmed him, and made it hard for him to say what he wished to say. There were, he knew, conflict- ing opinions amongst them—his best friends— as to his duty; they were candid in the matter, and spoke to him honestly, and he appreciated their honesty and their candour. He received one morning two important letters. The first was from one of the leading Nonconformists in the town, and urged him to remain behind, look- ing after those at home, for the sake of his con- gregation. He received the other by the same post. It was from a dear soldier, who had written it in the trenches, with the bullets fly- ing all around him. In that letter he said that, if there was one thing he wished to receive more than anything else, it was a message of cheer. The writer had once been a regular attender at that church. "These Soldier Lads Want Me."

"Yon see my difficulty," continued the Vicar. "I feel these soldier lads want me, and that I should be able to comfort them in their hours of sorrow and trouble, if only I went on active service. And so I am going. I shall go with my own battalion, and I promise the mothers, sisters and sweethearts of my lads that I will do my level best to cheer them up. My coun- try needs me. I am ordered to go! Therefore, whether it may be for a long or for a short period, I go; and you may depend upon it that I shall do my duty." Mr. Bracecamp concluded his statement by paying a tribute to the "wonderful ability" of the Rev. E. Downham, his colleague, and ex- pressed the hope that the congregation would "back up" Mr. Downham, whilst he (the speaker) was away. They would, he trusted, back up the finances of the church also; he was sure that his parish would not be neglected after his twelve years' service in it. THE TWO CLERICS LEAVE WARRINGTON

• Yesterday morning Mr. Braeeeamp left War- rington from Bank Quay Station by the 9.30 a.m. train, bound for the war station at which he joined the South Lancashire Division. The Rev. H. F. S. Collier also left the town yesterday morning to join his battalion of the " Liverpools," after receiving all good wishes for his safe return. Preaching at Padgate on Sunday evening, Mr. Collier took for his text: "Come; and they all began with one consent to make excuses." People were apt to forget, he said, what they owed to this country, and they must respond to the call now they were needed for her defence. The Rev. E. E. Chamberlain, of Rainhill, has been appointed curate-in-charge during the Vicar's absence. He will commence his duties on the Bth of November.

div.head: WELSH PASTOR FOR WELSH TROOPS.
div.p: WELSH PASTOR FOR WELSH TROOPS.

The Rev. It. Parry Jones, pastor of the Welsh Church, Crosfield-street, Warrington, having asked the church to relieve him for a month. left for Northampton last Friday to minister to the Welsh troops stationed there: few friends of the church subscribed and got to- gether a parcel of 150 Welsh Testaments, which, with 75 granted by the British and Foreign Bible Society, made a total of 225, for Mr. Jones to give out to the troops. Mr. Jones is a very popular missiongr, and we understand he is al- ready making ebod progress, and is to be con- gratulated upon offering his services at his own expense, which means a great sacrifice.

P.S.A. BROTHERHOOD'S PRAYERS. Ou behalf of his society, Mr. Benjamin Far- rar, secretary of the Wycliffe P.S.A., also for- warded to Mr. Bracecamp on Sunday a letter, in which he communicated the Brotherhood's sincere wishes. They prayed that God would shield him and protect him, and that He would bring him back in safety to all his dear people, giving victory to the cause of justice and right.

div.head: AMBULANCE .MEN ON DUTY.
div.p: AMBULANCE .MEN ON DUTY.

On Saturday a further body of the members of the Warrington Corps of the St. John Ambu- lance Brigade left the town for service at the First Western General Hospital, Fazakerley. They were Messrs. Wilmore, Ambrose, Kenning, Pritchard, Saunders and Walker, most of whom were members of the team which won the Crosfield Shield last year, while four of them took part in the National Competition in Lon- don laSt April. Three other members of the local corps—Messrs. Wilkinson, V. Raiford and J. A. Makin—left , for the same hospital on Tuesday morning.
HOSPITAL SHIP WRECKED.

Terrible scenes were witnessed yesterday off the Yorkshire coast at Whitby. The British hospital ship Rohilla was wrecked in a gale when bound for France with nurses, doctors, and ambulance men on board.

div.head: NOVEMBER ELECTIONS.
div.p: NOVEMBER ELECTIONS.
Labour Men Force a Contest IN THREE WARDS.

The November elections will take place on Monday, when three wards—St. John's, Bewsey and Orford—will be contested by the Labour party. In the other six wards the retiring mem- bers will be returned unopposed. The Liberals and Conservatives agreed to allow all retiring councillors a walk-over this year, so that there should be no strife during the period of the war; but the Trades and Labour Council decided to fight three wards, so that the proposed truce is to that extent broken. The sitting members are Councillor Lashford (C.), Councillor Dickenson (L.), and Councillor Halliwell (L.).
CONTESTS. The nominations are as follows:— ST. JOHN'S WARD.

Lashford, Fredk. Thomas, off-licence holder, 98, Battersby-lane. Proposers: W. A. McKee, B. Percival, A. Glover and S. Brown. Seconders: Joseph Taylor, T. Ice, G. D. Hotghton and W. Critchley. Helsby, John, insurance agent, 18, Hazel- street. Proposers: James Clare Wilkinson, James Jackson, Frederick Smith and Alfred Anderson. Lau-rinson, John Holden, Mary Robinson, Dominick McKay and Frank Boyle. Seconders: Josiah Richards, Thos. Hall, Wil- liam Green, Walter Ernest Brampton, E. Elwell, Thos. div.head: I WONDER!
div.p: I WONDER!
To the Editor of "The Examiner."

• Sir,—l wonder what is the subject matter that has cropped up at the present juncture to render it necessary for a contested election for the Counail? What are the qualifications of Mr. Dukes and his colleagues? Are they better than the representatives they are trying to supplant? Ido not think so. I think if the three sitting members are defeated, three of the best men, from the working man's point of view, will be lost to the interests of working men in general and trade unionism in par- ticular. I hope all will rally to the support of the three retiring councillors, for what they are we do know; but what Mr. Dukes and his friends may be is as yet a question of surmise.— Yours, &c., PHIL SQUOD.

div.head: BROKEN TRUCE.
div.p: THE BROKEN TRUCE.
To the Editor of "The Examiner."

Sir,—Let me tell Mr. Dukes at the outset that his inference that the Liberals and Tories of Warrington are trying to make capital out of the war is an accusation which cannot be sub- stantiated. The Liberals and Tories, when re- quested by Parliament to stop all controversy during the war, declared a truce, and if it had not been for the Socialist party there would not have been a fight of any description this November. Mr. Dukes tells us that the Labour Council is responsible for the candidature of himself and his satellites, and if there is any credit it must be given to them. What a satire upon the Labour Council! I presume that the decision that was arrived at last July, when Mr. Dukes tells us he and his friends were first chosen to stand, has since been ratified by the Labour Council, and they are still willing to run Labour candidates, despite the fact that war has broken out in the meantime. If that is so, I should like to ask whether the Labour Council has con- sulted the individual members of the Unions which they serve, whether they, by a majority, favour running Labour candidates and causing party strife during the grave national crisis through which we are passing. If they have not done so, they are taking •upon themselves a very grave responsibility, and if the members of the affiliated Unions are levied to meet the expenses of these contests, in the same manner as the Labour members of Parliament are sup- ported, the members of the Labour Council should not consider it too late even now to get at the real opinion of those they serve. Let me make a suggestion, or rather a chal- lenge to Mr. Dukes, that he, with his colleagues, visits every member of the Unions affiliated with the Labour Council in the three wards they are contesting, and withdraws, along with his friends, if a majority refuse their support. I venture to predict that Mr. Dukes will not ' trust his fellow trade unionists and that the poll will declare that he has not their support. Mr. Dukes tells us that the Labour party were not consulted in the matter of a party truce being declared owing to the war. I would inform Mr. Dukes that the Liberal, Tory and Labour parties in Parliament declared the truce and requested the parties all over the country to stop hostilities during the war. The Liberal and Tory agents .here appealed to the Labour party by letter for a truce, and the running of municipal candidates is tantamount to refusal. Does Mr. Dukes deny this? Mr. Dukes, in his election address, says "Union is strength," and he straightaway shows how disunited lie would have us appear in face of a national crisis. It is a character- istic weakness of the majority of that particu- lar type of Socialist, of which Mr. Dukes is a , sample. They preach comradeship and prac- tise snobbery; they ask for union and show how they lack the very elements of their gospel in the management of their own party; they talk and rave about helping the downtrodden and weak, but when they have the opportunity of doing a little to help the good work of caring for the remnants of that downtrodden little Belgian nation, they spend money on municipal elec- tions. .
Let every man who puts "Love of country first" record his vote against these disturbers of our national unity. VINCIT AMOR PATRI2E.

To the Editor of "The Examiner." Sir,—Your correspondent, " V.A.P.," has kindly sent me a copy of his letter to your paper, for which I am duly grateful. Its contents are a fair example of the opinions held by the aver- age Liberals or Tories, who are usually kept in the dark of the inner workings of their party. Every time I read a letter from these misguided sheep I feel pained at their simplicity. No, " V.A.P.," it was not the wicked Socialists who forced the election this time ; many dele- gates who are just Labour men, • pressed the matter forward at the Council meeting. You I seek to make capital by cheap satire through making reference to me and my satellites. ' I would rather be the central orb in the universe of Labour than the Ass of Balaara, when the sword of justice is about to fall. The Trades Council decided to fight. lam its servant, and as such accept its mandate. The rank and file have a voice in the Labour movement, and through their delegates the
