div.head: WAR ITEMS.
div.p: WAR ITEMS.

POLICEMEN WITH THE COLOURS. The Watch Committee reported to the Town Council at their meeting on Tuesday that P.S. Woodland and P.C. Cooke have joined the colours, and that the last-named has since got married. In each case it was recommended by the committee, and agreed to by the Council, that 15s. per week be allowed.
CROSFIELD'S TORCHLIGHT PROCESSION.

During the torchlight parade by Crosfield's Band and Boy Scouts on Saturday evening the handsome amount of £l6 14s. was collected. The whole amount has been paid to the Borough Treasurer for the local Soldiers' Tobacco Fund. A number of pipes and cigar- ettes was also given. £1,300 FOR LOCAL SERVICE MEN'S FAMILIES.

The work of relief by the Soldiers' and Sailors' Wives' and Families' Association con- tinues at the Parr Hall. This week assistance has been afforded in over 1,500 cases. This has been the figure for several weeks now. Over .21,300 has now been paid out locally.

div.head: WAR RESTRICTS WATER TRAFFIC. _
div.p: WAR RESTRICTS WATER TRAFFIC. _

The Rivers Committee reported to the Town Council on Tuesday evening that they had re- ceived a report from the Corporation's repre- sentative on the Upper Mersey Navigation Com- mission (Mr. R. T. Fairclough), which set forth that " the accounts received were £2OO less than last year, chiefly owing to the war." The report added: " The channels are good into Widnes Dock, West Bank Dock, and the Old Quay Lock. There is no channel into the Bridgewater or Weston Locks."

div.head: WHAT THE CORPORAL FOUND.
div.p: WHAT THE CORPORAL FOUND.

At the Borough Police Court on Tuesday, Joseph Mullen, of no fixed abode, was remanded for seven days on a charge of having been found on the enclosed premises of Orford Barracks for an unlawful purpose.—The Chief Constable said that a corporal at the barracks had found the man in his room that morning. Prisoner had the corporal's trousers in his possession, and when taxed with regard to his conduct he said he was in the same regiment as the corporal. That was quite false.—Prisoner said he had come from Manchester for some money due to him.

div.head: LANCE-CORPORAL'S LOST LEG.
div.p: LANCE-CORPORAL'S LOST LEG.

The friends of Lance-Corporal Gerald Ash- ton, of the South Lancashire Regiment, whose home is at 67, Forster-street, Warrington, have received intimation that he has been wounded, a piece of shrapnel striking him in the back and travelling downward to his leg, inflicting such injuries that the limb had to be ampu- tated.
Lance-Corporal Ashton, Who is only 22 years of age, is at present in hospital in France. Before becoming a soldier he served an appren- ticeship with Mr. Clare, painter and decorator, Forster-street.

THEATRE MANAGER AND THE BELGIANS The "Daily Telegraph" has organised a special fund called the King Albert Christmas Fund, for the benefit of the distressed Belgian people. Among the subscribers thereto is Mr. A. M. Loader, the manager of the Royal Court Theatre, Warrington, who wrote to the "Tele- graph" as follows:—" Many calls are made upon the theatrical profession just now, but my wife and I agree that we must not be among the defaulters to the King Albert Christmas Fund, and herewith I enclose our humble offering of twenty-five shillings from each of us. To-day I came across an autograph letter from the late Sir Henry Irving, which I purchased some time ago from a needy member of the profession. I herewith enclose it, and hope some collector may think it worth while to purchase, the pro- ceeds, of course, to go to the same fund."

div.head: PENKETH MAN AMONG THE _SLAIN.
div.p: PENKETH MAN AMONG THE _SLAIN.

The name of Private Charles Gandy, of the Ist Battalion of the South Lancashire Regiment, who made his home with his sister, Mrs. Arthur Watkins, of 236, Thelwall-lane, Warrington, has appeared in the list of those reported killed in action at Nalley Aure Aisne, between Septem- ber 19th and 29th. The gallant private was only 26 years of age, and was the son of Mr. and the late Mrs. John Gandy, of Penketh, in which township he was well known. He com- pleted his service in the Regular Army in January last—when he came home after a spell of duty in India—and was a member of the Reserve when the war broke out. Prior to being called up be worked for Messrs. Pierpoint and Bryant at .Latchford.

The last message his sister had from him was a postcard, dated September 18th, in which he said :—" We are having some very bad weather at present The shells have been dropping all around us for the last few days. It is not very nice and I wish it was all over."

div.head: COMFORTS FOR SOLDIERS.
div.p: COMFORTS FOR SOLDIERS.
Working* Parties Send Further Contributions.

Mrs. Fisher, honorary secretary of the War- rington Nursing Division of the St. John Ambu- lance Brigade, has received a letter of acknow- ledgment and thanks from Tier Majesty the Queen (president) and ladies of the Order for a consignment of various articles of useful clothing. MORE MITTENS WANTED.

Mrs. Edelsten reports another gratifying " haul" of clothing at the Town Hall on Thurs- day. Large parcels came from the Parish Church Working Party, the Penketh and San- key Working Party, Mrs. Mitchell, Mrs. Brace- camp, Mrs. Lindley, the Training College, the Women's Tariff Reform League, and the War- rington Branch of the National Union of Women's Suffrage Societies, per Mrs. Robert Pemberton.

_ Four substantial sacks of clothing were sent to Fazakerley Hospital, to the Mine Sweepers in the North Sea, to the Indian troops, and to Lady Barr for the hospitals at the Front. Warm mittens, without thumbs, ten inches long, are much needed.

div.head: NOVEMBER ELECTlONS—continued.
div.p: NOVEMBER ELECTlONS—continued.
Council register their views. It is not a matter of one or two wealthy patrons deciding for them. Fortunately the money bugs have no influence here.

Where the money will come from for the elec- tions is not the business of anyone outside the party. Those inside know quite well; at all events it will not be tainted with plutocratic stigma. It will represent honest desire. You ask if I deny that the Liberal and Tory parties offered a truce? I do not deny they offered what they thought a truce, but we do object to them meeting and asking us to accept their deliberations arrived at in our absence.

As a party we wanted representation. We are told by those who monopolise every seat that we cannot obtain representation only by contest, but they think we should defer our claim. We knew this before we asked; it only remained to convince the rank and file. The other people have done it for us. You speak of a national truce between Liberal, Tory and Labour. You might as well talk of mixing oil and water. Why the agitation to-day for the £1 per week minimum, if we can trust these people? "Don't come it." Whose leg are you trying to pull, you Simon .pure? Do you think we can forget history in a day? Yes, my action is characteristic of the Social- ist; therein lies the trouble. We can't be got at. lam proud to be a Socialist, more particu- larly now than ever before. The huge blunder "V.A.P." has made is in assuming that municipal activities can be sus- pended even during national crisis. As I have pointed out in the "Labour Gazette," Labour will require its men at a time when elections are impossible. We advise that preparation be made how. The question of Belgian relief is a national question; if it were municipal, then the support should come from the rates, and not depend on private charity. The very sug- gestion of postponing municipal contests so as to send money to the Belgian relief rankles of party cant. It is well to remind those who accept the views expressed by "V.A.P." that immediately hostilities broke out the Mora- torium was passed, granting fmancial interests security. This will cost the nation, according to the "Times." anything from £50,000,000 to ...t100,000,000. The relief of distress of the poor' including the refugees, is to depend upon private charity. When are we going to get out of the rut of charity-mongering? • _

You ask all who put love of country first to vote against the Labour candidates. I ask all who put the welfare of the people before flag worship and false patriotism to use their in- telligence.—Yours,
CHAS. DUKES.

div.head: TO IRONWORKERS.
div.p: TO IRONWORKERS.
Associated Iron and Steel Workers of Great Britain.

OUR DUTY DURING TRZ WAR. The following piece of good advice has been sent out by Mr. Jas. Cox, general secretary of the Associated Iron and Steel Workers o! Great . Britain. The suggestion that our workers should work to win while our soldiers are fighting to win will be acted upon to the full. It i& a com- plete victory we are striving for this time.

Fellow members,—lt is with confidence we • make this appeal to you regarding the duty of every workman during the present great war. In the first place we would urge you to think of all that the war and its results meaa to us as workmen. Its causes are too well known and need no recapitulation, but its effects are, we fear, too little realised. Either we must win for the triumph of political and industrial freedom, or be crushed by a military despotism—beneath whose iron heel all industrial freedom will be utterly destroyed. Thousands of our fellow workmen throughout the iron and steel trade have left home, friends, good positions, comparative comfort, to suffer hardships, risking life and limb for their coun- try's sake, and to hurl back the German despot, whose great desire is to ruin and conquer this great Empire. Our armies will be successful, however bitter and long the struggle may be; all honour to these gallant comrades of ours who rushed to the call of duty in Britain's need. We also who remain have our great fight, and that is to capture as far as we can the German iron and steel trade, built up by unfair, under- handed, and unscrupulous methods. The Ger- man nation would not only crush our Army, but would crush and cripple our industry. That is their aim! To beat them in the industrial fight is the great privilege of every industrial worker who stays at home. Now is the time, and now the opportunity, which may never occur again. Once missed, lost for ever! This industrial struggle is equally great with the military in which our comrades are risking their life and all. Employers are recognising this, and are throwing themselves into the great fight of cap- turing the German trade. Without our efforts their struggle will be useless! Just as astute and far-seeing generals need our brave soldiers to do, and dare, and conquer, so we workmen in the industrial struggle must do and dare if we are to succeed! Temporary inconvenience, loss I perhaps, we may have to suffer; new methods, greater and quicker adaptability may be neces- sary, the forbearance, pluck, and sacrifice of the soldiers in the field will be required from us, and the struggle will be equally keen; but it's up against us to win, just as surely as "Tommy Atkins" is going to win ! After our workmates have beaten the German despot, they will be coming back to work again, we must be capturing the Germans' trade to make plenty of work for us all when the war is over. We must beat the Germans in the trade fight as " Tommy " will beat them in the mili- tary struggle—we must both win! " Tommy " on the field fights to win, we in the works must work to win! " Tommy " suffers a lot, but he fights! • We may have to suffer a bit, but we must work!

No throwing down tools—suppose " Tommy " threw down his rifle?—No stopping away from work—" Tommy" doesn't stop away from the fight, he's eager to be in it !—We must be out to win. There is no room at the front for "Weary Willies" and "Tired Tims "; they take good care not to go. If we find them in our ranks at home, don't let them scotch our fight. They are Industrial Traitors—make it hot for them! Every reasonable difficulty can and will easily , be dealt with by and through our Association and Wages Boards—but they must be real! Don't manufacture or magnify them. Just as our workmates who have gone to the front, fights to conquer the vain German despot, so we at home must work to win and keep our indus- trial supremacy! Both fights are great, both are vital. In both shall we win—gloriously win, if we at home will but do our duty in the works, as our comrades will do their duty in the trenches. Issued by the Executive Council, October, 1914. *TAMES Cox, General Secretary. 5, Mount Pleasant, Darlington.

div.head: MR. CROSFIELD RE-ELECTED PRESIDENT.
div.p: MR. CROSFIELD RE-ELECTED PRESIDENT.
One of the most successful annual general meetings of the members of the Warrington Liberal Club ever held took place on Monday evening at the Liberal Club, when there was a large attendance.

The chair was occupied by Alderman David Tinnion, who, in a brief speech, made refer- ence to the European War, and to the agreed inactivity of the political parties. MEMBERSHIP MAINTAINED. Mr. H. Johnson, the hon. secretary, presented his report and balance sheet, from which it ap- peared that the membership had been main- tained, whilst the subscriptions were responsible for an increased income. The income derived from bowls and billiards also showed an ad- vance. The bowling green had been much im- proved and the bowling club had been a success under the leadership of Mr. George Marshall, who had acted as hon. secretary. The report and balance sheet were adopted. NEXT YEAR'S OFFICIALS ELECTED. On the proposition of Mr. Thomas Shaw, sec- onded by Mr. W. P. Ashton, Mr. A. H. Crosfield was unanimously re-elected president of the club for the ensuing year. His election was received with hearty cheers. Mr. J. Rudd spoke of the good wcvdc which had been done by the vice-presidents, Alderman Tinnion, Councillor John Wilkinson and Mr. Thomas Pemberton. He proposed their re- election. Mr. P. H. Brown seconded and the motion was carried with applause. The lion. secretary (Mr. Johnson) was re- ossirsnte dp, li and a elected, on the proposition of Councillor Firth Lindley, seconded by Mr. James Critchley, Brownwhilst c.x ursye)auditors r re-appointed, re the meeting showed its confidence in the com- mittee by re-electing the whole of the rerrilhg members, viz.: Messrs. J. T. Locker, Firth Lindley, Joseph Wilkinson, James Halliwell, William Hayes, Frank Ifullery, W. H. Pickup, Fred Walker, Joseph T. Smith and Thomas O'Brien. Two other nTembers, Councillor Samuel Gough and Mr. Peter Delaney, were nominated, but i were unsuccessful n the voting. FOR SOLDIER-MEMBERS. Mr. S. W. Jeffery proposed and Councillor John Wilkinson seconded the following resolu- tion: "That members of the Warrington Liberal Club who have rejoined the colours or have en- listed in Kitchener's Army or the Territorials, be admitted as full members to the club on their return." This was carried. _ _ _
Mr. J. T. Locker proposed and Mr. James Critchley seconded a hearty vote of thanks to the Chairman for presiding, an it was carried in an enthusiastic manner.

r:sh Tricks." rs there has been among us con- rtsearching as to the propriety and CPC, the second verse of our National rein, calling upon the Almighty to auemies and make them fall, we
- t

•. —.and their politics, • rate their knavish tricks," • For some time this vigorous lan- eighed somewhat heavily upon the • of the supersensitive in our midst, our public men took care to seize : ,ageons opportunity to urge that it astically modified. Here and there, ability that way submitted alterna- tims they thought might well be sub- . ••:a'..e.l .3: the lines to which they objected. n in which I lived a few years ago at o- • • .I..nbitious poetaster tried his 'prentice r. nprovement of the verse which had Lecome so offensive, and his "amend- inept" was printed in a version revised in view of an importvit ecclesiastical function, and those who approved of the change sang it in public. • After all, what is amiss with the original? Has not time vindicated the author and com- pletely justified his downrightness? Who of all the inhabitants of these parts is not ready earnestly and sincerely to echo the petition that the politics of Britain's enemies may be con- founded and their tricks—yes, their knavish tricks, most emphatically—frustrated? Brute Force v. Morality. In the opening leaderette in last week's "Examiner," under the cheerful and encourag- ing heading "All goes well," due stress was laid on the despicable part played by Germany since the outbreak of war—the deliberate and calcu- lated and systematic brutality of her soldiery, her diabolical violations of the recognised rules of civilised warfare, and her wanton and whole- sale d,emolition of priceless art treasures. The condition of the unfortunate Belgian refugees in our own district bears witness to the savagery of the inhuman German hosts. These cold- blooded crimes against peaceable civil popula- tions have opened the eyes of former admirers and well-wishers who little suspected the true character of the now unmasked foe. Difficult as it may be for the ordinary man in the street to understand it all, the explanation (as an able regular contributor to these columns made clear in the last issue) is simple enough to those who have read the books and studied the philosophy of Treitschke, Nietzsche, and Bernhardi. The Rev. H. Ogden, Mr. Parker, and others have plainly shown that such works have exercised a great influence over the Germati people, and that these as a whole must bear the blame and shame and everlasting infamy of the devastation and ruin wrought over so great a part of the European Continent in the course of the last two or three terrible months. " Undesirable Importation." This heading in the report of the proceedings against a Grappenhall farmer for failing to: notify wart disease amongst his potato crop somehow reminded me of another undesirable importation in the shape of an insect pest which caused home agriculturists much trouble, anxiety and loss many years ago. I refer to what was known as the Colorado beetle. I well remember how a gang of unscrupulous advertis- ing- wretches contrived to obtain a good deal of money from sufferers by means of a simple trick. Through the Press they announced the discovery of an infallible means whereby' the Colorado beetle might be destroyed, and confiding farmers who expectantly forwarded the sum demanded for the never-failing remedy received by return two bits of wood with instructions to place the obnoxious insect between these and press them together! It was similar to the amazing impu- dence of a gutter merchant whom I once came upon selling boxes of powder warranted to anni- hilate- fleas if the directions were striftly ob- serVed. When an inconveniently exacting pur- chaser returned with a complaint that there were no printed directions for the use of the stuff, the vendor coolly told him that all he had to do was to "catch the flea, squeeze it by the back of the neck till it opens its mouth, and put -a little of the powder on its tongue." Bachelorhood. In "Here and There" a week ago appeared the explanations of three or four bachelors as to why they remained single. I recollect how in a native magazine, Japanese women were in- vited to give their opinions on the ideal man. An English writer, summarising these, states that on the whole the qualities they most admire in a man are not strikingly different from our own.

He must not be miserly" is the very first point they insist on. This (commented the lady) is quite as it should be. Meanness spreads Like a blight over the whole nature, and it is a vice which tends to increase with the years. "I hate a mean man," said Theognis, "and I veil myself when I approach him, having the volatile spirit of a little bird." The pursuer of 'petty economies, the fighter over farthings, ought to remain a bachelor. He will never learn the secret of how to be happy though mar- ried. Moreover, miserliness is a defect which cannot be hidden. It continually obtrudes itself in the everyday affairs of life. As a matter of fact it is easier to lore a criminal of the grand sort than a mean man or a miser. Let me hasten to add that there are thousands upon thousands of admirable bachelors. The great majority of those who are at present fight- ing our battles on land and sea are single men. Of course, they are not by any means to be re- ' garded as confirmed bachelors. On Saturday evening last a very young lady confided to me that she had "started a bottom drawer." I ventured to interpose a question respecting the identity of the lucky prospective bridegroom. ".Oh," she replied, "that isn't decided yet, but, you know, the war will soon be over and there'll be lots of nice boys coming hack home—and then !"

Spiritualism. Mr. Tom Tyrrell's visit to the Spiritualist Society's rooms on Sunday caused me to turn up an old copy of "Broad Views" containing a paper by Mr. A. P. Sinnett on what is termed advanced practical psychology. It is part of the writer's argument that, while the cultured majority are sadly sceptical concerning all promises for the future, those who have their faiths fail to realise "the great fundamental truth " that the future life is "infinitely varie- gated." Quoting (or rather misquoting, as is the careless habit of writers and public speakers not a few) the old Shakespearian phrase con- cerning the undiscovered country from whose bonnie no traveller returns, the writer declares that it is not merely " disconcerted" every day by the return of cheerful travellers by the score or hundred, but that the other phrases of old-fashioned thinking which regards all the possibilities lying beyond the plane of the phy- sical senses as "unknowable," are equally ludi- crous in the sight of those who are aware that vast ranges of that region are daily explored by human consciousness still in the flesh, and have thus already become the subject of many text- books dealing with branches of science that once were clouded in mystery. A little further on this cocksure gentleman insists that there is no mystery at all about that Which happens to the average mortal after he has "passed through the experience which is the gateway of the new life," and he proceeds to describe his progress thus precisely: "He wakes to consciousness in surroundings still definitely belonging to this earth, although in- visible to the physical senses—surroundings described in the technical language of the occul- tist (of which we must make use in describing aspects of Nature with which only the occultist, so far, is practically se e or less protracted as the astral plane, and after a more sojourn amidst those surroundings, the disem- bodied entity passes on to a still more refined condition of existence, described by the term which occultism has borrowed from Oriental imagery, the 'neva Khan, the Home of the Gods. the Devachan Of modern theosophical ex- position. "Thence, in due time, but only after a pro- tracted rest of an exquisitely blieeful character, the disembodied entity returns once more to embodiment, to incarnation,' to the physical ex- periences of the earth life, and as compared with the cloudy suggestions of a feebly illumiu ated faith, this clear prospect of progressive ex- istence is eminently satisfactory to most inquir- ing minds." We are solemnly assured that this is no idle theory, but an actual statement of facts that may be verified by the many students of ad- vanced practical psychology. So there! And if you ask Mr. Sinnett what about penalties and rewards for bad or good deeds upon this earth, he has his answer ready. It may suffice just to mention that without reproducing more.

ILLE6ED IMPUDENT SWINDLE. Man With Two Aliases Sent for Trial.

At the Borough Police Court on Monday, before the Mayor (in the chair), Aldermen Bolton, Smethurst and James Evans, and Messrs. W. Roberts, S. Wright, W. Furness, G. Pilling and T. Locker, James Bibby, alias John Beverley, or Shaw, of no fixed abode, was charged with obtaining by false pretences 2s. 6d. from Mrs. Emily Stone, 51, Nicholson-street. _

Mrs. Stone stated that she was the wife of Alfred Thomas Stone, who was employed as a groom. Prisoner tame to her house on the 15th inst. and asked if that was Stone's house. She replied "-Ares," and prisoner said: "How funny I have found the right house first knock." She asked him what he wanted, and he answered: "Mr. Stone, myself and another man have had an accident with a tramcar. The other man has died. I have to go to the Post Office at 12 o'clock to draw £l5O. compensation." He also said that Mr. Stone had sent him to get some money for stamps and asked for a few shillings. She had no change, but gave him 2s. 6d., and he said his name was Phil Stone. She became suspicious and told her husband. She also went to the Post Office and in consequence of what she was told she reported the matter to the police. She had identified prisoner out of a number of other men. Alfred Thomas Stone said he did not know the prisoner at all. Detective-Sergeant Reddington said that he arrested the prisoner for druukenness, but see- ing that he answered the description of sonic one who was "wanted," he put him up for identifi- cation, and he was picked out by Mrs. Stone at once. When charged, prisoner replied: "I have nothing to say. I know all about it." The Chief Constable said that on the 3rd of June last year prisoner was sentenced to 18 months' hard labour and his time did not expire until December. He had served three terms of 12 months each, one of six months, and alto- gether his previous convictions Timbered 23. Prisoner was committed for trial.

div.head: BOROUGH POLICE COURT
div.p: BOROUGH POLICE COURT
SATURDAY.

Before Mr. R. if. Fairclough (in the chair), Alderman Tinnion, Mr. T. Pemberton and Mr. A. J. Jolley. " Bilked" the Landlady.—Albert Merchant, labourer, 149, Great Moor-street, Bolton, was charged with obtaining by false pretences food and lodgings to the value of ss. from Mary Alice Ingham, 5, White-street.—The Chief Constable said that on the, previous Saturday afternoon prisoner went to Mrs. Ingham and, stating that he was going to start work as a motor mechanic with Messrs, Bellian and Davies, obtained food and lodgings. He had not then received a promise of work, but it was ascertained that a few hours later, by representing himself as a motor mechanic, he had received a promise of work. On the Monday when he should have commenced work he told Mrs. Ingham ,that Messrs. Bellian and Davies would not start him because he could not drive a motor. He had told a story concerning a wife and family in South- port in order to get money, but he was unsuc- cessful. All his stories were false. When charged he said, "I had no intention of cheat- ing her. I was going to pay." As a matter of fact he had not enough money then.—This state- ment was borne out by prosecutrix, Mr. Davies ' and Detective-Sergeant Holland.—Prisoner said he had been working at Whitecross Works. He did not like telling Mrs. Ingham that he was a labourer because her house was a big one.— Several previous convictions were read out, and prisoner was sent to prison for two months.

div.head: TUESDAY.
div.p: TUESDAY.
Before Councillor (in the chair), Messrs. J. Rymer Young, T. Locker and C.
Jackson Holmes.

"A Disgrace to Her Sex."—Elizabeth Lavin, 24, Portland-street, again appeared before the .Bench.—The Clerk explained that she had been bound over on the 21st of July on two charges of theft, and she had not carried out her recog- nisances.-31r. Laws, police court missioner, said the woman had not been behaving herself at all, and she had broken the pledge many a time during the three months. He had cau- tioned her, and helped her, but it had been no use. She had been going about in a filthy con- dition, and had been discharged from a home because the doctor said she wai; more fit for a hospital. She ought to go there and be saved from herself. The police had warned and cautioned her, still she went about, a disgrfice to her sex.—Prisoner: I will go to the hospi- tal.—The Chief Constable: It is absolutely im- possible to keep her from drink. She has been pilfering penny and twopenny and threepenny artioles for the purpose of getting drink since she was placed under the care of Mr. Laws. She will receive the 'medical treatment, of which Mr. Laws speaks, in prison.—Prisoner was sentenced to three months' imprisonment. Detectives Upset Him.—Frank Edwards, 4, Pitt-street, was summoned for having travelled on the L. and N.-W. Railway between Earles- town and Warrington without having paid his fare.—Proseouting on behalf of the railway com- pany, Mr. Tait said that when be was stopped by the ticket collector the defendant had an old half of a ticket from Warrington to Earles- town, which he tendered.—Defendant said that on the day in question he lent a friend his bicycle to go home on and the friend gave him his return half, which had been issued that day. When he got to Warrington he gay, up an old half which he had in his pocket, and be was upset when the detectives started talking to him and did not mention. the half which had been given him by the friend, which was the proper ticket for that day.—Both halves of the tickets were produced.—The case was dismissed on payment of costs. Pushed His Wife Out.—For haling used obscene language, Philip Gandy, 11, Booth- street, was fined 10s. and costs.—lt was stated that he had pushed his' wife out into the street and had used disgusting language.

div.head: WEDNESDAY.
div.p: WEDNESDAY.
Before Messrs. J. W. Hayward (in the chair), C. Jackson Holmes, W. T. Williams, und 11.
Thornton.

Would-be Suicide Released.—Ellen Radbone, a married woman, of 9, Stanley-street, who had previously been charged with attempting to commit suicide by throwing herself in the Mersey at Warrington Bridge, again appeared before the magistrates.—The Chief Constable said she had been to the Workhouse on a 14 days' order, but had been discharged as being sane.—David Radbone, the woman's husband, announced his willingness to look after the woman, and she was handed over to his care.

Boy Who _Stole Brushes.—On giving an un- dertaking to go to the hostel at Messrs..C`ilking- ton's Glassworks, St. Helens, which is under the supervision of Mr. Firth (late Police Court Missioner at Warrington), the 15-year-old boy, who had previously been charged with stealing three brushes, value is. 6d., the property of Messrs. Peers and Morton, Market-street, was discharged.—The magistrates also bound him over for 12 months.
FRIDAY. Before Mr. S. Wright (in the chair), Alderman Pierpoint, Messrs. A. J. Jolley, W. Furness,
T. Locker.

Rifled a Gas Meter.—A 14-year-old boy was ordered to pay 125., the amount of damage he did to a slot gas meter when he stole eightpenee from it.—The magistrates also severely repri- manded him for the theft.

div.head: CHURCHES AND THE WAR.
div.p: CHURCHES AND THE WAR.
CANON WILLIS AND THE GERMANS.
"Pray For Them That Despitefully Use You."

Preaching at the Warrington Parish Church on Sunday morning, the Rector (the Rev. Canon Willis) said that one of the ways in which men could make the...roost of the present—a time of opportunities which should not be missed—was to enlist in the Army. Every man, he con- tinued, should ask himself if it was his duty to stay or go; in many cases, probably, just as much courage was required to refuse ls to vol- unteer. Most men were brave, and would be quite ready to sacrifice their lives for the sake of their country, were it not that they realised the duties they had at home. At the same time, there were many upon whom those obli- gations were not so pressing, and .who Might therefore go. The Duty of the Stay-at-homes. -

-.The question was a difficult one, and one which each, individual must answer for him- self. Those who remained behind must practice the severest self-denial, in order that the urgent calls for various funds might be answered. It was also tVeir duty to act as kindly and hos- pitably as possible to refugees, as well as their own sick and wounded.

13ut there was another duty, which was more difficult to perform; and that was to look im- partially upon the German nation. He did not wish to excuse it, for he recognised that both the nation and its rulers had acted cruelly and deceitfully, although reports might have 'been exaggerated, and there might have been repri- sals. Nevertheless, they must not hate them, nor return evil for evil. They must, instead, "pray for them that despitefully use you and persecute you." Britain's Bounden Duty.

The days were evil. But they were thankful that they might fight with a clear conscience. They did their utmost to avoid war, but he believed it had been their bounden duty to fight —a question of life and death for them, as for the Germans!

div.head: ANNIVERSARY OF AGINCOURT. . W. Bracecalinp Addresses Territorials.
div.p: ANNIVERSARY OF AGINCOURT. . W. Bracecalinp Addresses Territorials.

The new Reserve Battalion of the Territorials which is being raised in Warrington paraded at nine o'clock on Sunday morning and half-an- hour later attended a special service in St. Paul's Church, where they were briefly ad- dressed by their Chaplain (the Rev. W. Brace- camp).

'Tlie reverend gentleman reminded the men that Sunday was St. Crispin's Day, and that nearly 500 years ago that day the great Battle of Agincourt was fought—the great battle in which/ the English, under Henry the Fifth, vanquished the French, though outnumbered by ten to one. In the present struggle, happily, the French were on our side, and it was hoped that the successful results that followed Agin- court would be repeated now.

div.head: LEAGUE AGAINST FORCE. Britain Must Not Absorb the German Spirit.
div.p: A LEAGUE AGAINST FORCE. Britain Must Not Absorb the German Spirit.

Addressing a 'large congregation at the Bank Quay Mission on Sunday evening, Mr. E. Lloyd Jones, of Latchford, referring to the war, said that the present was a time of great conflict and trouble for the Kingdom of Jesus Christ. 'Every Christian was sore troubled as he read the daily records of what was happening. The world— the material spirit—in the words of the Psalm- ist, "put its trust in chariots and horses," but they as Christian people would remember the Name of the Lord., The world looked to chariots and horses, to arms and guns, but they, as Christians, would turn to the Lord their God, Who would, and did, help them. Ger- many to-clay boasted and gloried in her big siege guns and her large, well-trained forces. The spirit of vainglory was not absent in Bri- tain; indeed the jingo spirit was very much alive here and there were plenty of mil in the country who believed in force as the only means of conquering. The nations of Europe were in agony to-day because of the material, carnal, anti-Christian spirit which was so widespread. Materialism Must Be Destroyed._ —•

That creature, material, physical, anti-Chris- tian spirit—mighty, stormy and noisy as it was —must be destroyed. Whilst not belittling the part this nation was taking in the great war, he would remind them that they could not put their trust in weapons alone. They believed the part of England in the war to be inevitable and justifiable. They did not seek it or desire it, but, on the contrary, did all they could to avoid it, and failed. The honour and integrity of the country were at stake, and, as they could not avoid entrance into the quarrel, they thanked God for the courage, loyalty and self-sacrifice that had been revealed by the manhood of their race. If victory crowned their efforts, as they prayed God it would, they must be careful to see to it that the military spirit of force was not transferred from Germany to this country. It was the duty of Christian men and women to create such an atmosphere of thought that it would be impossible for the German disciples of the German spirit to foster it upon England. They must form a League against force.

div.head: PADGATE.
div.p: PADGATE.

Wesley Guild.—Several members of the Bold- street Wesley Guild, Warrington, paid a visit to Padgate on Monday, and gave an interesting sketch, entitled "Mock Brewster Sessions." The judge, counsel and witnesses are to be congratu- lated on the excellent manner in which they rendered the various parts allotted to them.— Mr. Hamblett, who replied to the vote of thanks on behalf of the Bold-street Guild, incidentally mentioned that, in his opinion, drinking in Warrington Was‘ on the increase, a remark which called forth a protest from Mr. Lunt, who stated that, although the actual quantity of t argument .his intoxicants produced might be on the increase, the actual consumption in "Warrington was On! the devease, and in support of lie pointed out the number of licences which had been surrendered in different parts of the town.—Mr. Morton, who occupied the chair, said that his acquaintance with the town was so short that he was unable to say anything for or against the views expressed, and suggested that an opportunity be given to Mr. Hamblett and Mr. Lunt to discuss the matter at another meeting of the Guild, a suggestion which seemed to meet with the approval of the major- ity of the members present.

div.head: 4.1174.0.. jr, IsTßicr .piEws • v_ ,•
div.p: 4.1174.0.. jr, IsTßicr .piEws • v_ ,•
LYMM.

Clock Lamps to be Fixed.—The Lymm Urban District Council at their meeting on Monday agreed to the recommendation of the Gas Com- mittee to fix automatic clock lamps on each side of Burford-lane Bridge. Proposed Hospital for Wounded Soldiers.—A movement is on foot to establish a hospital in Lymm to. accommodate a number of English wounded. soldiers. A provisional committee has been appointed.

Council Appointments.—At a meeting of the Lymm Urban District Council on Monday, Councillor Uotobed was appointed chairman of the Sanitary Comihittee and Councillor Mac- Intyre was placed on the Sewage Farm Sub- Committee.

Potato Thief.—At the Lymm Police Court on Thursday, before Messrs. S. W. Gould and S. Davies, a boatman was charged with stealing two cwt. of potatoes, the property of John Black- ledge, of Agden. He was committed to prison for one month. Territorials Return Thanks..—Mr. F. Evans, chemist, The Cross, Lymm, has received letters from Lieut. G. C. W. Hartley and Corporal Har- old Clare, returning thanks for a number of socks which have been sent to the Lymm Terri- torials in compliance with the wishes of the Lymm and District Defence Corps. New Rector of Oughtrington.—The induction of the new Rector of Oughtringfon (the Rev. Tudor Evans) took place on Wednesday evening. The Archdeacon conducted the service—assisted by the Rev. E. P. Withered (the retiring rector) —and afterwards gave a brief address. A num- ber of the new Rector's former parishioners from Lostock Gralam attended the service. Cross Roads Corner.—At a recent meeting or the Roads Committee of Lymm Urban District Copncil a letter was read from Mr. Clarke ask- ing what arrangements had been made with the other owners of the land at the cross roads corner. The Clerk was instructed to reply to the effect that the other owners would not treat with the Council. The Council endorsed the committee's action. -

Present at the council Meeting.—The mem- bers of. the Lymm District Council who were present at the meeting on Monday were Messrs. T. H. Warburton, R. H. Gotobed, C. E. Cowper, S. Critchley, G. H., Parker, W. H. Rershaw, F. Lockyer, W. G. Groves, and A. Maelntyre, to- gether with the following officials: Messrs. Wm. Mullard (clerk), Timperley (assistant clerk), D. Mort (surveyor), C. I. Barnes (water man- ager), T. H. West (gas manager), and Dr. De Jong (medical officer). • Concerning a Claim Against the Council.— The minutes of a recent meeting of the Sanitary Committee, which were read at the meeting of the Lymm District Council on Monday, stated that the surveyor reported that he had received a letter from Mr. Harold Garnett, writing on behalf of Mrs. Speight, claiming £l3 Ds. 4d., compensation for damages, loss of time, and materials in re:•peot of a drain to her cottage in Higher-lane, Lymm. The committee proposed that an offer of ..t8 be tendered, without preju- dice, on behalf of the Council to Mrs. Speight, as, in the opinion of the committee, the amount claimed was excessive. The Council, endorsed this proposal.

div.head: BELGIAN BELIEF :COMMITTEE. Should They have Consulted .the
div.p: BELGIAN BELIEF :COMMITTEE. Should They have Consulted .the
Council?

The Lymm Belgian Relief Committee came in for some criticism at the meeting of the Urban District Council on Monday evening. Councillor Cowper said he thought the Council should have been consulted by the committee. Circulars had been sent round with only Mr. Dixon's name on them and no sooner had the circular been received than a collector came round for money. He did not want ta be on the committee, but he thought the Council should be represented on it, seeing that they had come forward in a handsome manner. _
The Chairman (Councillor T. H. Warburton) : I think this is outside the business of the Council.

Councillor Gotobed said he could endorse what Councillor Cowper had said. The Belgians were coming on the Wednesday. They were to be taken to Beechwood direct. How nice it would be if the chairtnan of the Council could receive the refugees in that room and give them a civic welcome.

The Chairman said he was on the committee, but his numerous appointments prevented him serving on a sub-committee. The Clerk (Mr. Mullard) said that in addi- tion to the Chairman of the Council, Councillor J. 11. Holt was on the committee.

div.head: WELCOMED BACK.
div.p: WELCOMED BACK.
Mr. A. Alaelntyre Re-takes His Old
Seat on the Council.

At a meeting of the Lymm Urban District Council on Monday evening, a cordial welcome was extended to Mr. Alexander Maclntyre, farmer, of Burford-lane, who, after a prolonged absence from the Council Chamber, once more sits round the table as a representative of the electors of the Lymm Ward. The Clerk (Mr. Wm. Mullard) reported that Mr. Afaclntyre had been duly elected to fill the vacancy in the representation of the ward, caused by the resignation of the Rev. G. B. Thurston.

The Chairman (Councillor T. H. Warburton) said it gave him pleasure to welcome Mr. Maclntyre to the Council. He had had pre- vious experience of Council work, and there was no doubt that that experience would prove to be beneficial to the work of that body. Councillor Groves said he was pleased to see Mr. Maclntyre present. He sat with the new member before, and he was sure that his ser- vices would prove helpful. Councillor Cowper also added a few words of welcome, remarking that he always bad a great liking for farmers—(laughter)—and Mr. Mac- Intyre was one of the best in the district. There would be plenty of work for him•to do. Councillor Gotobed, as the senior member for the Lymm Ward, offered his good wishes and congratulated the Council upon having such a man as the new councillor in their midst.
Councillor Maclntyre, in acknowledgment, said that he would try to do his duty to the ratepayers of Lymm Ward and the district at large. He would do his best.

div.head: WATCHED WATERWORKS.
div.p: UN WATCHED WATERWORKS.

Council Decide to Dispense With Night Guards. The question as to whether or not it is ne&s- sary to continue to guard the Lymm water supply against the possibility of its being tam- pered with by agents of the enemy was raised in a discussion which took place at the monthly meeting of the Urban Distri. Council, held on Tuesday night. The Council answered the ques- tion propounded in the negative. From the minutes of the Water Committee it appeared that at a recent meeting a letter was read from the Chief Constable of.the county in- forming the Council that the constables who were engaged in watching at the Waterworks had been withdrawn as and from Saturday, October 17. The committee, in recommending that the Boy Scouts be withdrawn, proposed that the best thanks of the Council should be given to the Scoutmaster and boys for their services, which were highly appreciated. The Council agreed. ; Councillor Gotobed said he was led to under- stand that .it was 'a fact that the two Council watchmen who were doing duty at the Water- works stationed themselves down in the hollow and occupied the workshop. It seemed to him that the reservoir was the place which needed to be watched, and if the Council were to con- tinue paying the two watchmen they should, at least, demand that one of them should take up a position at the most dangerous poiltt.

div.head: Local Germans "_Bottled _Up."
div.p: Local Germans "_Bottled _Up."

_ Councillor Cowper: I do not think there, is any need for these men. The Chief Constable has taken his men away. If he thought there was any reason to have them there he would not have withdrawn them. We have got the Germans in the district pretty well bottled up. There are now only two about here, and they will have to go if they don't behave themselves! The Chairman (Councillor T. 11. Warburton): That is not the point raised.

Mr. Barnes (water manager) said that the watchmen occasionally went to the reservoir. Councillor Parker: How do you know? Are you there all night? Mr. Barnes:. Not likely, sir! I think that the most important things to be guarded are the works, as distinct from the reservoirN Councillor Parker: Suppose the water was poisoned? Mr. Barnes: That would be a very slow pro- cess ! _
Councillor Parker : Not so very slow if typhoid germs were used. Councillor Gotobed : Under whose directions are these men?

The Chairman: That's the point. Councillor Gotobed : I propose that they be under the charge of the Chairman of the Water Committee. Councillor Kershaw asked if he would be in order if he moved that the men be withdrawn. The Chairman said the committee had con- sidered withdrawing them, but had decided that they should be kept on. Councillor Kershaw would be in order all the same.
Councillor Kershaw;—"HZ-Ibeg to move that we dispense with the services of the men at the waterworks.
Councillor Cowper seconded.
On a vote being taken the majority of the Council voted in favour of dispensing with the watchmen.

div.head: OUR BELGIAN GUESTS.
div.p: OUR BELGIAN GUESTS.
Party of Thirty Arrive at Beechwood.

About thirty of the Belgian refugees arrived at Beechwood House, Lymm, on Wednesday afternoon and were given a hearty reception by a large crowd who turned out to witness their coming. They travelled by train to Bank Quay Station, Warrington, and from thence they were conveyed to their new place of abode in private motor cars, kindly, lent by local ladies and gentlemen. As they alighted at Beechwood House they were welcomed, on behalf of the local committee, by Mr. Alfred Watkin, and it was obvious that they were much touched by the cordiality of their reception. The refugees included in their numbers river pilots, a wounded sergeant-major of the Belgian Army, a commercial traveller, hotel attendants, trades- people, and a member of the Civil Guard from Ostend.

A Wounded Sergeant-Major. One of the men, who had been prosperous, has lost all his money through the Germans raiding the bank in which it was deposited, whilst his property was destroyed by shells. The ser- geant-major, who re-joined the colours after having been out of the Army for 16 years, fought at Diest andlle, and was wounded in the leg by a piece of shrapnel. The last time he heard tidings of his wife and family was two months ago, when they were in Brussels. A Civil Guardsman from Ostend was instrunlental in the capture of three German spies. The last of the trio, he told our representative, was carrying a bomb in a portmanteau when arrested.

Everything is being done to make the guests comfortable and happy at Beechwood House. The dining-room has been decorated with flags and with portraits and pictures calculated to interest the refugees. A smoke-room has been provided for the men, and in it is a billiard table, which proves a great source of attraction to the men. The bedrooms have been cosily fitted up, and a nursery, well-stocked with toys, has been provided for the children. Miss Healey'has been appointed matron, and she is doing her utmost to make the refugees as happy as possible.

, Those To Whom Thanks Are Due. All the arrangements for the accommoddtion of the refugees have been completed in a re- markably short time, and the committee, with I Mr. Alfred Watkin as chairman, and Messrs. W. MuHard and H. T. Mercer as honorary secretaries, and Mr. T. F. W. Dixon as honorary treasurer, deserve every praise for the great trouble they have taken in discharging their self-imposed tasks. / On Monday the house was thrown open for public inspection, at a charge of 6d. per head, the sum of £1 being realised.

div.head: STOCKTON HEATH
div.p: STOCKTON HEATH

St. Thomas' Band of Hope.—The St. Thomas' Church Band of Hope, under the superintend- ence of Mr. Hallows, met on Thursday evening, when there was a large attendance. A recita- tion, " The Way to Heaven," was nicely given by Miss Heath and was much appreciated. Mr. Rose told some stories, and inculcated some useful lessons by means of magnetic experi- ments. Mr. Hallows announced that various interesting competitions were being arranged for future meetings. The first rounders' match was held on Saturday, when, after a keen con- test, the honours fell to the boys.

div.head: PENKETH.
div.p: PENKETH.
Wesley Guild.--On Wednesday the members of the Wesley Guild listened to a most inter- esting lecture on "The Awakening of the Mind," by Mr. F. Littler.

Tennis Club; Annual Meeting.—The Lawn Tennis Club held their third annual meeting on Tuesday. After the balance sheet, which was of a very satisfactory nature, had been adopted; the election of officers took place. Mr. C. E. Parker was chosen president, and Miss E. Cook and Mr. G. J. Dale retain the offices of secretary and treasurer respectively. The mem- bership is limited to 36. It is hoped that a pavilion will be erected on the ground in readi- ness for the forthcoming season.. Orphan Band-boys' Entertainment.—ln the Wesleyan Schoolroom on Thursday night a musical entertainment was given by the hand of the National Children's Homes and Orphan- ages, founded by Dr. Stephenson. The youthful instrumentalists' playing was of a high order, and merited the praise the Chairman (Mr. Withinshaw) and audience gave them. The Rev. S. Carroll Myers, a former minister of this circuit, briefly addressed the meeting. The collection amounted to £5 is. 3d.

Belgian Party Settling Down.—Our Belgian visitors are settling down in their new home at Hall Nook. The committee and villagers have done all that is possible to make the compul- sory .exiles feel at home. They appear to be happy and comfortable, but their thoughts naturally frequently turn to their beloved Bel- gium, and papers that are supplied, both Eng- lish and French, are eagerly scanned to see how the great conflict progresses in a district they know so well. The men have been engaged in 'putting up conveniences in the house and in work in the grounds, while the women have gloried in a big wash—the first for many weeks. The children attend the village school, part- time, and join our children in their drill and play. On Thursday evening the party attended an entertainment given in the Wesleyan School by boys from the National Children's Home, and the Belgian National Anthem was played in honour of the visitors. We understand the ladies of the committee are arranging to pro- vide afternoon teas for those who have helped the undertaking, particulars of which are to be made public later.

div.p: GREAT SANKEY.
A FORTUNATE PARISH.
Only One Case of Distress Throullh War.
WORK AS USUAL.

Councillor W. Furness presided at a meeting of the Sankey Parish Council, held: in the Council Schools on Monday evening, when there were also present Councillors Pownall, Fair and Taylor, with Mr. J. Smith (clerk).
Dangerously-placed Telegraph Poles._

A letter was read from Mr.-P..H. Wright, in which he asked that something should be done to improve the road outside the Council Schools just beyond the turning to Penketh from Warrington. "I am -writing this letter," con- tinued Mr. Wright, "owing to the fact that on the previous Thursday night at 12 o'clock I was cycling with a friend to Warrington, when, just at the point named, we met a motor car with very powerful head-lights, 'which caused us to draw close in to the side. My friend was first, and owing to the sudden projection of the road and to the fact that a telegraph pole stands over the road, so to speak, it was im- possible to avoid a collision. The lights of the car quite obscured the pole, and in consequence my friend lies in Warrington Infirmary suffer- ing from a severe wound in the head. I think you will agree that this pole is standing in a dangerous position under the circumstances— in fact, the second one is also badly placed, and, in view of the possibility of another accident, which might be easily more serious than the present one appears to be, I would respectfully bring the matter to your notice, in the hope that something may be done to remove the danger." The Chairman: We all recognise that it is a dangerous quarter at the present time. I think it is to be deplored that the County Council have not made provision, as they pro- mised, with the object of widening the bridge; but, whilst that is so, we must not forget that these poles are put there by the Government. I suggested to the gentleman who was hurt that he shohld write to the Government Tele- graph Department and state his case. They could not give any compensation, because they are not legally entitled to do so. That, how- ever, did riot alter the moral aspect of the case. The poles had no right to be on the highway at this most awkward place, when there is no footpath. I think we should be justified in sending a strong letter to the Postal and Telegraph Department; asking them to make arrangements for the removal of the poles. I would also send a letter to the County Council enclosing the letter we have received from Mr. Wright. Councillor Pownall : A man using the road would take the wall of the bridge as being the boundary, but, if he does so, immediately he gets across the bridge he finds himself collid- ing with one of the poles, which seems to mark the boundary of the road. The Clerk: Both of the poles are in bad posi- tions. Councillor Pownall : There are three which ought to be set back. The Chairman suggested that a resolution should be sent to the County Council with reference to the widening of the bridge. Councillor Pownall : This does not apply to the Telegraph Department. The Chairman: Unless the bridge is widened and a footpath made, where can you put the poles? Immediately they begin to widen the bridge the Telegraph Department will remove the post. They will be bound to do it. Councillor Fair: I think the Telegraph De- partment ought to move in the matter. Councillor Pownall : Independent of the post, the bridge is in a dangerous state. I propose " that it be pointed out to the County Council that the bridge is in an unfinished state owing to the footpath being set back on the westerly side, and that the matter ought to be attended to at once. We have had more than one acci- dent there, and one man died from injuries received in an accident which took place at the spot some two years ago. The pole is practically on the road. The Clerk: And then there was that trap accident some years ago. After further discussion it was decided that the attention of the County Council be called to the unsatisfactory condition of the road at Barnes' Bridge, with an intimation that in the opinion of the Parish Council they should make arrangements for widening the bridge. The resolution also called attention to the fact that accidents had occurred there, and it was agreed to enclose with it a copy of the letter from Mr. Wright. It was also decided to send a similar com- munication to the Postal Telegraph Depart- ment. A Footpath Improved. The Chairman said he had some "good news" and went on to refer to Mr. E. Bennett's ac- count of ..eq for repairing the footpath at Hood-lane, which runs into Buttermilk Bridge. Councillor hair: And it is a vast improve- ment. Councillor Taylor: It is cheap, too. The Chairman: The distritt will be grateful to you, Councillor Fair, for what you have done in the matter. It having been intimated that the work had not been freely charged for, it was decided that the Council express their appreciation of the prompt and economical way in which Mr. Ben- nett had carried out the work.
Postmaster-General.
-John Rothwell, The Cocoa Factory, Colborne. Lancashire.--

div.head: Lord Lilford's Offer.
div.p: Lord Lilford's Offer.

In connection with the laying of water mains in Hood-lane, the Clerk read a letter from Mr. Sutton (clerk to the District Council), in which he stated: "Adverting to your letter of the 28th July, Mr. Selby writes to our inspector and arranges that if your Council will lay the water main in Hood-lane, northward from the pre- sent terminus as far as Peter Doraville's cot- tage, Lord Lilford will bear the cost of con- necting the same to Parsonage Farm, Bennett's House, and two cottages. The Clerk: A resolution was passed some time ago to the effect that the District Council would extend the main. It was decided to write further to the Dis- trict Council on the Matter.

- The Chairman: I have met several gentle- men who are anxious to get a Sunday delivery of letters. Nowadays you have to go to Mr. Knowles, the postmaster, and inquire for letters. div.head: MANCHESTER AND DISTRICT LEAGUE.
div.p: MANCHESTER AND DISTRICT LEAGUE.
First Division. RYLANDS' RECS. v. WARDLEY.

This match was played at Wardley last Satur- day, before a good crowd. Rylands' won the toss and decided to start off down the slope. From the opening kick they commenced to press, the full-back saving. A scrummage being formed close in, /Rylands' were penalised for "feet up." From the kick F. Horrocks fielded the ball, and, beating sseVeral men, made a splendid opening, and gave the ball to Rowlin- son, who score,d at the corner, Potter just failing at goal. After this reverse, Wardley played Strenuously, and the game became very keen, both teams struggling hard for the mastery, as neither of them had been beaten before. Rylands' were penalised, and the Wardley full- back landed a splendid goal from over the half- way line. Half-time arrived with the score: Rylancls',-1 try (3 points); Wardley, 1 goal (2 points). . .

With only a point separating them, both sides played for all they were worth, but over-eager- ness spoilt their efforts and caused the ball- to be frequently knocked on. Both sets of for- wards worked hard and the two sets of half- backs were penalised more than once. From one of the penalty kicks the Wardley full-back landed another fine goal, which gave his side the lead. Wardley then assumed the defensive, and Rylands' could not break through, the game ending in a well-deserved win for the homesters " 2 goals (4 points) to Rylands', 1 try (3 its). The full-backs both played a sterling ie.

The Warrington and District N.U. Inter- mediate League have written to the Town Hall, Parks and Baths Committee of the Town Coun- cil, thanking them for the use of Victoria Park. div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 31, 1914.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 31, 1914.
ANGLING.
Warrington Working Men's Association.
N.A. CENTRE.

The• lest sport obtained last week-end was at Waveran, 'Shropshire Union Canal. Roach were taken up to lib., and it would be wise at present for members who visit the Gowy at the Shaker end to cross over the meadows and try .the canal at Stoke if they are off in the Gowy. Those who Visited the Gowy failed to find any weighers, but reports to hand say that several perch were taken in the upper reaches beyond the mill. One angler took five on the Saturday, including one of about Boz. As these have only lately come into prominence in the stream they were carefully returned to the water. Chester, both river and canal, was " off," and from reports all round there is no place better for our local rods to go than the Gowy, even if it is not fishing up to expectations. The glorious uncertainty of the Gowy is better than visiting our canals, where the fish are entirely off.

div.head: CENTRE COMMITTEE.
div.p: CENTRE COMMITTEE.

A committee meeting was held at headquar- ters an Thursday to listen to our delegate's report. From several remarks in the report it seems that the N.A. of Warrington will be ex- ceedingly lucky if they are allowed to take either eels or pike during the coming close season by the F.F.P.L.; whose ruling the N.A.A. is pledged to adhere to up to the next general meeting at Tyldesley. If the ruling is not altered then, we in Warrington will be com- pelled to leave the above-mentioned fish alone, no matter what other anglers do. We still have the Gowy for trout, but is it worth while to pay even this fine trout stream a visit when we are debarred from taking either eels or pike? If pike and eel are detrimental to the coarse fisher, as well as the trout angler, why do not the F.F.P.L. meet on the matter and, put our minds at rest? If it is the wish of the F.F.P.L. to bar these fish in close season, and all soc- ieties agree on their decision, well, the N.A. of Warrington will uphold them as long as they pledge themselves to them as members.

Th-e delegate's report was listened to with great interest throughout, and after 'a hearty vote of thanks was passed to him, the Treasurer (Mr. E. Brookes) handed to him a beautiful gold albeit and medal for his past services to the club. ne was again elected delegate for season 1915. A. S.

div.head: ASSOCIATION.
div.p: ASSOCIATION.
FRIENDLY MATCHES. DARESBURY PARISH A.F.C. V. BANK QUAY A.F.C.

This match was played at Moore on Saturday, when the home team gained a: good victory. The visitors were somewhat younger than the home team, but for all that they played with spirit and strove hard to win. The home club had the best of the game, but many of their strong attacks were repulsed by the Bank Quay backs. R. Forster was a source of great strength to the visitors. Half-time arrived with the score: Daresbuu, 3 goals; Bank Quay, 2 goals. In the second half the home club had the hold a the visitors, and play was for the most part in their half. Nevertheless, the visitors

did not -consider themselves beaten until the whistle blew for time, the final score being: Daresbury, 6 goals; Bank Quay, 3 goals. The Daresbury scorers were: J. Lee-Jones (2), F. Forster, and W. M. Cartwright (3). MATCHES FOR TO-DAY.
