div.head: CxERM %NY'S NAVAL SUPERIORITY.
div.p: CxERM %NY'S NAVAL SUPERIORITY.
Whistling to Keep Their Courage Up.

The following items of naval interest occur among thb "news" circulated officially from Berlin by wifeless on Sunday and Saturday, and will be read with amusement in the light of Saturday's naval action : The " Nene Zuricher Zeitung " in an editorial article is very pessimistic regarding the British prospects of vanquishing the German Fleet. The excellent geographical conditions which our North Sea squadron enjoy and the fear of the tremendous activity of our submarines and torpedo-boats make it impossible for the British admirals to force the German Fleet into action. The disembarkation of land forces on the Ger- man North Sea coast appears to be about as unfeasible as could be the occupation of Ant- werp, for the transports would have to sail through a low depth of water. In addition to this there is the great superiority of the German " mantelringgeseheutze" (ring casing guns), which are able to fire 220 shots, while the British wire-bound guns are scaled after only 60 shots, and their accuracy of aim is destroyed. It would be impossible for English firms to make " niantelringgescheutze," as these firma are unable to produce sufficiently large blocks of steel for the quality required. In this re- spect also Germany is at a decided advantage. No confirmation is yet to hand from the Ger- man side of the London report of- the sinking of the British cruiser Hawke by a German sub- marine. There is a feeling of deep depression in London.

div.head: Longford United's Unbeaten Record Suffers.
div.p: Longford United's Unbeaten Record Suffers.
SUCCESS OF ST. BARNABAS,.
Notes by "Linesman."

On' Saturday there were some keen contests in the local League games, the chief interest being centred in the meeting of the Y.M.C.A. and St. Barnabas'. There was a good crowd present, many having travelled from town to see their favourites display their powers against th.e Y.M. The first portion was a very well con- tested half, being full of good and interesting football, in which the- home lot surprised the visitors by their exhibition. At the interval no score was made. The second half was as keenly contested until fifteen minutes from the finish, when both teams appeared to flag, with the visitors a shade the better. Martin, in the home goal, had more to do than Shaw, and it was owing to his good work that no score was re- corded until fifteen minutes had gone in the second half. The final score rested with the Saints, but on the general run of the game a draw wild have been a fitting result. Owing to the fact that the' Longford United team had not been defeated, their meeting with the Fairfield United team was an important en- counter for them, and the game was exciting and keenly contested. The visitors in the first portion of the game showed very indifferent form and their goal was subjected to heavy pres- sure. It was owing to the fine play of the de- fenders that the home team only saored once. In the second half the Fairfield players gave a very different display, and had a greater share of the game, and ultimately won by three goals against one... _ _ _ _

-Fairfield Athletic were visited by the Congre- gatiotalists from Newton, when a well-con- tested game was witnessed which resulted in favour of the visitors by.four goals against two. The Latchford Baptists journeyed to Padding- ton, and had to return defeated by 2 goals to nil. They have to thank their custodian, Wyatt, for his splendid display 'between the uprights, for he saved a penalty kick in excellent style, and many other difficult shots during the game. The Paddington players were not severely tested, and the Baptists will have to improve if they intend to win their first match.

There was another big crowd present at Lovely-lane, where the Recs. had The Central team as opponents. The game resulted in favour of the Recs., but the score by no means repre- sented the play, as on several occasions the simplest of chances were sadly missed by the Central forwards.

The Elmwood Congregationalists journeyed to meet the Mission, and were heavily defeated by seven goals against one. The Cons. gave a nook exhibition, and were easily overcome. Massey, in the home goal, was only troubled' twice dur- ing_the whole game. _

The Orford White Star. journeyed to Hollins Green and were victorious by scoring the odd goal in seven, a performance which is very satis- factory, as the •home team are a tough lot on their own ground.

efforts were successful, Hughes scoring, and at the interval the score was: Longford, 1 goal; Fairfield United, nil. From the commencement of the second half the visitors played as a new team; and their combination quite upset the home defenders, and Scott registered the first goal for the visit- ors. From the display of the home players it was evident they had over-exerted themselves in the first half, and the improved display of the visitors resulted in their having the greater share of the game. The home team were only able to make occasional visits to their oppo- nent's goal. Millward scored the second and Poulter the third goal for the visitors, and the home team, being unable to break down the visitors' defence again, had to retire defeated. Score: Fairfield United, 3 goals; Longford United, 1 goal.
PADDINGTON v., LATCHFORD BAPTISTS.

These teams met on Saturday on the ground of the former, before a good number of_spectaT tors. The Baptists won the toss, and Wood- head kicked off for the home team. During the first quarter of an hour the game was very evenly and well contested. Then the home lot made a strong attack on the visitors' goal, and in trying to clear Clark handled the ball inside the area. Craik took the kick and made a strong drive, but Wyatt made a great save and fully deserved the ovation he received from the spectators. From his clearance the visitors rushed towards the home goal, where George, the custodian,- came out to meet the ball, but missed. But for the timely effort of Chamber- lain by falling back a certain goal would have ensued. Wrench gained possession of the leather and passed out to Craik on the left, who made a splendid individual effort, and succeeded in opening the score for the home team. En- couraged by this. success, the home team were soon at close .quarters again with their oppo- nents, and Wyatt had a very busy time, saving many shots. The score at the interval was in favour Of Paddington by 1 goal to none. . . .

After changing ends the visitors improved in their play, but 'their forwards finished weakly, and were easily held in check by the home backs, the Baptists being inclined to try individual efforts instead of combining. Many chances were thus wasted, and the defenders of both teams kicked very well. One of the visitors conceded a corner. The flag kick was taken by Scarisbrick, and the ball dropped well in front of goal, where Wyatt again saved well. The home team appeared to revive themselves, and had the best of the exchanges. From another attack Woodhead increased the lead. The re- mainder of the game was mostly in favour of the home team. Result: Paddington, 2 goals; Latchford Baptists, nil.

div.head: WARRINGTON AND DISTRICT LEAGUE.
div.p: WARRINGTON AND DISTRICT LEAGUE.
EARLESTOWN Y.M.C.A. v. ST. BARNABAS'.
The meeting of these teams on the ground of the former had been keenly anticipated, as was shown by the crowd present. The teams turned out as follows:
_ Y.M.C.A.: Martin; Chambers and J. Atkin- son; Fairhurst, H. Martin and Goulden ; Taylor, Gilman, Riley. Hughes and Lee.

St. Barnabas' : Shaw; E. Glover and Long; J. E. Glover, Challinor and O'Neil; Darlington, Smith, Irons, Vernon and Houghton. Referee, J. Smith. The home captain won the toss and defended the railway goal. Irons set the ball in motion and it was very soon evident that the game would be keenly contested. The home defenders were quickly called upon, when they cleared their lines, and their own forwards raced away to the visitors' end, but were repulsed by the backs. The home men were quickly back again, and Shaw had to handle a long shot. H. Martin at centre-half, for the Y.M., was playing a good game, breaking up the attempts of the Saints and feeding his forwards in judicious manner, but their efforts were foiled by Glover and Long. Then the visitors' half-backs proved a very strong line, Challinor not allowing Riley much scope. The play gradually began to hover round the home goal, where Goulden had a stiff task to deal with in opposition to Smith and Darlington, when the former, after being beaten for the ball, regained possessioU.and sent in a surprise shot, which narrowly missed the top corner of the goal. The visitors were now hav- ing the best of the exchanges, but Chambers, Atkinson and Martin, in goal, defended splen- didly, the latter saving several shots in excellent style. Good work by the home forwards brought. relief to their defence. .The front line combined very well together, and at times the visitors' defence was hard pressed, but the home for- wards failed to score. Play was transferred by Vernon and Houghton, and, following an attack on the home citadel, the latter got in a very hot shot, which Martin put over the bar, being loudly applauded for the effort. At the inter- val no score had been made.

On resuming the game was contested more keenly and faster than in the first portion, and Riley was soon prominent with useful passes to his wing men, which put the Saints' goal in danger, and a splendid effort by Gilman was , very near capturing the Saints' citadel, Shaw just managing to put the ball round the post. The ensuing corner proved, fruitless, and from : another attack Shaw was penalised for carrying the ball. The free kick failed to materialise. The Saints relieved their area, and Smith and Darlington got away on the right, but owing to the narrowness of the field they could not operate together as well as expected. Vernon and Houghton proved the most dangerous wing. The latter, being well served by Vernon, scored with a shot which completely beat Martin. This reverse made the home players exert themselves more, and so well did they combine that they were soon swarming round the Saints' goal, and Shaw had to stir himself to clear. After the ball had been got away several times, Gilman sent across to Lee, who met it and crashed it into the net, equalising the score after twenty min- utes' play. The game now became a struggle between the opposing, half-back lines, all play- ing strongly, until Houghton outwitted Fair- hurst, but finally shot wide. Shortly after Ver- non was just wide with a long shot. The Saints , now appeared to be standing the strain better than their opponents, and from a free kick Houghton put them ahead. The home team again began to assert themselves, and their in- side trio were playing very well together. Chal- linor and H. Martin, ,the respective .centre halves, were doing a great amount of work. Off-side against the visitors spoiled many at- tempts, but after Darlington had been chal- lenged by Atkinson, he regained the ball and passed to Smith, who went forward and scored the Saints' third goal. Result: St. Barnabas', 3 goals; Earlestown Y.M.C.A., 1 goal.

div.head: LONGFORD UNITED V. FAIRFIELD UNITED.
div.p: LONGFORD UNITED V. FAIRFIELD UNITED.

These teams met on the ground behind the Horse and Jockey, Winwick-road, and when the teams turned out there was a good crowd of spectators, a hat of int Vest being centred in the game, as the homesters were as yet undefeated. From the opening exchanges the home team threatened danger, tut the visitors by good de- fensive play, prevented a score. Not to be denied, the home team came down again and from a shot at goal the ball rebounded out for a corner kick from one of the defenders. The flag kick was well placed, and after being headed out by one of the backs was returned into the goalmouth, where one of the home forwards, standing "in an off-side position, put the ball past the custodian. The point was rightly dis- allowed by the referee. The home team con- tinued to have the best of the game, and their

div.head: FAIRFIELD ATHLETIC v. NEWTON CONGREGATIONAL.
div.p: FAIRFIELD ATHLETIC v. NEWTON CONGREGATIONAL.

The above teams met on Saturday on the Orford-road ground. Teams:— Fairfield Athletic: Warburton; Jackson and Johnson; Leigh, Roberts and Hayes; Wood, Clark, Monks, Challinor and Short. Newton Cons.: Dagnall; Tithers and Law- rence; W. Clark, C. Clark and Porter; Beres- ford, Pritchard, Rowbottom, Jones and Gleave. Referee, B. Howell.

The visitors won the toss and from the kick off they at once made an attack on the home goal, but a free kick to the home team relieved the danger. Monks, receiving the ball, raced away on the wing, only to be defeated by Law- rence, and the leather was transferred to the home area, where Gleave and Beresford did good work for their respective sides. Even play fol- lowed for a short time. The Cons.' forwards were again seen to advantage and the Athletic were penalised for hands against Chaninon Lawrence took the ensuing kick, but hit the upright, and from the rebound the ball went over the line. The home team showed im- proved form and by good combination they gained ground in their opponents' goal area, and from a scrimmage in goal Short opened the score. Directly from the centre-kick the Cons. became aggressive, and Tones equalised the score. Mid-field play followed, and then from a free kick C. Clark gained the lead for the visit- 'ore. Monks was next prominent with a good 1 clearance, and Hardy came to the rescue when the home goal was in danger, while at the other end Lawrance followed suit. Jones and Gleave, on the visitors' left, were very noticeable for a good passing movement, and the Fairfield goal was hotly besieged, Warburton having to save several times. Monks had hard lines with a shot which hit the upright, and then Porter by good play placed Clark in a good position, but the latter hit the cross-bar and directly after Short equalised for the home team after twenty- five minutes' play. Play now became exciting, and free kicks against the home team were numerous, and from a free kick Porter gave the Cons. the lead. The visitors' half-backs gave a good display, and the home forwards did not make much headway, and at the interval .the Cons. were leading by 3 goals against 2. On resuming the game was eyenly contested, each end being quickly visited. Warburton mulled a shot, which nearly let the visitors in, when Monks came to the rescue, and the home forwards raced away, for Short to give Dagnall a warm handful. The home team were now pressing very hard, but they could not defeat Tithers and Lawrence, whilst Porter proved too good for Challinor aid Clark, and then a corner kick to the Athletic was headed wide by Jack- son. A far better display was being shown now than in the first half, but the home lot could not pierce the visitors' defence. A corner kick to the visitors was next cleared by Roberts, and a brief visit was paid to the visitors' end, and good play by Beresford, Pritchard and Row- bottom transferred the play again to the home quarters, which resulted in Jones scoring the Cons.' fourth goal. The visitors continued to have the best of the game. Monks played a grand defensive game for the Athletic. At the call of time the result was: Newton Cons., 4 goals; Fairfield Athletic, 2 goals.

div.head: BANK QUAY RECS. v. WARRINGTON
div.p: BANK QUAY RECS. v. WARRINGTON
CENTRAL.
These teams met on the Lovely-lane ground, and consequent of the Recs.' meritorious victory of the previous week over their rivals, there was another great crowd present to witness the game.

- Referee G. Bamber had charge of the follow- ing players : Recs.: Bushill : Rowlinson and F. Millington; Worrell, Lagar and Long; Eccleston,Milling- ton, Banner, Webb and Lemons. Central: Roberts; Emson and Williams; Goulden, Guest and Williams; Mason, Hands, Holmes, Collins and Farrell. The Recs. won the toss and Holmes started ' the ball; After a spell of give-and-take play, the home, forwards attacked in determined fashion, and Roberts made a grand save from Banner. The visitors' defence had a busy time, and after. Roberts had brought off another good save from Webb, Lemons received the ball and scored with a low shot. Roberts touched, but failed to hold the ball. After this' reverse the visitors made a strong effort to equalise, and Hands, with an easy opening, dallied in front of goal and lost his chance of equalising. Good play by- Lagar enabled Webb and Lemons to get off, and the latter scored a second goal for the Recs. The Central were now playing a hard game, but failed to hold the home for- wards in check, and J. Millington added a third goal. Half-time score: Recs., 3 goals; Central, nil. After changing ends the game was contested at a fast pace, the Central having the best of the exchanges, and from a clearance by Bushill, Holmes missed an open goal. Following this let- off the Recs. raced to the visitors' end and Webb notched a fourth goal. The custodian made no effort to save. Guest, the visitors' centre-half, was playing a good effective game, holding Ban-

ner, the home centre-forward, well in check. Although the visitors received plenty-of en- couragement from their supporters, their for- wards failed to accept some very easy opportu- nities. Banner was successful in scoring a fifth goal for the Recs., and at the call of time the result was: Bank Quay Recs., 5 goals; Warring- ton Central, nil.
EARLESTOWN ST. JOHN'S MISSION V. ELM WOOD CONGREGATIONALISTS. _
Played on the Mission ground.- The following players turned out:—

Mission: Massey; Winders and Griffiths; Tay- lor, F. Eaton and Theobald; Wallace, Jarrett, A. Eaton, Sherlock and Plumpton. Elmwood Cons.: Ashton; Jos. Plicenix and Jas. Mellor; Pritchard, E. B. Mellor and Hall; W. Phcenix, Gleave, Ellam, Wells and Smith. Referee, W. Bennett.

The visitors won the toss and the home team attacked straight from the centre kick. Sher- lock, heading through from a corner kick, scored the first goal after five minutes' play. The visitors continued more on the defensive, and only made brief visits to the home end. Jarrett scored again. Half-time: Mission, 2 goals; Cons., nil.

On resuming, the home forwards again monopolised the game, and in trying to clear a shot one of the visitors' backs put through his own goal. This was followed with a fourth by A. Eaton. The visitors now made several at- tempts to score and were awarded a penalty, from which Pritchard scored their only goal, and A. Eaton, Jarrett and Wallace scored for the Mission. Result: Mission, 7 goals; Cons., I goal.
HOLLINS GREEN v. ORFORD WHITE STAR.--

These teams met onil;e.ground of the former club, with the following players:— Hollins Green: Perrin; Clark and Kilshaw; Cleworth, Adams and Buckley; Atkinson, Bil- lington, Pritchard, Mellor and Brooks.
white Star: Ashton; Miller and Pilling; Gifford, Denny and Caldwell; Smith Hunbobin, 3leachin, Hankinson and Gregory. Referee, R. G. Brandreth. —. .

The visitors won the toss and from the centre kick the home team at once pressed. After several futile attempts, Billington succeeded in opening the score. Then the visitors made a strong effort to get on level terms, but were driven back, and even play followed. During another attack on the visitors' goal Gifford handled inside the area. Billington was en- trusted .with the kick and drbve the ball past Ashton for a second goal. This reverse nerved the visitors to stronger efforts, and after a spell of attack Hankinson scored for the White Star. The score at the interval was in favour of the home team by 2 goals to 1. _

_ The second portion opened very evenly, and after each end had been visited the visitors im- proved greatly on their game, and pressed heavily. The ball was put past Perrin, but off- side against Hankinson nullified the point. How- ever, the visitors would not be driven back, and Hankinson made the scores equal with a fast shot. In a great effort to get the lead the home team gained ground, but failed to get past the defence. Good work by the visitors' half-backs set their forwards going and Smith increased the lead, and a few minutes later Meachin added the fourth. The home team did not give up hope, and made an attempt to reduce the ar- rears, but Denny and Pilling cleared the danger. Kilshaw was penalised, but Perrins saved the resultant kick, from which the home forwards broke away and Mellor scored. The game con- tinued to be keenly contested, but no further scoring was done. Result: Orford White Star, 4 goals; Rollins Green, 3 goals.

CHESTER AND RUNCORN LEAGUE. PRESTON BROOK ALBION v. FRODSHAM. These teams niet on the ground of the former club in the above competition, under the con- trol of Mr. S. C. Essenhigh. From the kick-off it was soon evident that the home team were not much trouble to their more. experienced opponents, and the game proved to be a very one-sided contest. The visitors scored five 'times before the interval, Spencer, Formston (two), Plant and Dodd securing the goals. After change of ends the visitors had the slope in their favour and kept up a continued attack on the home goal, and corner-kicks were numerous. The home team only made two or three visits to the visitors' end, but failed to get past their defence, and further goals were added for Frodsham by Formston, D. If ughes (four) and Plant (three). The end came with the result :—Frodsham, 11 goals; Preston Brook, none.

div.head: FRIENDLY MATCHES. EMMANUEL INSTITUTE v. WALTON.
div.p: FRIENDLY MATCHES. EMMANUEL INSTITUTE v. WALTON.

Played at Walton. After some even play in mid-field Cliffe dashed away and put in a good centre. Marsh shot, but the visitors' goal- keeper saved in masterly style. . The visitors were now being outplayed,- the home forwards being too strong for their backs. Walton opened their scoring after ten minutes' play, Jones leaving the goalkeeper helpless, with a strong shot. Emmanuel now visited the home end, and after some neat play between Ayres, Eaton and Bevan came near to scoring, the latter putting the ball out to Roberts, who shot hard, but missed the mark. Walton again be- came dangerous, and after an individual effort by Marsh, another goal was registered. Pick- ering put on a third goal from long range. Half-time: Walton, 3; Emmanuel, nil. Resuming, Emmanuel looked like wiping off the arrears, for they made straight for the home goal, where Bevan brought Barlow down to his knees. The visitors' forwards played a good combination game and the Walton efforts were checked by Banner, who continually broke up their movements. Both the home wing men were playing well, but were being well looked after by T. Hughes and Ayres. Emman- uel broke away, and following a good centre by Oakes, Bevan scored, but it was disallowed owing to an infringement. The home team, by some clever work between Andrews, Jones and Bretherton, made the visitors' goalkeeper concede a corner to save. This was well placed by Cliff e, but Crosier cleared. Emmanuel were pressing to the end, but could not score. Walton thus won a good, clean game by 3 goals to nil.

div.head: WILDERSPOOL JUNIORS v. BEWSEY ALBION.
div.p: WILDERSPOOL JUNIORS v. BEWSEY ALBION.

Played on the Wilderspool ground. The first half was evenly contested. Play was fast and exciting. On the teams turning round the game was one-sided, the visitors completely over-running the home team. The Juniors scored through Powell, Whitby and Jones, while the visitors scored through C. Lee (3), L. Doncaster (2) and It White. A good game ended in favour of the visitors by 6 goals to 3.
CADISHEAD WESLEYANS v. HALEBARNS.

These teams met on Saturday at Cadishead. The visitors won the toss and decided to play with the slope in their favour. From the oPening stages of the game the home team asserted their superiority, and at the interval were leading by 4 goals to none. - In the second half the home team continu- ally attacked, and, had their shooting abilities been anything ,like good, they would have scored many times. The home goalkeeper only handled the ball once during the game, and just before the finish one of the visiting for- wards hit the cross-bar. Final score:— Cadishead Wesle3-ans, 11 goals; Halebarns, nil.
SANKEY ATHLETIC v. CHESHIRE_ LIN.ES.

.. - These teams met on the ground sif the latter club at BeWsey-road. The first portion, of the game was evenly contested and the Athletic scored first from a penalty by Kenyon. Then the Cheshire Lines equalised, but the Athletic regained the lead before the interval. Half- time: Athletic, 2 goals; Cheshire Lines, 1 goal. The second portion proved to be a very one- sided game, and the Athletic had the game all their own way, and further goals were scored by Kenyon (2), Hill (2) and Hunt. Result:— Sankey Athletic, 7 goals; Cheshire Lines, 1 goal.

Ask Martin what he thinks of lioughton'a volleys! Lee scored with a clinker; Shaw never saw it. The Orford White Stars are still shining brightly. A great performance to secure-a victory at Hollins Green.

Latchford Baptists have not yet secured a victory. Stan. Craik missed scoring from a penalty. Wyatt gave a good display between the up- rights. Fairfield succumbed at home to Newton Cons. Dagnall and Coy proved too good for the Athletic.

A " Derby " Day on the Cons.' ground to-day! They meet the Earlestown Mission team. Chamberlain, Wrench and Craik were the pick of the Paddington eleven. Wyatt's first appearance in goal for the visi- tors was an exceptionally good one. The Recs. are in their best form at present. A 5-0 victory on Saturday against Central! Their victory over St. Barnabas' was no fluke. Longford United at last came a cropper to the Fairfield United. They missed their chances in the first half. The Elmwood Cons. suffered another reverse last week. They have lost 12 goals to 1 to the Earles- town Mission team. Ashton, Jos. Phcenix and James Mellor had a gruelling time of it. ' The Mission team all played well. Some of our local teams are beginning to quake. There is some talk of Great Sankey re- forming. Don't mention this in Lovely-lane district or Fairfield United area. Let us all say—" Good luck to Great Sankey" if they succeed in their application to the Chester and Runcorn League.

div.head: ITEMS.
div.p: ITEMS.
The game between Y.M.C.A. and St. Barna- bas' was the best seen in Earlestown this season. -

Martin,. in goal, did excellently. H. Martin and Challinor, the respective centre-halves, played very well throughout the game, Riley must have lost his shooting boots. Gilman had hard lines With a surprise shot. Shaw did very well to save it. Shaw gave his best display of the season. Glover and Long proved strong defenders.

div.head: Summary of Authentic News From All Involved Areas,
div.p: Summary of Authentic News From All Involved Areas,
SPECIALLY COMPILED FOR "THE EXAMINER.",
THIRTEEN'
FRANCO-BELGIAN FRONTIER.
RUSH TO CALAIS STOPPED BY ALLIES.

Germany has been concentrating all her ener- gies upon getting round the Allies' left by way of the Western Belgian frontier in order to get to Calais, and so—perhaps—to Paris. Endless reinforcements have been brought up, and are being brought up, but the Belgian, British and French troops on land have presented an un- breakable front to the enemy, while the British fleet has taken a hand in the fighting, and ac- cording to various reports, inflicted great losses on the Germans. .

The Allied line was in a rough semi-circle that passes through Dixmude and the district south-east of RouTers, going thence south through Armentieres and to the east of Lille. The French military authorities in their bul- letin issued on Saturday afternoon revealed the fact that the enemy had made some impres- sion north of Dim:nude and round La Bassee, with Allied advances near the coast and between Armentieres and Lille.

-- Fighting continued to be severe and contin- uous. Ground was gained, and one British division captured two guns. Many prisoners were taken by our troops. On the whole, the positions remained much as they were. The Germans got across the Yser, but their losses were terrible.

On Monday night the Press Bureau confirmed the favourable impressions gathered from the Paris reports that in spite of severe and con- tinuous fighting, the situation continued to be favourable. Ground was being gained and many prisoners had been taken. KAISER'S " ORDER " DISOBEYED.

_ The fighting in Flanders, said Tuesday's re- ports, was still very severe. The enemy was being held in the district of the Yser, while he had been thrust back again in the country be- tween Ypres and Roulers. Report says the Kaiser ordered his generals to take Calais no matter what the cost. Already the cost of the effort has been terrible, and the taking promises to be long deferred. On Tuesday the German attacks between Arras and the sea coast at Nieuport were much less vigorous than they had been. The British troops were still forcing their way forward north and east of Ypres. South-west of La Bassee, where the enemy met with considerable success several days ago, the French were mak- ing progress. BELGIAN BRAVERY.

In this co-a-s—t—fi—gi:iiing—the Belgian Army has shown the greatest bravery. For several days its soldiers held the enemy at bay, and although they were finally compelled to give ground they did not withdraw far. Then, with the help of reinforcements they held up the advance. The German report said: "Our attacks were main- tained," which showed how little had been gained by the enemy." A report front the headquarters of the Bel- gian Army, stated that Monday before noon saw the critical moment of the violent attacks , made by the Germans on the Belgian troops holding the line of the Yser. At this time the , Belgians had begun to give ground, but before the evening the position on their front was again secure. Yesterday it was reported that all the German efforts to break through had been unsuccessful, while the Allies had made progress at certain points. . . .
Yesterday it was reported that the British had been attacked by superior forces, but had largely held their own. Progress was made at practically all important points.

div.head: FLEET GIVES INVALUABLE AID.
div.p: FLEET GIVES INVALUABLE AID.
Great Havoc in the Enemy's Lines.

British warships continued to tZssist the land forces by shelling the Germans within reach of the coast. The Germans brought up long- range guns, but they were no match for our naval weapons. BATTLESHIP JOINS THE MONITORS. _ .
A battleship; joined the fleet off the Belgian coast, and brought her 12in. guns to bear on the German trenches, and the Germans were compelled to withdraw some of their guns a distance.

Our Fleet on the Belgian coast seemed to enjoy a charmed life. Shells fell all around, one falling about ten feet from one of the ships, but none of the vessels were struck. ACCURATE AND GALLING FIRE. -

The Secretary of the Admiralty made the following announcement on Thursday night "British Naval Flotilla continues to support the Allied Left, and since the morning of the 27th the fire of 12in. guns has been brought to bear upon the German position and bat- teries."
Reports received from the shore testify to the effective accuracy of the fire and to its galling character. The flank is thus thoroughly main- tained.

Yesterday and the day before the enemy brought up heavy guns and replied vigorously to the fire of Admiral Hood's ships. The ves- sels only received trifling structural damage. Yesterday the opposition from the shore had practically ceased, and the preponderance of the naval gunnery seems to be established. The casualties have been very slight through- out. One shell exploded on the destroyer Falcon and killed one officer and eight men and wounded one officer and 15 men. One killed and several wounded are also reported from the Brilliant, and eight wounded from the Rinaldo. The enemy's submarines have also been re- ported seeking an opportunity to attack the bombarding ships, which are covered by British destroyers.

div.head: GERMAN SUBMARINE SUNK.
div.p: GERMAN SUBMARINE SUNK.
H.M.S. Badger, Commander Charles Fre- mantle, rammed and sunk a German submarine off the Dutch coast.

div.head: ON THE AISNE FRONT.
div.p: ON THE AISNE FRONT.
SUBSTANTIAL PROGRESS MADE.

Along the Aisne both armies are content to wait. Further east in the Meuse country the French have done well. Beyond the river they have made good their gains, and near Thiau- court have established themselves within 20 miles of Metz. In the Argonne the French have occupied Melzicourt, a village to which they attach much importance. They believe that by holding the place, some 22 miles north-west of Verdun, they make difficult communication between the armies of the German Crown Prince and General von neeringen. Good roads through the Argonne are scarce, and one of them is commanded by Melzicourt. In the neighbourhood of Soissons and around Berry-au-Bac an artillery engagement turned in our favour and resulted in the destruction of several of the enemy's batteries. In the district east of Nancy between the Forest of Bezange and that of Parroy we have taken the offensive and driven the enemy across the frontier. Between the Aisne and the Argonne the Allies captured some of the enemy's trenches. At other points the Germans made " partial attacks," which were uniformly unsuccessful. An advance of Allied troops is also reported in the forest of Apremont.

div.head: RUSSIAN VICTORY GERMANS IN_ttETREAT SUFFER
div.p: RUSSIAN VICTORY GERMANS IN_ttETREAT SUFFER
HEAVILY.
The German invaders of Poland are still re- tiring before the Russian Armies which de- feated them on the Vistula.
The Russians by their rapid pursuit compelled

div.head: 'II WEEK.
div.p: 'II WEEK.
the Austro-German centre to stand and give battle.

A stand made by the Austrians, who had re- ceived "unexpected reinforcements" gave the Russians some trouble. The fighting here "assumed considerable dimensions," but the Russian advance continued. _ _

A strong cavalry force pushed rapidly west- wards to Lodz, and from there threatened the German rear. About Radom, on their advanced right, the enemy have prepared a defensive line, but they can hardly remain in possession while danger draws near from Lodz. On the Vistula, east of Radom, the Russians have taken 3,000 prisoners, cannon, and machine guns. The Russian Armies continued to push on in all parts of their long front. A counter-attack attempted by the retreating enemy north of Radom was overwhelmed and cost the Germans a loss of 49 officers, about 5,000 men, and many guns.

div.head: RUSSIAN CAVALRY ENTER RADOM._
div.p: RUSSIAN CAVALRY ENTER RADOM._

The Headquarters Staff at Petrograd issued a communique on Wednesday which stated We have broken the resistance of the last units of the enemy who were still attempting to maintain themselves on the north of the Pilitsa. At present, on the front beyond the Vistula, all ' the Austro-German army corps are in retreat. We have occupied Strykow, Ezhow, and Nowe Miasto. The Russian cavalry has entered Radom. We have captured several thousand prisoners, guns, about 10 machine guns, and a train of motor waggons. In Galicia no change is reported. On the East Prussian front the German First Army Corps, supported by other units, has con- ducted during the last four days fruitless at- tacks in the neighbourhood of Bakalarzewo. The losses sustained by the enemy are very great.

div.head: SOUTH AFRICAN REBELS.
div.p: SOUTH AFRICAN REBELS.
REVOLT SPREADS, BUT IS BOLDLY TACKLED.

Maritz, the ex-commander of a South African column, who went over to the Germans, has been attacked at Kakamas by the South African forces and totally defeated. He has fled for refuge to German territory. It is announced that 121 and a further batch of 120 of Maritz's rebels, including five officers, surrendered to Colonel Van Der Venter at Onderstedoorne, midway between Calvinia and Kenhardt. No sooner was Maritz defeated than other Boer leaders took the field against us. Chris- tian de Wet, the famous antagonist of Lord Kitchener during the last war, and Mr. Beyers, formerly Commandant-General of the Citizen Forces under the Crown, have become rebels.

BOTHA SWIFT AND SURE. General Botha has been swift to meet the rebel generals in South Africa. A column under his personal command has attacked Beyers near Rustenburg, in the Transvaal. Beyers was evidently unprepared to meet this movement. General Botha drove him in head- long pursuit all day on Tuesday, and in the evening forced him to make some attempt at a stand. In this fighting Beyers lost 80 men, fully armed, taken prisoners. General Ffertzog, who has in the past been a close associate of Beyers and The Wet, and Mr. Merriman, an ex-prime Minister of the Cape Colony and the doyen of South African states- men, are using their influence to induce the rebels to abandon a hopeless enterprise. General Brits reports that the invasion of the Cape Province has finally broken down, he hav- ing defeated the combined rebel and German force at Scuit Drift-

div.head: ENTER TURKEY,.
div.p: ENTER TURKEY,.
Turkey has attacked Russia. Two of her cruisers, the Breslau and the Hamidieh, have appeared off the Russian Black Sea coast and bombarded one unfortified town and summoned another to surrender.

div.head: PORTUGAL INVOLVED
div.p: PORTUGAL INVOLVED

The African exploits of Germany now include an invasion of Portuguese territory. German forces have invaded Angola, the Portuguese colony which borders on the north German South-West Africa. This step has not taken the Lisbon Government by surprise.

div.head: MINES AT SEA.
div.p: MINES AT SEA.
IN THE CHANNEL AND THE NORTE OF IRELAND.

The steamer Amiral Cauteaune, while on pas- sage from Calais to Havre with some 2,500 French refugees, struck a mine near Cape Gris Nez. The Channel steamer Queen rescued most of the passengers, but between 30 and 40 were drowned or crushed to death. Off the north coast of Ireland a British mer- chantman of over 5,000 tons, the Manchester Commerce, struck a German mine and foun- dered. The captain and 13 of the crew perished, but 30 survivors were picked up.
GERMAN LOSSES. OVER QUARTER OF A MILLION
IN SIX WEEKS.
The enemy's loses have been continuously heavy since the beginning of the war. Up to the middle of September 251,000 are officially
admitted.

div.head: PRINCE KILLED.
div.p: PRINCE KILLED.
Prince Maurice of Battenberg, the youngest son of Princess Henry of Battenberg and a cousin of the King and Queen, has died of wounds received in action.

div.head: PRINCE LOUIS RESIGNS.
div.p: PRINCE LOUIS RESIGNS.

Admiral lI:S.H. Prince Louis of Battenherg has resigned his position as First Sea Lord of the Admiralty. Admiral of the Fleet Lord Fisher has been appointed to succeed him. Prince Louis, who was born in Austria of Ger- man parents—his grandfather was Grand Duke. of Hesse—sixty years ago, entered the British Navy in 1868. He has been Director of Naval Intelligence, Second Sea Lord, and First Sea Lord—the last two in immediate succession—at the Admiralty, and has held several important commands afloat. He was appointed to the post he now resigns in 1912. Before the war, Sir John Jellicoe was Second Sea Lord, who left the Board to become Commander-in-Chief of the Grand Fleet, and was succeeded early in August by Vice-Admiral Sir Frederick Hamilton.

div.head: Ell/DEN AGAIN.
div.p: Ell/DEN AGAIN.
CRUISER AND DESTROYER SUNK,

The German cruiser Emden, said to have been disguised by means of an additional dummy funnel and flying the Japanese flag, approached the roadstead at Penang, an island of the Straits Settlement, and torpedoed a Russian cruiser and French destroyer before her real character was discovered.—Eighty-five of the cruiser's crew perished.

div.head: R, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 31, 1914
div.p: R, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 31, 1914
PUBLIC AMUSEMENTS.
ROYAL COURT THEATRE. A Thrilling Sims' Drama.

"The Staircase of Fortune," from the pen of Mr. G. R. Sims, is attracting large audiences to the Royal Court Theatre this week, and is proving decidedly popular. It is a highly dra- matic production, providing many "thrills" and exciting situations. The ups and downs of an inveterate gambler forms one of the many themes introduced into a sound plot woven round a really striking love story, and the two elements of adventure and love are presented in admirable fashion. An accept- able amount of comedy of the true Lancashire variety helps in no small degree to relieve the heavier aspects of the piece. The company is an excellent one and spares no effort in making the drama go with a swing. A dasAing hero is found in Mr. Kendal Chalmers, who appears as Dave Mellish, whilst Miss Edith Rutland makes a successful appeal to the emotions .as the charming Barbara Vane; and Mr. R. S. Trelawney endows the part of John Kintrea with as much repulsiveness as possible, with- out in any way straining too much after effect. Miss Beatrice Wynn as Stella Kintrea also shares in the execrations of the popular parts of the house. Mr. Ernest Street Porter and Miss Emily Stevens give most realistic imper- sonations of a Lancashire couple and cause much laughter. Mr. Sydney T. Russell contri- butes largely to the comedy as Nat Mellish, and he is ably assisted by Miss Winifred Preece as Tilly Spraggs. The other characters are in the very able hands of Mr. Leslie Grey, Mr. Leonard Thackery, Mr. Victor C. Moors, and Miss Edie Martin.

div.head: Big " Hit " for Next Week.
div.p: Big " Hit " for Next Week.

The management have secured a striking attraction for next week, in the shape o. Walter Howard's emotional drama, "The Story of the Rosary.", The play has been enormously successful. During twelve nights when it ran at the Pavilion Theatre, Liverpool, 56,557 people attended the performances, and in six weeks it was witnessed by 114,743 persons. Few new plays in the provinces have ever had such a run.
More than one play has been written round the theme of that beautiful song, "The Rosary," and Mr. Howard's is spoken of as quite the best.

div.head: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.
div.p: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.

Patrons of the popular Barbauld-street house are more than delighted with the extremely good programme presented this week. The large audiences, which have been the order so far, have fully appreciated the talents of the six skilled musicians, who appear in the Corner-Grey musical novelty, "Symphonia." The violin, 'cello, piano, celeste and mustel organ are all played with great skill, and Mr. Henry Corner, along with his /ady partner, score a decided success with many well-chosen duets. " Captain Careless, V.C. "is the title of a clever one-act play, presented in admirable fashion by Messrs. George Sheldon's and Raw- son Buckley's Company. There are many ex- Citing incidents in the playlet, and they are all brought out in a striking manner. Jock Mills is an amusing Scottish Comedian, whose gags and songs are both new and witty. Jimmie Pullin is a clever comedian, who knows how to entertain, and his "School Board-man" and ." Tram Conductor" numbers are exceptionally good. The Brothers Erard are smart acrobatic violinists; whilst James Dixon is a brilliant baritone, and entertains with many ballads and operatic selections. Sims and Hurste cause much laughter in their duologue, "The Captain and the Mate," and sing remarkably well.

Next Week's Attractions. Next week's programme will include Woody, Wood and Well, in an acrobatic sketch, en- titled "At the Perch Club"; F. V. St. Clair, in famous war songs; Conn and Conrad, in "An Exciting Time in the Jungle"; Mr. A. Toose, in "Bill's Last Chance"; Takes°, a Japanese magician; Tim Carlisle, light comedian; and Jenny Robbins, comedienne and dancer.

div.head: PICTUREDRONIE.
div.p: PICTUREDRONIE.

At the Picturedrome this week grand bills of fare were provided. That for the first three days included another instalment of the thrilling serial "Lucille Love," which this week showed how that girl of mystery saved a ranch—and afterwards herself—from raiders. Another fine drama was "The Changeling," whilst a rousing war-song, "The Battle Eve," was illustrated. An abundance of comedy was provided in the films "The Forgotten Watch," "Innocent, but Awkward," and "Lost Child." The "Gaumont Graphic" depicted topical war happenings, and " Marvellous Light Effects on Italian Lakes" showed some beautiful scenery. The second programme, now showing, in- cludes the dramas, "Her Great Scoop," "The Little Sheriff," and "The Signal "; the come- dies, "A Model of Perseverance," "An Innocent Victim," and "Fanny's brelodrama"; and "In the Maritime Alps," a fine scenic film.
For Next Week. Two splendid romantic films have been booked for next week's performances at this popular house, viz., "From the Flames" and "A Queen's Love."

div.head: PICTURE HOUSE.
div.p: PICTURE HOUSE.

Fine sets of pictures were shown this week at the Picture House. In the first programme the chief interest centred round "If England were Invaded," a thrilling war film based on Wil- liam Le Queux's famous " Invasion of Eng- land." Other engrossing dramas were: "When the Wheels of Justice Clogged," "Little He and She," and "The Basket Habit." "Peter's Patent Pipe-lighter," and "The Also Hans" were real mirth-provokers; whilst the topical item " Beleagured Antwerp" proved a real-life war-film of great interest. The items that go to make up the second strong programme are: "Was She Right in Forgiving Him?" a problem film; "Blind Man's Buff," and " Broncho Billy—Outlaw," two other thrilling dramas; and the excellent comedies: "A Barnyard Flirtation," "Pimple's Last Re- source," "Never Send Your Boots," and "The Bully Boy."

div.head: Next Week's Fare.
div.p: Next Week's Fare.

"The Isle of Abandoned Hope"; is the attrac- tive title of the "star" among the many ex- cellent films to be shown next week. His Country's Bidding" is well spoken of by the cinema Press and should also prove a big draw.

div.head: STAR KINEMA.
div.p: STAR KINEMA.

The high standard of the Star Kinema pro- grammes is fully maintained this week. Many fine pictures shown during the first three days included: "Child o' My Heart," a pathetic drama whjch vividly contrasted high .and humble life and concluded by blending the two very happily, "The Harvest of Sin" was another fine drama dealing with life in the "Wild West." "The Girl at the Lunch Counter" and. "Hearts and pwords" were two highly entertaining comedies whilst the Gaumont Graphic" and " Pathe's Animated Gazette" detailed recent happenings in differ- ent parts of Europe in a very, interesting manner. The second set of films, which is to be seen this week-end, is a very strong one, including "The Jew," and many other dramas and fine comedies. Next Week. On the first three nights of next week another long ineltalment of the enthralling cinema-serial "The Adventures of Kathlyn" will be given, whilst the big film booked for the latter half of the week is entitled " The Shadows of a Great City."

div.head: POLICE DOCTOR'S DEPUTY.
div.p: POLICE DOCTOR'S DEPUTY.

The Watch Committee reported to the Town Council on Monday night that they had resOlved to appoint Dr. E. C. Bowden as deputy police surgeon to act during the absence of the Police Surgeon on active service with the 4th Battalion of the South Lancashire Regiment.

div.head: ORPHANED INSTRUMENTALISTS
div.p: ORPHANED INSTRUMENTALISTS
Give Successful Concert in Warrington.

Warringtonians responded generously to the appeal of the National Children's Home and Orphanage for a large audience, at the enter- tainment given by their Farnborough Boys' Band and Choir at the Co-operative Hall on Wednesday evening. The concert, over which Mr. C. E. Parker presided, was held in War- rington chiefly through the instrumentality of the Rev. W. Thompson Derry, and was arranged by Mr. Appleton; whilst Miss Weaver provided the list of local houses at which the boys spent the night. It had for its object the financial assistance of the deserving institution founded in South London by Dr. Stephenson some fifty years ago. The homes are at present in special need of increased funds, since they are receiving many of the orphan children of soldiers and sailors fallen in battle. They have also ad- mitted a number of orphan Belgian refugees. The Chairman said he was led to believe that the boys from Dr. Stephenson's homes needed no introduction to a Warrington audience; they not only occupied a warm place in the hearts of Wesleyans, but they were known amongst other denominations also. There was a danger of these organisations they had known so long being seriously affected by the war. Not only was there a danger of the funds being dimin- ished, but many more little children would be sure to need the care of the institutions—even the orphaned children of the people of other nations.

In their little village of Penketh they had now a small family of about thirty. (Laughter.) He felt like a sort of father to them. The age of the eldest "child" was about seventy. (Laugh- ter.) But they had also a little fellow of about eight, who had been separated from all relatives except his grandmother. There were many cases such as this needing their help. (Ap- plause.) A SPLENDID PROGRAMME. The Farnborough Boys' Band and Choir then proceeded with a splendid musical programme, commencing with the "Eliza E. Claudio" over- ture. That well-known baritone song, "The Admiral's Broom," was adapted into a rousing chorus, specially applicable to the present stir- ring times. A spirited rendition of "The Girl in the Taxi" selections was followed by "The Last Post "—a recitation by one of the boys. An "Impressionist Picture of the N.C.H.0." was quite a novel feature, each boy bearing a shield representative of one of the branches of the home, and reciting about it; the whole fin- ishing with a tableau. The cornet solo, "Land of Hope and Glory," was sympathetically given, the band providing a subdued accompani- ment. "The Tailor," an action song, produced roars of laughter, as did also the humoresque, "Who's Next?" which followed the " Valse Trieste." The well-trained voices of the choir blended very effectively in the part-song, "Out with the Tide," but perhaps the best rendering of all was that of Bucalossi's "A Hunting Scene," a descriptive fantasia which was per- fectly interpreted from start to finish. At the conclusion of the musical programme, - The Chairman heartily congratulated the band upon its creditable performance. - -

A FAMILY OF 2,250 CHILDREN. The Rev. S. Carroll Myers, assistant principal of the Orphanage, delivered a short address upon the history and aims of the institution. Since its foundation, he said, the original home had gradually expanded, until there were now branches all over England, in the form of homes, sanatoria, farms and other industrial settlements. They even had a Canadian branch. There were now 2,250 boys and girls in the homes, all of whom had come to them solely on the grounds of need, and irrespective of creed or locality. Naturally, in doing work like that, they were confronted with very grave responsibilities, but he was convinced that, without those homes, very many of the girls and boys would go to swell the ranks of the unemployables and the inmates of the prisons. But, given their right, the children would follow the path in which their feet were directed. The work of the homes, he contended, was national service of the first order; for by doing this work they were helping the nation's chief asset, and cutting off the entrail of evil. (Applause.) A musical gymnastic display followed, into which many novel drills were introduced. An effective flag-tableaux conclnded the exhibition, after which the audience sang the National Anthem and dispersed.

ETERNAL ENGLAND. . (By JESSIE Salm.) There's a country which never shall fall, . • Be her enemies ever so strong; ' For, responsive to Liberty's call, She will vanquish the wrong. . And the country is England, dear England, the land of my song. , There's a, glory which never shall fade, But is constant and clear as the sun.. It was earned by the Englishman's blade, When that great fight begun For the freedom of all upon earth. And the fight will be won. There's a flag that shall never be furled Till the firmament's rolled like a scroll. It will flutter all over the world, And the world be made Whole. ' 'Tis the flag of Old England. Thus leads she . the world to, its goal. . . • Ai44AT IS SHRAPNEL? WELSH DOCTOR ON GERMS AND GERMANS. Dr. R. Owen Morris, tuberculosis lecturer to the Welsh National Memorial, speaking at New- town, Montgomeryshire, on Tuesday night, on germs and Germans, said that even with per- fected instruments of destruction soldiers were more likely to be killed by germs than by Ger- mans, and it was far more important to train young soldiers to fight typhoid, dysentery and pneumonia than Germans. Local Territorials did not take enough sleep. which was essential for physical fitness.' Referring to local factory girls working from six till eight at night, he said it was rank madness for the sake of a few extra pence to open the door for disease.

RESERVE TERRITORIALS. Drums and Bugles Wanted. Capt. Max Woods makes an appeal to War- ringtonians to supply him with funds with which to provide the reserve battalion of our Territorials with drums and bugles. We com- mend this appeal to the attention of our readers as one of the most worthy of all the appeals with which they will have to deal. To the Editor of "The Examiner." Sir,—l venture to appeal to the generosity of the people of Warrington on behalf of the 4th Reserve Battalion South Lancashire Regiment. The Battalion is handicapped when on the march by the lack of drums and bugles, which are a necessity for their cheering effect on the spirits of the men, fatigued by long marches.. I shall be very grateful for any subscriptions towards the cost of the drums and bugles, which will amount to the sum of £3O. Subscriptions should be sent to me at the Drill Hall. I beg to remain, &c., MAX WOODS, Captain commanding 4th (Reserve) Battalion South Lancashire Regiment.

PROGRESS OF THE WAR.

DRINK IN WAR TIME. Warrington Public-Houses to Open " as Usual." A COUNCILLOR WHO THINKS THEY SHOULD. The question of whether Warrington should close its public-houses earlier during the war was referred to briefly at the Council meeting on Tuesday night. On the private agenda the following minute of the Watch Committee appeared "The Chief Constable produced a petition praying that the Intoxicating (Liquor Restric- tion) Act, 1914, should be acted upon," and it was resolved: "That the Chief Constable be re- quested to lay the petition before the Licensing Justices." The petition, which was signed bSi. 2,500 per- sons, and was influentially supported by the churches, was so submitted, and we understand that it was reported to the Licensing Justices that there had been no increase in the number of cases of drunkenness since the outbreak of the war. As we reported last week, it was decided that, while the intentions of the petitioners were fully appreciated, there was no need at present to comply with their request. "A VOTE OF CONFIDENCE." Councillor Broadhurst, alluding to the min- utes and evidently to the decision of the magis- trates, which, of course, formed no portion of the business of the Council, Said he thought the committee, the Chief Constable and the Licens- ing Justices might congratulate themselves on the action they had taken in the matter of the petition. He took the action of the Licensing Committee as being a kind of vote of confidence in the working classes of the town, and he was certain that it would be found that confidence which had been reposed in them had not been misplaced. Steps such as that proposed by the Temperance party were calculated to create a panic throughout the districts in which they were adopted, and the action of the Licensing Justices in Warrington would do something to- wards preventing any panic from arising in this town. BAND OF HOPE QUEEN'S DISAPPOINT- MENT. To the Editor of "The Examiner." Sir,—Will you kindly allow me a small space in your paper to say how very disappointed I was to read in your last Saturday's issue that the petition for the early closing of public- houses was not successful? I think that while the country is in such an unsettled condition, it is very necessary that all licensed houses should be closed earlier. After reading Lord Kitchener's appeal for sober soldiers, I think it is the duty of all British subjects, young and old, to do whatever they can to keep our soldiers fit and healthy, and to reduce temptation as much as possible. When we hear that other countries have set us such an example, surely we can do our little share, if it is only by closing an hour or two earlier. I feel sure that my disappointment will be shared by many persons in Warrington, and I sincerely hope it is not too late even now for the matter to be re-considered.—Yours faithfully, EVA A. TANNER, Band of Hope Queen. 27, Winwick-street, Warrington, October 27th, 1914.
